## Pronunciation

- {主角|zhǔ jué} zhǔ jué: jué, not jiǎo. {中奖|zhòng jiǎng} zhòng jiǎng: zhòng, not zhōng.
- {散|sàn} sàn (to break up), {散步|sàn bù} sàn bù; lesson 12's {散|sǎn} sǎn (to come apart).
- {当天|dàng tiān} dàng tiān (that same day): fourth tone, as in {当作|dàng zuò}.
- {属|shǔ} shǔ (born in the year of) and {数|shǔ} shǔ (to count, HSK 5): the same sound.
- {撒|sǎ} sǎ (to sprinkle) and {洒|sǎ} sǎ (to spill, HSK 5): the same sound and close meanings.
- {灯笼|dēng lóng} dēng long: the second syllable is often light in speech.
- {元宵|yuán xiāo} yuán xiāo, {汤圆|tāng yuán} tāng yuán, {粽子|zòng zi} zòng zi.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{早|zǎo}{不|bù}{来|lái}{晚|wǎn}{不|bù}{来|lái}，{正好|zhèng hǎo}{这|zhè}{时候|shí hou}{来|lái}{了|le}，{太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}~~: the format is a complaint. For a lucky moment, say {来|lái}{得|de}{正好|zhèng hǎo}.
- ~~{一再|yí zài}~~ after the verb: ~~{感谢|gǎn xiè}{一再|yí zài}~~. Only {再三|zài sān} can follow ({考虑|kǎo lǜ}{再三|zài sān}); {一再|yí zài} goes first: {一再|yí zài}{感谢|gǎn xiè}.
- For your zodiac animal, say {我|wǒ}{属|shǔ}{兔|tù} or {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{属|shǔ}{兔|tù}{的|de}; {属|shǔ} is the verb that does the work.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{中奖|zhòng jiǎng}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{电脑|diàn nǎo}~~: {中奖|zhòng jiǎng} takes no object. Say {我|wǒ}{中奖|zhòng jiǎng}{了|le}，{奖品|jiǎng pǐn}{是|shì}{一|yì}{台|tái}{电脑|diàn nǎo}, or {我|wǒ}{中|zhòng}{了|le}{一|yì}{台|tái}{电脑|diàn nǎo}.
- Flowers take {枝|zhī}, {朵|duǒ} or {束|shù} rather than {个|gè}: {一|yì}{枝|zhī}{梅花|méi huā}, {一|yì}{朵|duǒ}{菊花|jú huā}, {一|yí}{束|shù}{兰花|lán huā}.
- ~~{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}{祖国|zǔ guó}~~: {唱|chàng}{歌|gē} takes no object. {歌唱|gē chàng} can ({歌唱|gē chàng}{家乡|jiā xiāng}), and so can {唱|chàng} ({唱|chàng}{一|yì}{首|shǒu}{歌|gē}).

## Key points

- {早|zǎo}{不|bù} X {晚|wǎn}{不|bù} X，{偏偏|piān piān}…: of all times (a complaint): {雨|yǔ}{早|zǎo}{不|bú}{下|xià}{晚|wǎn}{不|bú}{下|xià}，{偏偏|piān piān}{这|zhè}{时候|shí hou}{下|xià}.
- {一再|yí zài} (before the verb) and {再三|zài sān} (before or after): again and again.
- {一|yì}{枝|zhī}{梅花|méi huā} (on its stem), {一|yì}{朵|duǒ}{花|huā} (a flower head), {一|yí}{束|shù}{花|huā} (a bunch). {我|wǒ}{属|shǔ}{兔|tù}. {宴会|yàn huì}{散|sàn}{了|le} (sàn).
- Festivals: {拜年|bài nián}, {团圆|tuán yuán}, {元宵|yuán xiāo} / {汤圆|tāng yuán}, {粽子|zòng zi}, {灯笼|dēng lóng}, {民俗|mín sú}, {吉祥|jí xiáng}, {祝福|zhù fú} / {祝愿|zhù yuàn}, {心愿|xīn yuàn}, {盼望|pàn wàng}, {来临|lái lín} (written).
- Ceremonies: {仪式|yí shì}, {典礼|diǎn lǐ}, {宴会|yàn huì}, {招待|zhāo dài}, {布置|bù zhì}, {气氛|qì fēn} / {氛围|fēn wéi}, {抽奖|chōu jiǎng} / {中奖|zhòng jiǎng} / {奖品|jiǎng pǐn} / {券|quàn}; {捧|pěng}, {撒|sǎ}, {泼|pō}, {添|tiān}, {跪|guì}.
- Films: {剧本|jù běn}, {情节|qíng jié}, {题材|tí cái}, {场景|chǎng jǐng}, {镜头|jìng tóu}, {字幕|zì mù}, {改编|gǎi biān}, {塑造|sù zào}, {主演|zhǔ yǎn}, {主角|zhǔ jué} zhǔ jué, {喜剧|xǐ jù}, {场次|chǎng cì}.
- New characters: {薯|shǔ} {烫|tàng} {添|tiān} {吞|tūn} {脂|zhī} {肪|fáng} {粥|zhōu} {笼|lóng} {氛|fēn} {旗|qí} {柴|chái} {跪|guì} {菊|jú} {吉|jí} {祥|xiáng} {兰|lán} {梅|méi} {盼|pàn} {捧|pěng} {券|quàn}.

lessons.title: Heritage: arts, crafts and relics
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

{安娜|Ān nà} Anna now works at an art museum as a guide and translator. This lesson follows her through the
galleries: the porcelain, the paintings and the workshop where old paintings are restored, and the
master who has spent his life there. It has the words for relics and historic sites, for painting and
calligraphy, and for the performing arts, from folk songs to traditional opera and crosstalk.

The grammar is written Chinese, the language of labels, guidebooks and reports:

- **structural particle {所|suǒ}**: {所|suǒ} + verb ({我|wǒ}{所|suǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{的|de}: what I know) and {为|wéi}…{所|suǒ} ({为|wéi}{人们|rén men}{所|suǒ}{熟悉|shú xī}: familiar to
  people);
- **{以便|yǐ biàn}** (so that) and {以免|yǐ miǎn} (so as not to), the written purpose clauses, which lesson 27 brings back;
- the same information in a written label and in a guide's spoken words.

## {所|suǒ}: the written particle before a verb

**{所|suǒ}** stands before a verb to turn it into a description of that verb's object. It is written
Chinese, and it can always be left out in speech:

{我|wǒ}{所|suǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{的|de}{情况|qíng kuàng}{就是|jiù shì}{这些|zhè xiē}。 — That's all I know about it. (Spoken: {我|wǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{的|de}{情况|qíng kuàng}{就是|jiù shì}{这些|zhè xiē}。)

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我们|wǒ men}{馆|guǎn}{所|suǒ}{收藏|shōu cáng}{的|de}{最|zuì}{古老|gǔ lǎo}{的|de}{一|yí}{件|jiàn}{瓷器|cí qì}。 — This is the oldest piece of porcelain in our museum's collection.

{大家|dà jiā}{所|suǒ}{关心|guān xīn}{的|de}{问题|wèn tí}，{我们|wǒ men}{会|huì}{一一|yī yī}{回答|huí dá}。 — We will answer, one by one ({一一|yī yī}, lesson 27's word), the questions everyone is concerned
about.

- The pattern is (subject +) {所|suǒ} + verb + {的|de} + noun: {他|tā}{所|suǒ}{说|shuō}{的|de}{话|huà} (what he said), {我们|wǒ men}{所|suǒ}{看|kàn}{到|dào}{的|de} (what we see).
  The noun can be left out when it's clear: {我|wǒ}{所|suǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{的|de} (what I know).
- {所|suǒ} goes only before a verb that takes an object: {所|suǒ}{说|shuō}, {所|suǒ}{看|kàn}{到|dào}, {所|suǒ}{收藏|shōu cáng}, {所|suǒ}{关心|guān xīn}. Not ~~{所|suǒ}{睡觉|shuì jiào}~~ or ~~{所|suǒ}{高兴|gāo xìng}~~.

### {为|wéi}…{所|suǒ}: the written passive

{为|wéi} wéi + the doer + {所|suǒ} + verb is a formal passive, "is (verb)ed by…". HSK 5 met it; here it is in the
language of heritage:

{这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{技艺|jì yì}{早已|zǎo yǐ}{为|wéi}{人们|rén men}{所|suǒ}{熟悉|shú xī}。 — This craft has long been familiar to people.

{他|tā}{的|de}{作品|zuò pǐn}{为|wéi}{海内外|hǎi nèi wài}{的|de}{收藏家|shōu cáng jiā}{所|suǒ}{喜爱|xǐ ài}。 — His work is loved by collectors at home and abroad.

   art of the past alive for people today.
2. So as not to harm the original picture ({以免|yǐ miǎn}{伤|shāng}{到|dào}{原来|yuán lái}{的|de}{画面|huà miàn}): what they handle was left by people
   centuries ago, and once damaged it's gone for ever.
3. Not making the painting new but keeping it as it was: new paper as old-looking as the original, new
   colour slightly paler, so later people can see what was repaired.
4. Because the craft can't be rushed: as he says, only a calm heart gives a steady hand ({心|xīn}{静|jìng}{了|le}，{手|shǒu}{才|cái}{稳|wěn});
   she was eager to start too soon.

"The man who brings old paintings back to life. When you walk into the museum's conservation room, the
first thing you notice is a faint smell of paper and ink. On the table lies a Ming dynasty landscape
painting that has just come in: the paper has yellowed, it is full of holes, and in places the colour
can hardly be made out. Master He, in his glasses, is cleaning the picture bit by bit. He has worked
here for thirty-two years, and he has restored more than five hundred paintings and works of
calligraphy. Once a painting arrived in dozens of pieces, and he and his colleagues spent two whole years
putting it back together piece by piece. Restoring an old painting often takes several months, even years. The first step is
cleaning, so as to remove the dust and water stains; the second is to peel off the old backing paper
layer by layer; then the holes are filled, and only at the end can the colour be retouched. Every step
must be done with great care, so as not to harm the original picture. 'What we are dealing with,' says
Master He, 'was left by people hundreds of years ago: if it's damaged, it's gone for ever.' In the
restoration trade there is a principle everyone agrees on: 'restore the old as old'. That is,
restoration doesn't make an old painting new but keeps it as close as possible to how it was. Paper
added must be as old in colour as the original, and colour added must be slightly paler, so that later
generations can see at once what has been repaired. Visitors often ask him, 'Isn't it
frustrating, being so slow?' He always smiles and says, 'These paintings have waited hundreds of
years: a few more months won't matter.' 'We're not painters,' says Master He. 'Our job is
to let the work of the ancients live on, not to leave our own names on it.' The craft is hard to learn
from books: it's mainly passed on by a master showing you with his own hands. When Master He was
young, he studied with his master for five whole years before he was allowed to work on his first
painting. Now he too has taken on two apprentices. One, Xiao Ou, trained in fine art, and when she
first came she was impatient to get started, but Master He had her practise 'peeling paper' for six
months first. 'You can't rush this craft,' Xiao Ou says. 'My master always says: only when your
heart is calm is your hand steady.' People today live at an ever faster pace, and slow work like this
is rare. Yet it is pairs of patient hands like these that let paintings and calligraphy hundreds of
years old still be enjoyed by people today."
</details>

## Speaking: retell a passage

The exam's first speaking task gives you a passage to retell in your own words (as reported: two
passages, about a minute and a half each). Read this one twice, cover it, and retell it: who, what they
did, why it matters.

```speak

{在|zài}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小|xiǎo}{山|shān}{村|cūn}{里|lǐ}，{住|zhù}{着|zhe}{一|yí}{位|wèi}{七十|qī shí}{多|duō}{岁|suì}{的|de}{老|lǎo}{奶奶|nǎi nai}。{她|tā}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{会|huì}{唱|chàng}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{当地|dāng dì}{的|de}{民歌|mín gē}，{这些|zhè xiē}{歌|gē}{没有|méi yǒu}{写|xiě}{在|zài}{书|shū}{上|shàng}，{都|dōu}{是|shì}{一代|yí dài}{一代|yí dài}{口口相传|kǒu kǒu xiāng chuán}
{下来|xià lái}{的|de}。{前|qián}{些|xiē}{年|nián}，{村|cūn}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{年轻|nián qīng}{人|rén}{大多|dà duō}{去|qù}{城|chéng}{里|lǐ}{打工|dǎ gōng}{了|le}，{会|huì}{唱|chàng}{这些|zhè xiē}{歌|gē}{的|de}{人|rén}{越|yuè}{来|lái}{越|yuè}{少|shǎo}。{老|lǎo}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{很|hěn}{着急|zháo jí}，{她|tā}{担心|dān xīn}{自己|zì jǐ}{不|bú}{在|zài}{了|le}，{这些|zhè xiē}{歌|gē}{也|yě}
{就|jiù}{没有|méi yǒu}{了|le}。{于是|yú shì}，{她|tā}{每|měi}{个|gè}{周末|zhōu mò}{都|dōu}{把|bǎ}{村|cūn}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}{叫|jiào}{到|dào}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}，{一|yí}{句|jù}{一|yí}{句|jù}{地|de}{教|jiāo}{他们|tā men}{唱|chàng}。{一|yì}{开始|kāi shǐ}，{孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{觉得|jué de}{这些|zhè xiē}{歌|gē}{太|tài}{老|lǎo}{了|le}，{不|bú}{愿意|yuàn yì}{学|xué}。

{录|lù}{了|le}{下来|xià lái}。{现在|xiàn zài}，{这些|zhè xiē}{民歌|mín gē}{不但|bú dàn}{在|zài}{村|cūn}{里|lǐ}{传唱|chuán chàng}，{还|hái}{被|bèi}{放|fàng}{到|dào}{了|le}{网上|wǎng shàng}，{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{听|tīng}{到|dào}{了|le}{这么|zhè me}{好听|hǎo tīng}{的|de}{歌|gē}。
= In a small mountain village lives an old woman of over seventy. Since she was a child she has known many local folk songs; they were never written down, but passed on by word of mouth from generation to generation. In recent years most of the village's young people have gone to work in the city, and fewer and fewer people can sing them. She grew worried that when she was gone the songs would be gone too. So every weekend she called the village children to her home and taught them line by line. At first the children thought the songs were too old and didn't want to learn, but after hearing the story behind each song, they gradually came to love them. "This is a story about handing down folk songs. An old woman in a village knows many local folk songs,
```

## Write it: a request

Write a letter of 150–200 characters to a museum asking it to arrange a guided visit for your class:
who you are, when you'd like to come, how many people, what you'd like to see, and what you need. Use
{以便|yǐ biàn} once, and three of {讲解|jiǎng jiě}, {陪同|péi tóng}, {文物|wén wù}, {书画|shū huà}, {瓷器|cí qì}, {浓厚|nóng hòu}.

(when, how many), thanks the reader, and ends with the name and the date.

## Say it


## Pronunciation

- {曲|qǔ} qǔ (a tune) and {弯曲|wān qū} wān qū (bent): third and first tone.
- {乐器|yuè qì} yuè qì and {乐曲|yuè qǔ} yuè qǔ: {乐|yuè} is yuè for music, lè for happiness.
- {散文|sǎn wén} sǎn wén: {散|sǎn} sǎn, as in lesson 12.
- {师父|shī fu} shī fu and {师傅|shī fu} shī fu: the same sound, a light second syllable.
- {相声|xiàng sheng} xiàng sheng: a light second syllable; {相|xiàng} is xiàng here, not xiāng.
- {塔|tǎ} tǎ: third tone. {铜|tóng} tóng and {同|tóng} tóng sound the same.
- {所|suǒ} suǒ: third tone; in {我|wǒ}{所|suǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{的|de} the 3+3 of {我|wǒ}{所|suǒ} is said wó suǒ.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我们|wǒ men}{所|suǒ}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}~~: {所|suǒ} needs a verb that takes an object, and {睡觉|shuì jiào} takes none; "the room we sleep in" is {我们|wǒ men}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}.
- {被|bèi}{大家|dà jiā}{所|suǒ}{熟悉|shú xī} is also seen in print, but the classic written pattern is {为|wéi}{大家|dà jiā}{所|suǒ}{熟悉|shú xī}; in speech, drop {所|suǒ} altogether.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{对|duì}{书画|shū huà}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{浓厚|nóng hòu}{兴趣|xìng qù}~~: {浓厚|nóng hòu} needs {的|de} before the noun: {浓厚|nóng hòu}{的|de}{兴趣|xìng qù}.
- {师父|shī fu} for a taxi driver is wrong: drivers and repairmen are {师傅|shī fu}. {师父|shī fu} is your own master in a craft.
- {以便|yǐ biàn} doesn't belong in a chat: it's written. In speech, {好|hǎo} + verb or {这样|zhè yàng}…: {早|zǎo}{点儿|diǎnr}{来|lái}，{好|hǎo}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{安排|ān pái}.
- ~~{这个|zhè ge}{瓷器|cí qì}{很|hěn}{宏大|hóng dà}~~ for a small vase: {宏大|hóng dà} is for great size or scale ({宏大|hóng dà}{的|de}{建筑|jiàn zhù}, {规模|guī mó}{宏大|hóng dà}).

## Key points

- {所|suǒ} + verb (+ {的|de} + noun), written: {我|wǒ}{所|suǒ}{知道|zhī dào}{的|de}, {我们|wǒ men}{馆|guǎn}{所|suǒ}{收藏|shōu cáng}{的|de}{文物|wén wù}. {为|wéi} + doer + {所|suǒ} + verb: {为|wéi}{人们|rén men}{所|suǒ}{熟悉|shú xī}.
- {以便|yǐ biàn} (so that) and {以免|yǐ miǎn} (so as not to): written purpose clauses after the main clause.
- Heritage: {遗产|yí chǎn}, {文物|wén wù}, {古迹|gǔ jì}, {名胜|míng shèng}, {遗址|yí zhǐ}, {国宝|guó bǎo}, {现存|xiàn cún}, {历经|lì jīng}, {起源|qǐ yuán}, {闻名|wén míng}, {考古|kǎo gǔ}, {鉴定|jiàn dìng}, {修复|xiū fù}, {收藏|shōu cáng}, {痕迹|hén jì}.
- Arts: {书画|shū huà}, {绘画|huì huà}, {描绘|miáo huì}, {手法|shǒu fǎ}, {图案|tú àn}, {对称|duì chèn}, {精美|jīng měi} / {精致|jīng zhì}, {宏大|hóng dà}, {鲜明|xiān míng}, {浓厚|nóng hòu}, {审美|shěn měi}, {古典|gǔ diǎn}, {当代|dāng dài}; {师父|shī fu} (your master) and
  {徒弟|tú dì}, {传授|chuán shòu} (teach a skill), {传承|chuán chéng} (hand down).
- Performance: {戏曲|xì qǔ}, {相声|xiàng sheng}, {民歌|mín gē}, {乐器|yuè qì}, {乐曲|yuè qǔ}, {演奏|yǎn zòu}, {排练|pái liàn}, {扮演|bàn yǎn}, {悲剧|bēi jù}; literature: {散文|sǎn wén}, {诗词|shī cí}, {诗歌|shī gē}.
- A label (written, four-character phrases) and a guide (spoken, short sentences) say the same thing.
- New characters: {撒|sǎ} {宴|yàn} {仪|yí} {宵|xiāo} {枝|zhī} {粽|zòng} {瓷|cí} {痕|hén} {绘|huì} {宏|hóng} {审|shěn} {塔|tǎ} {铜|tóng} {徒|tú}.

lessons.title: History: dynasties, war and peace
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The module ends in the distant past. David's company is taking a group of British students to Xi'an,
and he asks {安娜|Ān nà} Anna, who studied art history, to help him tell its story: the first emperor and his
terracotta army, the Tang capital Chang'an, the Great Wall. You'll learn the words for dynasties and
rulers, for armies and wars of long ago, and for the peace and civilisation that followed them, and the
way history is told: as fact, as legend, and as the origin of things we still do.

The grammar:

- **concession with {却|què}**: {虽然|suī rán}…{却|què}… (although…, still…): {秦朝|Qín cháo}{虽然|suī rán}{很|hěn}{短|duǎn}，{却|què}{影响|yǐng xiǎng}{了|le}{两千|liǎng qiān}{多|duō}{年|nián};
- {相传|xiāng chuán} (according to legend), for stories that may not be history;
- {源于|yuán yú} (to originate from, written) and {由来|yóu lái} (the origin of something).

## {虽然|suī rán}…{却|què}…: although…, yet…

You know {虽然|suī rán}…{但是|dàn shì}… from HSK 2. **{却|què}** què (HSK 4) can replace {但是|dàn shì}, or join it, and puts the surprise
in the second half:

{秦朝|Qín cháo}{虽然|suī rán}{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{十|shí}{几|jǐ}{年|nián}，{却|què}{影响|yǐng xiǎng}{了|le}{后来|hòu lái}{两千|liǎng qiān}{多|duō}{年|nián}{的|de}{历史|lì shǐ}。 — Although the Qin dynasty lasted only some fifteen
years, it shaped the next two thousand years of history.

{这|zhè}{座|zuò}{城|chéng}{虽然|suī rán}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}，{历史|lì shǐ}{却|què}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}。 — The town is small, but its history is long.

{他|tā}{虽然|suī rán}{是|shì}{将军|jiāng jūn}，{却|què}{从来|cóng lái}{不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{打仗|dǎ zhàng}。 — Although he was a general, he never liked fighting wars.

- {却|què} is an adverb: it goes after the subject of its clause and before the verb or adjective ({历史|lì shǐ}{却|què}{很|hěn}{长|cháng},
  {他|tā}{却|què}…). {但是|dàn shì} goes before the subject ({但是|dàn shì}{历史|lì shǐ}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}). So: {虽然|suī rán}{这|zhè}{座|zuò}{城|chéng}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}，{但是|dàn shì}{历史|lì shǐ}{很|hěn}{长|cháng} / {这|zhè}{座|zuò}{城|chéng}{虽然|suī rán}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}，{历史|lì shǐ}{却|què}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}.
- {但是|dàn shì} and {却|què} can appear together ({但是|dàn shì}{他|tā}{却|què}{不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}), which stresses the contrast; ~~{却|què}{他|tā}{不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}~~ is wrong.
- {却|què} also works without {虽然|suī rán}: {大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{去|qù}{了|le}，{他|tā}{却|què}{没|méi}{去|qù} (everyone went, but he didn't).
- In written Chinese, {虽然|suī rán} is often shortened to {虽|suī} (lesson 27): {城|chéng}{虽|suī}{小|xiǎo}，{历史|lì shǐ}{却|què}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}. That is the style of
  guidebooks and essays.

## {相传|xiāng chuán}: according to legend

{相传|xiāng chuán} xiāng chuán (it is said, according to tradition) begins a story that has been handed down and may
not be history. It is how you tell a legend honestly:

{相传|xiāng chuán}，{端午节|Duān wǔ jié}{吃|chī}{粽子|zòng zi}{的|de}{习俗|xí sú}{源于|yuán yú}{纪念|jì niàn}{诗人|shī rén}{屈原|Qū Yuán}。 — According to tradition, the custom of eating zongzi at the
Dragon Boat Festival comes from remembering the poet Qu Yuan.

{相传|xiāng chuán}，{长城|Cháng chéng}{是|shì}{秦始皇|Qín Shǐ huáng}{修|xiū}{的|de}。{其实|qí shí}，{长城|Cháng chéng}{是|shì}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{个|gè}{朝代|cháo dài}{修|xiū}{的|de}。 — Legend has it that the First Emperor built the
Great Wall. In fact, many dynasties built it.

- {相传|xiāng chuán} usually starts the sentence, followed by a comma. {据说|jù shuō} (it is said, HSK 4) is the everyday partner:
  {据说|jù shuō} can report recent news; {相传|xiāng chuán} is for old stories.
- Lesson 12's {过桥米线|guò qiáo mǐ xiàn} had a legend too, introduced with {据说|jù shuō} ({据说|jù shuō}{在|zài}{很|hěn}{久|jiǔ}{以前|yǐ qián}…) and told as a story, not as fact.

## {源于|yuán yú} and {由来|yóu lái}: where things come from

- {源于|yuán yú} yuán yú: to originate from (written). It takes the origin as its object: {这个|zhè ge}{节日|jié rì}{源于|yuán yú}{古代|gǔ dài}{的|de}{农业|nóng yè}{生活|shēng huó} (this
  festival comes from the farming life of ancient times). In speech: {是|shì}{从|cóng}…{来|lái}{的|de}.
- {由来|yóu lái} yóu lái: the origin (of a name, a custom). It is a noun: {这个|zhè ge}{名字|míng zi}{的|de}{由来|yóu lái}, {春节|Chūn jié}{的|de}{由来|yóu lái}. {你|nǐ}{知道|zhī dào}"{长安|Cháng ān}"{这个|zhè ge}{名字|míng zi}{的|de}
  {由来|yóu lái}{吗|ma}？
- {起源|qǐ yuán} (lesson 14) is close to both: a noun (the origin) and a verb ({起|qǐ}{源于|yuán yú}, to originate in). {源于|yuán yú} is only the
  verb; {由来|yóu lái} is only the noun.

"Chang'an: a world city of long ago. In Chinese history there is one city whose name later generations
have always remembered: Chang'an, today's Xi'an. From the Han to the Tang, one dynasty after another
built its capital here. The origin of the name Chang'an is simple: people of old hoped the place would
have 'lasting peace'. Yet in history Chang'an went through many wars; it was damaged by war several times and
rebuilt several times. Tang Chang'an was one of the largest cities in the world at the time. The city
covered more than eighty square kilometres, and by one estimate its population may have reached about a
million. Its design was very orderly: wide streets, one after another, divided the city into blocks,
like a sheet of paper covered with squares. The widest street in the city is said to have been more
than a hundred metres wide, wider than the roads of many cities today. In the north was the palace where the emperor lived, and the
officials' offices lay just south of it. Ordinary people lived in the rest of the city. There were two
great markets in Chang'an, the East Market and the West Market. The West Market was livelier than the
East, because many foreign merchants lived near it. They came from far away, bringing spices, gems and
horses, and took Chinese porcelain, tea and cloth back to their own countries. In the West Market you
could hear all kinds of languages and eat food from all over. In those days the West Market had people selling clothes, medicine and wine,
and many little shops run by foreigners. At that time Chang'an had not only
merchants but many envoys and students from other countries. The Tang was fairly open to foreigners: people from
different countries could trade and study here. Japan sent people to study in Chang'an
many times. When they went home, they took back many books and new knowledge. Some foreigners lived in
Chang'an for decades, and some even became officials of the Tang. Although Tang Chang'an is long gone,
its traces remain. Walk the streets of Xi'an today and you can still see many historic sites. More
important still, it shows us that more than a thousand years ago, people of different countries and
civilisations were already living together, exchanging ideas and learning from one another."

(lesson 21's); {对话|duì huà}: a dialogue; {未来|wèi lái}: the future.)

Checklist: a thesis that answers the question ({我|wǒ}{却|què}{认为|rèn wéi}…); two reasons with examples ({首先|shǒu xiān}…{比如|bǐ rú}…; {其次|qí cì}…); a
concession ({当然|dāng rán}…{但是|dàn shì}…); a conclusion that returns to the thesis ({总之|zǒng zhī}…), here with {虽然|suī rán}…{却|què}; written words
({认为|rèn wéi}, {面对|miàn duì}, {启发|qǐ fā}), no {吧|ba} or {啊|a}.

## Say it

## Pronunciation

- {剑|jiàn} jiàn and {箭|jiàn} jiàn: the same sound. {将军|jiāng jūn} jiāng jūn: {将|jiāng} is jiāng here, as in {将来|jiāng lái}.
- {率领|shuài lǐng} shuài lǐng: {率|shuài} is shuài, not the lǜ of {效率|xiào lǜ}.
- {打仗|dǎ zhàng} dǎ zhàng: zhàng, fourth tone.
- {埋|mái} mái: second tone.
- {势力|shì lì} shì lì and {视力|shì lì} shì lì (eyesight, lesson 08): the same sound.
- {兴起|xīng qǐ} xīng qǐ: {兴|xīng} is xīng here, as in {兴奋|xīng fèn}; {高兴|gāo xìng} has xìng.
- {公元前|gōng yuán qián}{二二一|èr èr yī}{年|nián}: read the year digit by digit, èr èr yī nián.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{虽然|suī rán}{城|chéng}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}，{却|què}{它|tā}{的|de}{历史|lì shǐ}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}~~: {却|què} goes after the subject: {它|tā}{的|de}{历史|lì shǐ}{却|què}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}.
- ~~{这个|zhè ge}{习俗|xí sú}{由来|yóu lái}{于|yú}{古代|gǔ dài}~~: {由来|yóu lái} is a noun ({这个|zhè ge}{习俗|xí sú}{的|de}{由来|yóu lái}). The verb is {源于|yuán yú} or {起|qǐ}{源于|yuán yú}: {这个|zhè ge}{习俗|xí sú}{源于|yuán yú}{古代|gǔ dài}.
- ~~{相传|xiāng chuán}，{他|tā}{昨天|zuó tiān}{来|lái}{了|le}~~: {相传|xiāng chuán} is for old stories handed down; for recent news, {据说|jù shuō} or {听说|tīng shuō}.
- ~~{他|tā}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{兵马俑|Bīng mǎ yǒng}{的|de}{将军|jiāng jūn}~~: a figure in the army is {一|yí}{个|gè}{兵马俑|Bīng mǎ yǒng}; {将军|jiāng jūn} is a real general.
- ~~{率领|shuài lǐng}{朋友|péng you}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}~~ sounds oddly formal: {率领|shuài lǐng} is for troops and delegations. Say {带|dài}{朋友|péng you}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}.
- {剑|jiàn} (with 刂) is a sword; {箭|jiàn} (with ⺮) is an arrow: the same sound, different radicals.

## Key points

- {虽然|suī rán}…{却|què}…: although…, yet… ({却|què} after the subject): {秦朝|Qín cháo}{虽然|suī rán}{很|hěn}{短|duǎn}，{却|què}{影响|yǐng xiǎng}{了|le}{两千|liǎng qiān}{多|duō}{年|nián}. Written: {虽|suī}…{却|què}.

lessons.title: The gardens of Suzhou
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 14 met the word {园林|yuán lín}, the classical garden. This honors lesson goes to the city most famous for
them: {苏州|Sū zhōu} Suzhou, west of Shanghai, where {安娜|Ān nà} Anna spends a weekend with {王芳|Wáng Fāng} Wang Fang. You'll read how
a Chinese garden is designed (rocks, water, buildings and plants arranged so that a small space feels
like a landscape), meet two of its best-known gardens, and learn the words people use to talk about
them: {借景|jiè jǐng} (borrowing a view), {漏窗|lòu chuāng} (lattice windows) and {移步换景|yí bù huàn jǐng} (the view changes with every step).

## A landscape in a courtyard

The classical gardens of Suzhou were made by scholars, officials and merchants, mostly between the
Song dynasty and the end of the Qing (roughly the eleventh to the nineteenth century). They are private
gardens, built beside the owner's house inside the city walls, and many are small. Their aim was to
bring {山水|shān shuǐ} (mountains and water, the Chinese word for a landscape) into the city: a pond for a lake, a
pile of rocks for a mountain, so that the owner could "live in the city and still be in the hills".

In 1997 four of them were listed by UNESCO as World Heritage ({世界文化遗产|shì jiè wén huà yí chǎn}), and in 2000 five more were
added: nine gardens in all, listed together as the Classical Gardens of Suzhou ({苏州古典园林|Sū zhōu gǔ diǎn yuán lín}).

The four things every garden has:

| Element | Chinese | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| rocks | {石|shí} / {假山|jiǎ shān} jiǎ shān | an "artificial mountain" built of rocks; the most prized are {太湖石|Tài hú shí} Tài hú shí, stones from Lake Tai, full of holes |
| water | {水|shuǐ} / {池|chí} chí | a pond at the centre, which reflects the buildings and the sky |
| buildings | {亭|tíng}, {廊|láng}, {楼|lóu} | pavilions ({亭|tíng} tíng) to stop in, covered corridors ({廊|láng} láng, {走廊|zǒu láng}) to walk along, halls and towers |
| plants | {花木|huā mù} | trees and flowers chosen for each season, and for meaning: {竹|zhú} (bamboo), {梅花|méi huā}, {兰花|lán huā}, {菊花|jú huā} |

## Four ideas behind the design

- {借景|jiè jǐng} jiè jǐng, borrowing a view: using something outside the garden as part of it. From the
  Humble Administrator's Garden ({拙政园|Zhuō zhèng yuán} Zhuō zhèng yuán), the old pagoda of a temple outside the garden's walls
  rises behind the trees as if it belonged to the garden.
- {漏窗|lòu chuāng} lòu chuāng, lattice windows: openings in a wall filled with patterns of tile or brick, so that
  you glimpse the next courtyard without seeing all of it. A plain opening that frames a view like a
  picture is a {窗景|chuāng jǐng} or {框景|kuàng jǐng}.
- {移步换景|yí bù huàn jǐng} yí bù huàn jǐng, the view changes with every step: paths, corridors and bridges turn, so
  that each few steps show a new picture. You never see the whole garden at once.
- {小中见大|xiǎo zhōng jiàn dà}, the large within the small: walls, rocks and winding paths divide a small space so that it
  seems bigger than it is.

## Two gardens

{留园|Liú yuán} Liú yuán, the Lingering Garden, dates from the late Ming dynasty (1593). It is known for its long
covered corridors, some seven hundred metres of them, which lead from courtyard to courtyard past
lattice windows, and for a tall Taihu stone that stands in a courtyard of its own.

{网师园|Wǎng shī yuán} Wǎng shī yuán, the Master-of-Nets Garden, is one of the smallest of the nine: its name means a
fisherman's garden, the owner's way of saying he would rather live simply. Its buildings stand round a
small pond, and it is often given as the best example of {小中见大|xiǎo zhōng jiàn dà}.

## Reading: a weekend in Suzhou

Anna writes about her trip for her museum's newsletter. It's a travel piece with explanation in it:
notice how she moves from what she saw to why the garden is designed that way.

> {一下子|yí xià zi}{看|kàn}{完|wán}。{两|liǎng}{种|zhǒng}{花园|huā yuán}{没有好坏之分|méi yǒu hǎo huài zhī fēn}，{只是|zhǐ shì}{审美|shěn měi}{不同|bù tóng}。{不过|bú guò}，{我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{明白|míng bai}{了|le}{为什么|wèi shén me}{那么|nà me}{多|duō}{人|rén}{说|shuō}，{苏州|Sū zhōu}{园林|yuán lín}{要|yào}{慢|màn}{慢|màn}{地|de}{走|zǒu}，
> {慢|màn}{慢|màn}{地|de}{看|kàn}。

New words: {高铁|gāo tiě} (the high-speed train), {目的|mù dì} (purpose), {池子|chí zi} chí zi (a pond), {代表|dài biǎo} (to stand for), {堆|duī} (to pile
up), {篮球场|lán qiú chǎng} (a basketball court), {暗|àn} (dark), {窄|zhǎi} (narrow), {拐|guǎi} (to turn, lesson 09), {效果|xiào guǒ} (an effect), {惊喜|jīng xǐ} (a
pleasant surprise), {水波|shuǐ bō} (ripples), {透过|tòu guò} (through: lesson 26's word), {院子|yuàn zi} (a courtyard), {屋顶|wū dǐng} (a roof), {忍不住|rěn bu zhù}
(can't help), {挤|jǐ} (crowded), {水面|shuǐ miàn} (the surface of the water, lesson 17's word), {围|wéi}{着|zhe} (round), {挡|dǎng}{住|zhù} (to block), {显得|xiǎn de} (to seem), {实际|shí jì} (real, actual), {西方|xī fāng} (the
West), {花园|huā yuán} (a garden), {一眼|yì yǎn} (at a glance), {打鱼|dǎ yú} (to fish), {日子|rì zi} (days, life), {往西|wǎng xī} (westwards), {眼光|yǎn guāng} (one's gaze: lesson 24's word), {弯弯曲曲|wān wān qū qū} (winding), {没有好坏之分|méi yǒu hǎo huài zhī fēn} (neither is better).

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"The gardens of Suzhou: a new view at every step. By Anna. Last weekend my friend Wang Fang and I took
the high-speed train to Suzhou. From Beijing it takes under five hours. The main reason we went was to
see the gardens. Most of Suzhou's gardens were built by scholars, officials and merchants of the past.
They lived in the city but wanted to live among mountains and water, so they built gardens beside their
homes: a pond stood for a lake, and a few rocks piled up made a mountain. None of the gardens is large;
some are only the size of a basketball court. But once you're inside, you feel it's much bigger than it
looks. We went to the Lingering Garden first. Just inside the gate is a long corridor, dark and narrow.
Just as I was thinking it a bit odd, the corridor suddenly turned right and everything was bright: a
pond, a few pavilions and the rock mountain opposite, all in front of me at once. Wang Fang said this
was exactly the effect the designer wanted: 'dark first, then light': first you can't see anything
clearly, then you get a sudden surprise. The Lingering Garden's corridors are very long, with lattice
windows all along the walls. Every window has a different pattern: some like flowers, some like
ripples. Through them you can see a little bamboo in the next courtyard or a corner of a roof, but never
all of it, so you can't help wanting to go and look. After walking a while, I noticed that every few
steps the view in front of me changed, as if I were looking at a very long painting. Chinese calls this
'the view changes with every step'. In the afternoon we went to the Master-of-Nets Garden. It's even
smaller, but it doesn't feel crowded at all. The buildings stand round a little pond, and the rocks and
trees at its edge hide part of the water, so you can't see where the pond ends, and it looks bigger
than it really is. Standing by the pond, looking at the pavilion, the white walls and the clouds
reflected in the water, I felt as if time had slowed down. The
Master-of-Nets Garden's name is interesting too: a 'master of nets' is a fisherman, and the owner chose
the name to say that he wanted a simple, quiet life. The next morning we went to the Humble
Administrator's Garden. Standing by the pond and looking west, you see an old pagoda in the distance that
seems to be in the garden, though in fact it's far outside it. Wang Fang told me this is 'borrowing a
view': a garden may have walls, but your eyes can travel a long way. All the way back to Beijing I kept thinking:
many Western gardens like symmetry, and you can see the whole thing at a glance; the gardens of Suzhou
prefer winding paths and won't let you see everything at once. Neither kind is better: they just have
different ideas of beauty. But now I understand why so many people say that the gardens of Suzhou are
for walking slowly and looking slowly."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# In a Suzhou garden
{苏州|Sū zhōu}{园林|yuán lín}{是|shì}{世界文化遗产|shì jiè wén huà yí chǎn}。
= The gardens of Suzhou are World Heritage.
{这个|zhè ge}{园林|yuán lín}{虽然|suī rán}{不|bú}{大|dà}，{却|què}{让|ràng}{人|rén}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。
= This garden isn't big, but it feels big.
{透过|tòu guò}{漏窗|lòu chuāng}，{可以|kě yǐ}{看|kàn}{到|dào}{隔壁|gé bì}{的|de}{院子|yuàn zi}。
= Through the lattice window you can see the next courtyard.
{每|měi}{走|zǒu}{几|jǐ}{步|bù}，{风景|fēng jǐng}{就|jiù}{变|biàn}{一|yí}{次|cì}，{这|zhè}{叫|jiào}{移步换景|yí bù huàn jǐng}。
= Every few steps the view changes: that's called "the view changes with every step".
{远处|yuǎn chù}{的|de}{古|gǔ}{塔|tǎ}{也|yě}{被|bèi}{借|jiè}{到|dào}{了|le}{园子|yuán zi}{里|lǐ}。
= The old pagoda in the distance has been "borrowed" into the garden too.
```

## Key points

- Suzhou's classical gardens: private gardens of scholars, officials and merchants, from about the
  Song to the late Qing; nine listed by UNESCO (four in 1997, five more in 2000).
- The elements: {假山|jiǎ shān} and {太湖石|Tài hú shí} (rocks), {池|chí} (water), {亭|tíng} and {廊|láng} (buildings), {花木|huā mù} (plants).
- The ideas: {借景|jiè jǐng} (borrowing a view), {漏窗|lòu chuāng} (lattice windows), {移步换景|yí bù huàn jǐng} (a new view at every step), {小中见大|xiǎo zhōng jiàn dà} (the
  large in the small).
- {留园|Liú yuán} (1593): long corridors and lattice windows. {网师园|Wǎng shī yuán}: small, built round a pond.
- Chinese gardens hide and reveal ({先暗后亮|xiān àn hòu liàng}, {弯弯曲曲|wān wān qū qū}); the contrast with symmetrical Western gardens is one of
  {审美|shěn měi}, not of better or worse.

This honors lesson adds no new vocabulary: its words are glossed where they appear.

lessons.title: Xu Xiake, traveller
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Most travellers in old China moved for a reason: officials to a new post, merchants to a market,
soldiers to a war. {徐霞客|Xú Xiá kè} Xú Xiá kè travelled to see. For some thirty years in the late Ming dynasty he
walked across much of China, wrote down what he found every day, and left diaries that geographers
still read: 《{徐霞客游记|Xú Xiá kè yóu jì}》, *The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake*. This lesson tells who he was, where he went,
what he recorded, and why it matters.

## Who he was

| | |
|---|---|
| Name | {徐弘祖|Xú Hóng zǔ} Xú Hóng zǔ, best known by his literary name {徐霞客|Xú Xiá kè} ("guest of the rosy clouds") |
| Dates | 1587–1641, the late Ming dynasty |
| Home | {江阴|Jiāng yīn} Jiāng yīn, a town on the Yangtze in today's Jiangsu |
| Family | well-off and educated; his father died before his travels began, and his mother encouraged him to go |
| Work | some thirty years of journeys, written up day by day as diaries |

Educated young men of his time studied for the imperial examinations ({科举|kē jǔ} kē jǔ) to become officials.
Xu Xiake didn't: from his early twenties he set out on journeys instead. One story, told by later
writers, is that his mother sent him off with the words {儿可游矣|ér kě yóu yǐ} (my son, you may travel now), an old
written way of saying {你|nǐ}{可以|kě yǐ}{出去|chū qù}{旅行|lǚ xíng}{了|le}.

## Where he walked

- The famous mountains: his surviving diaries open with a trip to {天台山|Tiān tāi shān} Tiān tāi shān in Zhejiang
  in 1613, and he went on to {黄山|Huáng shān} Huáng shān and many others.
- The south-west: his last and longest journey, at about fifty, took him through {广西|Guǎng xī} Guǎng xī,
  {贵州|Guì zhōu} Guì zhōu and {云南|Yún nán} Yún nán, regions few scholars of his day had seen.
- On foot: he walked most of the way, often off the roads, climbing into caves and following rivers,
  with a servant or two and very little money. He fell ill on that last journey and was carried home,
  where he died.

The day his diaries begin, 19 May 1613, is now {中国旅游日|Zhōng guó lǚ yóu rì}, China Tourism Day, which is held on 19 May
every year in his memory.

## What he recorded

- Karst landscapes: the limestone country of the south-west, where water dissolves the rock into
  steep hills, caves and underground rivers. He went into dozens of caves ({山洞|shān dòng}), estimated their size as best he
  could, and described their shapes, their water and how they seemed to have formed. Geographers
  call his account one of the earliest detailed descriptions of karst anywhere.
- Rivers and their sources: classical books said the Yangtze ({长江|Cháng jiāng}) began at the {岷江|Mín jiāng} Mín jiāng. In an
  essay on the river's source, Xu argued from what he had seen that the {金沙江|Jīn shā jiāng} Jīn shā jiāng, further
  west, was its true upper course. Historians note that he wasn't the first to know this, but he was
  among the first to say so clearly and give his reasons.
- Everything else: the weather, the plants, the roads, the people he met, the prices of food. His
  diaries are a record of daily life in late Ming China as well as a book of geography.

## Why it matters

Before Xu Xiake, most Chinese writing about geography repeated what older books said. He went and
looked: {实地考察|shí dì kǎo chá}, studying a place on the spot, and recording what he saw even when it disagreed with
the classics. That is why his diaries are read today as a work of science, and why his name is attached
to China's tourism day. They are also a pleasure to read: clear, exact, and full of the excitement of
someone seeing a waterfall or a cave for the first time.

## Reading: a man who travelled to see

New words: {双脚|shuāng jiǎo} (both feet), {地形|dì xíng} (landforms, lesson 18's word), {走遍|zǒu biàn} (to walk all over), {出远门|chū yuǎn mén} (to go on a long journey), {出生|chū shēng} (to be born), {梦想|mèng xiǎng}
(to dream of), {亲眼|qīn yǎn} (with one's own eyes), {支持|zhī chí} (support), {背|bēi} bēi (to carry on one's back), {弄清楚|nòng qīng chu} (to work out),
{火把|huǒ bǎ} huǒ bǎ (a torch), {整理|zhěng lǐ} (to put in order, edit), {思考|sī kǎo} (to think), {形成|xíng chéng} (to form), {学者|xué zhě} (a scholar), {详细|xiáng xì}
(detailed), {源头|yuán tóu} (a source), {提出|tí chū} (to put forward), {上游|shàng yóu} (the upper reaches), {理由|lǐ yóu} (a reason), {长途|cháng tú} (long-
distance), {迷路|mí lù} (to get lost), {放弃|fàng qì} (to give up), {沿|yán}{着|zhe} (along), {去世|qù shì} (to pass away), {了不起|liǎo bu qǐ} (remarkable), {定为|dìng wéi} (to designate as), {篇|piān} (a piece of writing), {亲自|qīn zì} (in
person).

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"The man who walked across China. In ancient China, many people never left their home towns in their
whole lives. Even those who went on long journeys mostly did so to take up a post, to trade or to fight.
But in the late Ming dynasty one man set out in order to see: Xu Xiake. Xu Xiake was born into a well-off
family of scholars in Jiangyin. In those days the most important thing for an educated man was to take
the examinations, so as to become an official one day. Xu Xiake had no interest in examinations. From
childhood he loved reading geography books and looking at maps, and he dreamed of one day seeing with his
own eyes the mountains and rivers the books described. In his twenties, with his mother's support, he
shouldered a little luggage and set off. Over the next thirty-odd years he travelled through most of
China. He hardly ever took a cart, and sometimes went by boat, but he relied mainly on his own feet. Sometimes he walked
for days to see one mountain; to find out how deep a cave was, he would carry a torch all the way to the
far end. In the evening, however tired he was, he wrote down what he had seen that day: how high the
mountains were, which way the rivers flowed, whom he had met on the road, what he had eaten. These diaries
were later edited into a book: the famous Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake. Along the way he often met danger: once he got lost in the
mountains, and once he was robbed of the money he carried, but he never gave up. Why does the book matter so much?
Because Xu Xiake didn't just look at the scenery: he observed and thought carefully. In Guangxi, Guizhou
and Yunnan he saw many strange stone hills and caves, recorded their shapes in detail and tried to work
out how such landscapes formed. Many scholars regard this as one of the earliest detailed studies of this
kind of landscape anywhere in the world. Besides, the old books said the source of the Yangtze was the
Min River. From his own observations, Xu Xiake put forward the view that the Jinsha River was the
Yangtze's true upper course. Although he wasn't the first to know this, he was among the first to set out
his reasons clearly in writing. On his last long journey Xu Xiake fell seriously ill. He was
carried back to his home town, and died in 1641. He never held office and left little property, but he
left later generations a remarkable book. Today China has made 19 May 'China Tourism Day', because it is
the day the first piece of his diaries begins. Xu Xiake's story tells us that what we learn from books
matters, but seeing for ourselves and thinking for ourselves matter just as much. To this day, many people take his book and travel along the roads he walked."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Xu Xiake
{徐霞客|Xú Xiá kè}{用|yòng}{双脚|shuāng jiǎo}{走遍|zǒu biàn}{了|le}{中国|Zhōng guó}{的|de}{大部分|dà bù fen}{地方|dì fang}。
= Xu Xiake walked across most of China.
{他|tā}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{都|dōu}{把|bǎ}{看|kàn}{到|dào}{的|de}{东西|dōng xi}{写|xiě}{下来|xià lái}。
= Every evening he wrote down what he had seen.
{他|tā}{根据|gēn jù}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{考察|kǎo chá}，{提出|tí chū}{了|le}{新|xīn}{的|de}{看法|kàn fǎ}。
= From his own observations he put forward a new view.
{五|wǔ}{月|yuè}{十九|shí jiǔ}{日|rì}{是|shì}{中国旅游日|Zhōng guó lǚ yóu rì}。
= 19 May is China Tourism Day.
{书|shū}{上|shàng}{的|de}{知识|zhī shi}{很|hěn}{重要|zhòng yào}，{亲眼|qīn yǎn}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{也|yě}{同样|tóng yàng}{重要|zhòng yào}。
= What we learn from books matters, and seeing for ourselves matters just as much.
```

## Key points

- {徐霞客|Xú Xiá kè} ({徐弘祖|Xú Hóng zǔ}, 1587–1641), late Ming: a traveller who went to see, not to serve, trade or fight.
- 《{徐霞客游记|Xú Xiá kè yóu jì}》: some thirty years of journeys written up as daily diaries; 19 May, the day they begin
  (1613), is {中国旅游日|Zhōng guó lǚ yóu rì}.
- He described the karst landscapes and caves of the south-west in detail, and argued that the {金沙江|Jīn shā jiāng}, not
  the {岷江|Mín jiāng}, is the Yangtze's upper course (not the first to know, among the first to argue it clearly).
- His method was {实地考察|shí dì kǎo chá}: going to look, and recording what he saw even against the old books.
- {虽然|suī rán}…{却|què} and {以便|yǐ biàn} from this module, in a real story: {他|tā}{虽然|suī rán}{不|bú}{是|shì}{第|dì}{一|yī}{个|gè}…，{却|què}{是|shì}{最|zuì}{早|zǎo}…; {参加|cān jiā}{考试|kǎo shì}，{以便|yǐ biàn}{将来|jiāng lái}{当官|dāng guān}.

This honors lesson adds no new vocabulary: its words are glossed where they appear.

lessons.title: The digital world and AI
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about computers, networks and artificial intelligence, and about how Chinese builds
the words for them. {李明|Lǐ Míng} (Li Ming), now a translator at a company, tells {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (Wang Fang) about the AI
translation system his office has brought in, and the reading is one of {王芳|Wáng Fāng}'s commentary pieces for
the website: what AI can and can't do. You'll learn:

- **[[word formation]]**: the prefixes {超|chāo}- {多|duō}- {反|fǎn}- {无|wú}- {亚|yà}- {准|zhǔn}-, and the suffixes -{化|huà} -{式|shì} -{型|xíng} -{性|xìng} of lesson
  01 again, with -{率|lǜ} (rate), so that you can work out words you've never met ({多功能|duō gōng néng}, {无线|wú xiàn}, {数字化|shù zì huà});
- the words of numbers and chance: {概率|gài lǜ} (probability), {乘|chéng} (to multiply), {相等|xiāng děng}, {相差|xiāng chà}, {对应|duì yìng}, {图表|tú biǎo};
- about sixty words of the digital world: what's on the screen ({窗口|chuāng kǒu}, {浏览器|liú lǎn qì}, {文档|wén dàng}, {链接|liàn jiē}), what you do
  ({点击|diǎn jī}, {粘贴|zhān tiē}, {查询|chá xún}, {压缩|yā suō}, {转换|zhuǎn huàn}), networks ({联网|lián wǎng}, {流量|liú liàng}, {实时|shí shí}, {远程|yuǎn chéng}, {中断|zhōng duàn}) and AI ({人工智能|rén gōng zhì néng}, {识别|shí bié}, {生成|shēng chéng}, {模拟|mó nǐ},
  {优化|yōu huà}).

The module's first essay task is near the end: an argued piece of 300–400 characters.

## Word formation: building words from parts

Most Chinese words are built from parts that keep their meaning: {电|diàn} (electricity) + {脑|nǎo} (brain) is a
computer, {网|wǎng} (net) + {站|zhàn} (station) is a website. This is **[[word formation]]**, and at HSK 6 it becomes
a real reading skill: in a news article you'll meet words that no dictionary list gives you, but
whose parts you know. Two kinds of part are worth learning as a set: a **[[prefix]]** comes before a
word and a **[[suffix]]** after it.

### Six prefixes

| Prefix | Meaning | Words |
|---|---|---|
| {超|chāo}- chāo | super-, extra-, beyond | {超市|chāo shì} (a supermarket: {超级|chāo jí}{市场|shì chǎng} shortened), {超级|chāo jí} (super), {超大|chāo dà} (extra-large), {超长|chāo cháng} (extra-long) |
| {多|duō}- duō | multi- | {多媒体|duō méi tǐ} (multimedia), {多功能|duō gōng néng} (multifunctional), {多样|duō yàng} (varied) |
| {反|fǎn}- fǎn | counter-, anti-, reverse | {反作用|fǎn zuò yòng} (a counter-effect, a backlash), {反面|fǎn miàn} (the reverse side), {反对|fǎn duì} (to oppose) |
| {无|wú}- wú | without, -less, un- | {无线|wú xiàn} (wireless), {无人|wú rén} (unmanned: {无人机|wú rén jī}, a drone), {无限|wú xiàn} (unlimited), {无关|wú guān} (unrelated) |
| {亚|yà}- yà | second, sub- | {亚军|yà jūn} (runner-up: lesson 29), {亚健康|yà jiàn kāng} (not ill but not well: "sub-health") |
| {准|zhǔn}- zhǔn | -to-be, about to be | {准妈妈|zhǔn mā ma} (a mother-to-be), {准大学生|zhǔn dà xué sheng} (someone about to start university) |

These prefixes belong to a written, modern style: you see them in product names, adverts and news
({多功能|duō gōng néng}{电饭锅|diàn fàn guō}, {无线|wú xiàn}{网络|wǎng luò}, {超长|chāo cháng}{待机|dài jī}: a multifunction rice cooker, a wireless network, an extra-long standby time). Two warnings:

- Not every {无|wú} or {亚|yà} at the start of a word is a prefix. {无论|wú lùn} is "no matter (how)", and {亚洲|Yà zhōu} is
  "Asia", from the old foreign name; neither is built on a word after it.
- {准|zhǔn} is also "accurate" ({准确|zhǔn què}, and this lesson's {精准|jīng zhǔn}). {准|zhǔn} + a person ({准妈妈|zhǔn mā ma}) is the prefix; {准|zhǔn} + a verb
  or adjective is usually "accurate" or "allowed" ({准时|zhǔn shí}, on time).

### Suffixes: -{化|huà} -{式|shì} -{型|xíng} -{性|xìng}, and -{率|lǜ}

Lesson 01 brought the four suffixes; here they are with this lesson's words.

| Suffix | Meaning | Words |
|---|---|---|
| -{化|huà} huà | -ise, -ify: becoming so | {数字化|shù zì huà} (digitalisation: becoming digital), {优化|yōu huà} (to optimise: make better), {现代化|xiàn dài huà} (modernisation), {智能化|zhì néng huà} (becoming "smart") |
| -{式|shì} shì | -style, a way of | {中式|Zhōng shì} / {西式|xī shì} (Chinese- / Western-style), {自助式|zì zhù shì} (self-service) |
| -{型|xíng} xíng | type, model | {新型|xīn xíng} (a new type of), {大型|dà xíng} / {小型|xiǎo xíng} (large- / small-scale) |
| -{性|xìng} xìng | -ness, -ity: the quality of | {可能性|kě néng xìng} (possibility), {重要性|zhòng yào xìng} (importance), {安全性|ān quán xìng} (safety), {积极性|jī jí xìng} (enthusiasm) |
| -{率|lǜ} lǜ | rate, ratio | {频率|pín lǜ} (frequency), {概率|gài lǜ} (probability), {效率|xiào lǜ} (efficiency), {准确率|zhǔn què lǜ} (accuracy rate), {成功率|chéng gōng lǜ} (success rate) |

{率|lǜ} is lǜ as a suffix, but shuài in {率先|shuài xiān} (to be the first to: lesson 20) and {率领|shuài lǐng} (to lead an army:
lesson 15). The suffixes make nouns you can count and compare: {这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{方法|fāng fǎ}{的|de}{成功率|chéng gōng lǜ}{很|hěn}{高|gāo} (this method's
success rate is high); {我们|wǒ men}{要|yào}{优化|yōu huà}{系统|xì tǒng} (we need to optimise the system). A word with -{化|huà} can be a
verb ({优化|yōu huà}{系统|xì tǒng}) or a noun ({实现|shí xiàn}{数字化|shù zì huà}, achieve digitalisation).

## Numbers and chance

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {乘|chéng} chéng | to multiply | {三|sān}{乘|chéng}{四|sì}{等于|děng yú}{十二|shí èr}。 (3 × 4 = 12.) In sums people also say {乘以|chéng yǐ}: {三|sān}{乘以|chéng yǐ}{四|sì}. |
| {概率|gài lǜ} gài lǜ | probability | {扔|rēng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{硬币|yìng bì}，{正面|zhèng miàn}{朝|cháo}{上|shàng}{的|de}{概率|gài lǜ}{是|shì}{百分之|bǎi fēn zhī}{五十|wǔ shí}。 (Toss a coin: the probability of heads is 50 %.) |
| {相等|xiāng děng} xiāng děng | to be equal | {这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{数|shù}{相等|xiāng děng}。 (These two numbers are equal.) |
| {相差|xiāng chà} xiāng chà | to differ (by) | {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{城市|chéng shì}{的|de}{气温|qì wēn}{相差|xiāng chà}{十|shí}{度|dù}。 (The two cities' temperatures differ by ten degrees.) |
| {对应|duì yìng} duì yìng | to correspond (to) | {一|yí}{个|gè}{汉字|hàn zì}{对应|duì yìng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{音节|yīn jié}。 (Each Chinese character corresponds to one syllable.) |
| {图表|tú biǎo} tú biǎo | a chart, a graph | {从|cóng}{图表|tú biǎo}{上|shàng}{看|kàn}，{用户|yòng hù}{越|yuè}{来|lái}{越|yuè}{多|duō}。 (From the chart, there are more and more users.) |

{乘|chéng} chéng "to multiply" is a second item beside HSK 4's {乘|chéng} "to ride, to take" ({乘|chéng}{车|chē}, {乘|chéng}{飞机|fēi jī}): same
character, same sound, different words. Division is {除以|chú yǐ} ({十|shí}{除以|chú yǐ}{二|èr}{等于|děng yú}{五|wǔ}); {加|jiā} and {减|jiǎn} you know. {硬币|yìng bì} is a
coin; {正面|zhèng miàn} (lesson 10) is "the front", here heads, and {反面|fǎn miàn} tails.

## Words for the digital world

**On the screen.** {窗口|chuāng kǒu} (a window on a screen; also a service counter at a bank or a station), {浏览器|liú lǎn qì}
(a browser), {文档|wén dàng} (a document, a file you write in), {版本|bǎn běn} (a version: {新|xīn}{版本|bǎn běn}, {中文|Zhōng wén}{版本|bǎn běn}), {图像|tú xiàng} (an image),
{摄像头|shè xiàng tóu} (a camera on a computer or a street: a webcam), {多媒体|duō méi tǐ} (multimedia), {动漫|dòng màn} (animation and comics,
anime), {科幻|kē huàn} (science fiction: {科幻|kē huàn}{小说|xiǎo shuō}, {科幻|kē huàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}), {科普|kē pǔ} (popular science: {科普|kē pǔ}{文章|wén zhāng}).

**Doing things.** {点击|diǎn jī} (to click: {点击|diǎn jī}{链接|liàn jiē}), {粘贴|zhān tiē} (to paste: {复制|fù zhì}{和|hé}{粘贴|zhān tiē}, copy and paste), {放大|fàng dà} (to
enlarge, zoom in), {隐藏|yǐn cáng} (to hide), {提示|tí shì} (a hint, a prompt; to prompt), {查询|chá xún} (to look up, inquire: {查询|chá xún}
{信息|xìn xī}, {查询|chá xún}{成绩|chéng jì}), {输出|shū chū} (to output, to export: the opposite of HSK 5's {输入|shū rù}), {扫描|sǎo miáo} (to scan: {扫描|sǎo miáo}{二维码|èr wéi mǎ}, {扫描|sǎo miáo}{文件|wén jiàn}), {存储|cún chǔ} (to store data:
written; in speech {保存|bǎo cún} or {存|cún}), {压缩|yā suō} (to compress: {压缩|yā suō}{文件|wén jiàn}), {转换|zhuǎn huàn} (to convert, to switch: {把|bǎ}{文档|wén dàng}{转换|zhuǎn huàn}{成|chéng}
{别的|bié de}{格|gé}{式|shì}), {传输|chuán shū} (to transmit: {传输|chuán shū}{数据|shù jù}), {生成|shēng chéng} (to generate), {提取|tí qǔ} (to extract: {提取|tí qǔ}{信息|xìn xī}), {采集|cǎi jí} (to collect,
gather: {采集|cǎi jí}{数据|shù jù}).

**Networks.** {网|wǎng} (a net; the network: {上网|shàng wǎng}, {网上|wǎng shàng}, and a net for fish, {一|yì}{张|zhāng}{网|wǎng}), {联网|lián wǎng} (to go online, to be
networked), {下线|xià xiàn} (to go offline, to log off), {链接|liàn jiē} (a link; to link), {流量|liú liàng} (data, traffic: {手机|shǒu jī}{流量|liú liàng};
also the flow of water or people), {容量|róng liàng} (capacity: {存储|cún chǔ}{容量|róng liàng}), {频率|pín lǜ} (frequency: {使用|shǐ yòng}{频率|pín lǜ}), {远程|yuǎn chéng} (remote:
{远程|yuǎn chéng}{办公|bàn gōng}, working remotely), {实时|shí shí} (real-time: {实时|shí shí}{翻译|fān yì}), {定时|dìng shí} (at a set time; a timer: {定时|dìng shí}{发送|fā sòng}),
{定位|dìng wèi} (to locate; positioning: {手机|shǒu jī}{定位|dìng wèi}), {跟踪|gēn zōng} (to track, follow), {对接|duì jiē} (to link up, connect two
systems or two sides), {中断|zhōng duàn} (to break off, cut out), {间隔|jiàn gé} (an interval, a gap), {通讯|tōng xùn} / {通信|tōng xìn} (to
communicate; communications), {通话|tōng huà} (to talk on the phone).

**AI and security.** {人工智能|rén gōng zhì néng} (artificial intelligence), {识别|shí bié} (to recognise, identify: {语音识别|yǔ yīn shí bié},
{人脸识别|rén liǎn shí bié}), {模拟|mó nǐ} (to simulate), {数字化|shù zì huà} (digitalisation), {优化|yōu huà} (to optimise), {辅助|fǔ zhù} (to assist; auxiliary),
{借助|jiè zhù} (with the help of), {验证|yàn zhèng} (to verify: {验证码|yàn zhèng mǎ}, a verification code), {干扰|gān rǎo} (to interfere; interference),
{攻击|gōng jī} (to attack; an attack), {精准|jīng zhǔn} (precise), {清晰|qīng xī} (clear, sharp: of an image or a voice), {视觉|shì jué} (sight,
vision), {听觉|tīng jué} (hearing).

**Speed.** {便捷|biàn jié} (quick and convenient), {快捷|kuài jié} (quick: {快捷键|kuài jié jiàn}, a keyboard shortcut), {飞速|fēi sù} (at great
speed: {飞速|fēi sù}{发展|fā zhǎn}), {频繁|pín fán} (frequent: written).

Pairs to keep apart:

- {通讯|tōng xùn} / {通信|tōng xìn} are "communications" as a field ({通讯|tōng xùn}{技术|jì shù}, {通信|tōng xìn}{公司|gōng sī}) and {通信|tōng xìn} is also "to write to each
  other"; {通话|tōng huà} is to talk on the phone ({他们|tā men}{通话|tōng huà}{了|le}{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}).
- {借助|jiè zhù} is "with the help of" a thing or a method, before the main verb: {借助|jiè zhù}{翻译|fān yì}{软件|ruǎn jiàn}，{我|wǒ}{看|kàn}{懂|dǒng}{了|le}{这|zhè}{篇|piān}{文章|wén zhāng}.
  {帮助|bāng zhù} (HSK 2) is help from someone: {朋友|péng you}{帮助|bāng zhù}{了|le}{我|wǒ}.
- {精准|jīng zhǔn} and {准确|zhǔn què} are both "accurate"; {精准|jīng zhǔn} is "precise, to the point", more written, and common in
  technology and business ({精准|jīng zhǔn}{定位|dìng wèi}). {清晰|qīng xī} and {清楚|qīng chu} are both "clear"; {清晰|qīng xī} is written and describes
  images, voices and thinking ({图像|tú xiàng}{很|hěn}{清晰|qīng xī}, the image is sharp; {思路|sī lù}{清晰|qīng xī}, clear thinking: {思路|sī lù} is lesson 26's).
- {便捷|biàn jié} adds "easy" to "quick" ({便捷|biàn jié}{的|de}{服务|fú wù}); {快捷|kuài jié} is just quick ({快捷|kuài jié}{的|de}{方式|fāng shì}). Both are written; in speech
  you'd say {方便|fāng biàn} or {快|kuài}.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Traditional | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 捷 | quick | jié | 扌 | 11 | 捷 | {便捷|biàn jié}, {快捷|kuài jié} |

In traditional, {辅|fǔ} is 輔 (14 strokes, with 車), {踪|zōng} is 蹤 (18: {足|zú} + 從), {链|liàn} is 鏈 (18: {金|jīn} + 連), {拟|nǐ}
is 擬 (17: 扌 + {疑|yí}) and {讯|xùn} is 訊 (10, with {言|yán}). {链|liàn} stands for two traditional characters: 鏈 for
a chain or a link ({链接|liàn jiē}, 鏈接) and 鍊 in {项链|xiàng liàn} (a necklace, lesson 22: 項鍊, 17 strokes).

- **Sound parts.** {辅|fǔ} is {车|chē} + {甫|fǔ} fǔ, and {甫|fǔ} gives a whole family: {辅|fǔ} fǔ, {捕|bǔ} bǔ (to catch, lesson 17)
  and {铺|pū} pū (to spread, lesson 07). {踪|zōng} is {足|zú} (foot) + {宗|zōng} zōng: {踪|zōng} zōng and {综|zōng} zōng ({综合|zōng hé}, HSK 5).
  {晰|xī} is {日|rì} + {析|xī} xī ({分析|fēn xī}): the same sound exactly. {讯|xùn} is 讠 + {卂|xùn} xùn, as in {迅|xùn} xùn ({迅速|xùn sù}, quick, HSK 5).
  {攻|gōng} is {工|gōng} gōng + 攵 (a hand with a stick): {工|gōng} gives gōng to {攻|gōng} and {功|gōng} ({成功|chéng gōng}), and hóng to {红|hóng} and {虹|hóng} (a
  rainbow, lesson 17).
- **{粘|zhān}** is {米|mǐ} (rice: sticky rice) + {占|zhàn} zhàn, which also has the reading zhān (to divine); {占|zhàn} is also in {站|zhàn} zhàn and
  {战|zhàn} zhàn.
- **{链|liàn}** is 钅 (metal) + {连|lián} lián (to join): a chain is joined metal. A memory aid, but the sound is
  close too (lián, liàn).
- **{拟|nǐ}** is 扌 + {以|yǐ} yǐ, with the sound drifted to nǐ.
- **Look-alikes**: {幻|huàn} huàn and {幼|yòu} yòu (young: {幼儿园|yòu ér yuán}, HSK 5) share {幺|yāo}; {幼|yòu} has {力|lì} on the right, {幻|huàn} a
  single hooked stroke. {攻|gōng} gōng and {功|gōng} gōng: 攵 (attack) or {力|lì} (effort).

### Stroke order

- **{辅|fǔ}** (11): {车|chē} first; on the left, its last stroke is a rising stroke. Then {甫|fǔ} (7), with the
  long vertical through the middle and the dot last.
- **{攻|gōng}** (7): {工|gōng}, its bottom stroke rising to the right, then 攵 (left-falling, horizontal,
  left-falling, right-falling).
- **{幻|huàn}** (4): {幺|yāo} (three strokes), then the right part in one stroke: across, down and hooked.

4. Balanced: it's a useful tool, neither good nor bad in itself; use it for repetitive work, check

"**What can AI do, and what can't it?** Lately 'artificial intelligence' has become a hot topic.
Open your phone and it can look up the weather and plan a route for you; click once online and in a
few seconds it can generate an article or an image. Some say that before long a great many jobs
will be taken over by machines; others say it's just a passing fuss, and in a few years nobody will
mention it. So what, in the end, can AI do, and what can't it?

First, what it can do. AI's greatest strength is processing huge amounts of data in a very short
time. With the help of a camera and image-recognition technology, for example, a phone can
identify several thousand kinds of plants with quite a high accuracy rate; map software can locate
drivers using real-time road conditions and warn them where the traffic is jammed ahead;
translation software can convert a document of dozens of pages into another language in a few
minutes. Work like this is slow and tiring for people, but quick and precise for machines. In these
areas AI really is a handy helper.

But its shortcomings are obvious too. First, it doesn't truly 'understand' what it's saying. It
calculates the probability of the next word from past data, then outputs one word after another.
So it sometimes states wrong information very confidently, in a way that's hard to spot. Second, it
learns from what people have written, and where people's writing has biases, so will it. Third, it
finds it hard to do well at things that need experience and feeling: why a joke is funny, how to
say a word of comfort, machines often can't explain.

Others worry that AI will cost many people their jobs. The worry isn't groundless: in some
factories machines have already replaced quite a few workers, and many companies' service lines
are now answered first by a machine. But look at history and you'll find that every new technology
has made some jobs disappear while new ones appeared. Once computers became common, there were
fewer jobs just typing, but more and more people making websites and software. So the key isn't to
refuse new technology but to keep learning new skills.

Besides this, there's a safety problem in using AI. The photos, documents and call records we
upload may be stored; if the system is attacked, our personal privacy may fall into other people's
hands.

So how should we see it? My view is this: AI is a tool; in itself it's neither good nor bad, and
the key lies in the people who use it. We can let it help us with repetitive, time-consuming work,
and spend the time we save where thinking and creating are needed. But we must check the answers
it gives ourselves, and important decisions should still be made by people. Rather than worrying
about whether machines will replace people, we'd do better to think: how can we make good use of
them?

Wang Fang"

- {干扰|gān rǎo} gān rǎo: gān here (to interfere), as in {干燥|gān zào} (dry, lesson 17), not gàn.
- {通讯|tōng xùn} tōng xùn, {通信|tōng xìn} tōng xìn, {通话|tōng huà} tōng huà: one syllable tells them apart.
- {下载|xià zǎi} xià zǎi (to download): the dictionaries give zǎi; xià zài is also heard.
- {摄像头|shè xiàng tóu} shè xiàng tóu: tóu keeps its tone here (a "head", the camera unit), unlike the light tou of {石头|shí tou}.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{很|hěn}{无线|wú xiàn}~~: {无线|wú xiàn} sorts things into a kind (wireless or not), so it can't be graded with {很|hěn}. Say {无线|wú xiàn}{网络|wǎng luò} (a
  wireless network), {这个|zhè ge}{耳机|ěr jī}{是|shì}{无线|wú xiàn}{的|de} (these headphones are wireless).
- {借助|jiè zhù} needs an object and a main verb: {借助|jiè zhù}{翻译|fān yì}{软件|ruǎn jiàn}，{我|wǒ}{看|kàn}{懂|dǒng}{了|le}{这|zhè}{篇|piān}{文章|wén zhāng}. ~~{我|wǒ}{借助|jiè zhù}{了|le}~~ alone doesn't finish.
- {存储|cún chǔ} is written and technical ({存储|cún chǔ}{数据|shù jù}, {存储|cún chǔ}{容量|róng liàng}); for "save your file" in speech say {保存|bǎo cún} or {存|cún}{一下|yí xià}.
- {通话|tōng huà} is talking on the phone; ~~{我们|wǒ men}{通话|tōng huà}{了|le}{邮件|yóu jiàn}~~ is wrong: emails are {发|fā} ({我们|wǒ men}{互相|hù xiāng}{发|fā}{了|le}{邮件|yóu jiàn}), and letters
  are {通信|tōng xìn}.
- {亚洲|Yà zhōu} isn't a prefix word: {亚|yà} there is just a sound in a foreign name. And {无论|wú lùn} is "no matter", not
  "no argument".
- {率|lǜ} after a noun: ~~{率|lǜ}{成功|chéng gōng}~~ is wrong: {成功率|chéng gōng lǜ} (the success rate). The suffix comes last.

## Key points

- Word formation: prefixes {超|chāo}- ({超大|chāo dà}), {多|duō}- ({多媒体|duō méi tǐ}, {多功能|duō gōng néng}), {反|fǎn}- ({反作用|fǎn zuò yòng}, {反面|fǎn miàn}), {无|wú}- ({无线|wú xiàn}, {无人|wú rén}), {亚|yà}- ({亚健康|yà jiàn kāng}),
  {准|zhǔn}- ({准妈妈|zhǔn mā ma}); suffixes -{化|huà} ({数字化|shù zì huà}, {优化|yōu huà}), -{式|shì} ({自助式|zì zhù shì}), -{型|xíng} ({新型|xīn xíng}), -{性|xìng} ({可能性|kě néng xìng}), -{率|lǜ} ({频率|pín lǜ}, {概率|gài lǜ}, {成功率|chéng gōng lǜ}).
- Numbers and chance: {乘|chéng} ({三|sān}{乘|chéng}{四|sì}{等于|děng yú}{十二|shí èr}), {概率|gài lǜ}, {相等|xiāng děng}, {相差|xiāng chà}, {对应|duì yìng}, {图表|tú biǎo}.
- The screen: {窗口|chuāng kǒu}, {浏览器|liú lǎn qì}, {文档|wén dàng}, {版本|bǎn běn}, {图像|tú xiàng}; doing: {点击|diǎn jī}, {粘贴|zhān tiē}, {扫描|sǎo miáo}, {查询|chá xún}, {压缩|yā suō}, {转换|zhuǎn huàn}, {传输|chuán shū}, {生成|shēng chéng}, {提取|tí qǔ}; networks:
  {联网|lián wǎng}, {下线|xià xiàn}, {链接|liàn jiē}, {流量|liú liàng}, {远程|yuǎn chéng}, {实时|shí shí}, {中断|zhōng duàn}; AI: {人工智能|rén gōng zhì néng}, {识别|shí bié}, {模拟|mó nǐ}, {辅助|fǔ zhù}, {借助|jiè zhù}, {验证|yàn zhèng}, {精准|jīng zhǔn}, {清晰|qīng xī}.
- New characters: {捷|jié} {辅|fǔ}✎ {踪|zōng} {攻|gōng}✎ {幻|huàn}✎ {链|liàn} {拟|nǐ}✎ {晰|xī} {讯|xùn}✎ {粘|zhān}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Space, sea and the planet
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson goes up into space and out to sea. {王芳|Wáng Fāng} and {李明|Lǐ Míng} take a boat to an island for the
weekend, and the reading is a piece of popular science about the moon: why we only ever see one
side of it. You'll learn:

- **{一同|yì tóng}** (together: written) and the pattern **{一时|yì shí}…{一时|yì shí}…** (now…, now…);
- the measure words **{艘|sōu}** (for ships) and **{株|zhū}** (for plants), and how {船只|chuán zhī} counts;
- **{结|jiē}** jiē and **{结果|jiē guǒ}** jiē guǒ, "to bear fruit", beside {结果|jié guǒ} jié guǒ "a result" (HSK 4), and **{露|lù}** lù, dew
  (lesson 23 brings {露|lòu} lòu);
- the words of space ({太空|tài kōng}, {月球|yuè qiú}, {轨道|guǐ dào}, {运行|yùn xíng}, {探索|tàn suǒ}), the poles ({北极|běi jí}, {南极洲|Nán jí zhōu}), the coast ({海岸|hǎi àn}, {港口|gǎng kǒu}, {码头|mǎ tou}, {岛|dǎo},
  {沿海|yán hǎi}, {海拔|hǎi bá}), water ({漂|piāo}, {浮|fú}, {渡|dù}, {水流|shuǐ liú}, {水面|shuǐ miàn}), the weather ({晴朗|qíng lǎng}, {潮湿|cháo shī}, {干燥|gān zào}, {彩虹|cǎi hóng}) and describing the natural
  world ({广阔|guǎng kuò}, {神奇|shén qí}, {构造|gòu zào}, {形态|xíng tài}, {密度|mì dù}, {垂直|chuí zhí}, {弯曲|wān qū}, {延伸|yán shēn}, {覆盖|fù gài}).

The module's retelling task is near the end.

## {一同|yì tóng}: together (written)

{一同|yì tóng} is a written {一起|yì qǐ}: it goes before the verb and says that people do something together.

{这|zhè}{次|cì}{会议|huì yì}，{两|liǎng}{家|jiā}{公司|gōng sī}{的|de}{经理|jīng lǐ}{一同|yì tóng}{参加|cān jiā}。 — The managers of both companies will attend the meeting together.

{请|qǐng}{大家|dà jiā}{明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{在|zài}{码头|mǎ tou}{集合|jí hé}，{一同|yì tóng}{出发|chū fā}。 — Please gather at the pier at eight tomorrow morning, and we'll set off together.

In notices, reports and formal invitations you'll see {一同|yì tóng}; in chat, say {一起|yì qǐ} ({明天|míng tiān}{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{吧|ba}). {一同|yì tóng}
is read yì tóng: {一|yī} before a second tone.

## {一时|yì shí}…{一时|yì shí}…: now…, now…

{一时|yì shí} (for a moment: lesson 25's word) used twice describes something that keeps changing, from one
state to another and back:

{海|hǎi}{上|shàng}{的|de}{天气|tiān qì}{一时|yì shí}{晴|qíng}{一时|yì shí}{雨|yǔ}，{谁|shéi}{也|yě}{说|shuō}{不|bu}{准|zhǔn}。 — At sea the weather is sunny one moment and rainy the next: nobody can tell.

{他|tā}{一时|yì shí}{说|shuō}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{一时|yì shí}{又|yòu}{说|shuō}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{了|le}。 — One minute he says he wants to go, the next he says he doesn't.

Each {一时|yì shí} is followed by an adjective or a verb phrase, and the two are usually opposites ({晴|qíng} and
{雨|yǔ}, {想|xiǎng}{去|qù} and {不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}). The pattern is a little written; in speech, {一会儿|yí huìr}…{一会儿|yí huìr}… does the same job
({一会儿|yí huìr}{晴|qíng}{一会儿|yí huìr}{雨|yǔ}).

## Ships and plants: {艘|sōu} and {株|zhū}

| Measure word | For | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {艘|sōu} sōu | ships and large boats | {一|yì}{艘|sōu}{轮船|lún chuán}, {两|liǎng}{艘|sōu}{船|chuán} |
| {株|zhū} zhū | plants, trees (written) | {一|yì}{株|zhū}{小|xiǎo}{树|shù}, {几|jǐ}{株|zhū}{花|huā} |

- {艘|sōu} is for ships; a small boat in speech is often {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{船|chuán} or {一|yì}{只|zhī}{船|chuán}.
- {株|zhū} is written: in a report on a garden or a farm ({这里|zhè lǐ}{种|zhòng}{了|le}{三百|sān bǎi}{株|zhū}{苹果|píng guǒ}{树|shù}). In speech, trees are {棵|kē} ({一|yì}{棵|kē}{树|shù},
  HSK 4).
- {船只|chuán zhī} (vessels, shipping) is a collective word, like {车辆|chē liàng}: on its own it means ships in general
  ({来往|lái wǎng}{的|de}{船只|chuán zhī}{很|hěn}{多|duō}, there's a lot of shipping). It never takes {个|gè}: ~~{三|sān}{个|gè}{船只|chuán zhī}~~ is wrong. News reports
  count it with {艘|sōu} ({三|sān}{艘|sōu}{船只|chuán zhī}); in speech, say {三|sān}{艘|sōu}{船|chuán} or {三|sān}{条|tiáo}{船|chuán}.

## {结|jiē} jiē and {结果|jiē guǒ} jiē guǒ: to bear fruit

{结|jié} jié (to tie; to form, HSK 5) and {结果|jié guǒ} jié guǒ (a result, HSK 4) have a second reading, jiē, for
plants:

{这|zhè}{株|zhū}{苹果|píng guǒ}{树|shù}{种|zhòng}{了|le}{三|sān}{年|nián}，{今年|jīn nián}{终于|zhōng yú}{结果|jiē guǒ}{了|le}。 — This apple tree was planted three years ago, and this year it finally bore fruit.

{树|shù}{上|shàng}{结|jiē}{了|le}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{苹果|píng guǒ}。 — The tree is full of apples.

{结|jiē} jiē takes the fruit as its object ({结|jiē}{苹果|píng guǒ}, {结|jiē}{了|le}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{苹果|píng guǒ}); {结果|jiē guǒ} jiē guǒ takes none ({树|shù}{结果|jiē guǒ}{了|le}). Read the
sentence for the meaning: {结果|jiē guǒ} after a plant is jiē guǒ; {结果|jié guǒ} at the start of a clause is jié guǒ ({结果|jié guǒ}，
{我们|wǒ men}{没|méi}{赶上|gǎn shàng}{船|chuán}: as a result, we missed the boat).

## {露|lù} lù: dew; to show

{露|lù} lù is dew, more often {露水|lù shuǐ} in speech: {早上|zǎo shang}，{草|cǎo}{上|shàng}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{露水|lù shuǐ} (in the morning the grass is wet with dew).
As a verb, {露|lù} lù is "to show, to come into view", usually with {出|chū} or a direction complement:

{云|yún}{散|sàn}{了|le}，{月亮|yuè liang}{露|lù}{了|le}{出来|chū lái}。 — The clouds cleared and the moon came out.

{露|lù} has a second reading, {露|lòu}, in everyday phrases about showing yourself ({露面|lòu miàn}, to show your face):
that's lesson 23's word. {散|sàn} here is sàn (to disperse: lesson 13).

## Words for space

{太空|tài kōng} (outer space), {月球|yuè qiú} (the moon: the astronomer's word; {月亮|yuè liang} is the everyday one), {天文|tiān wén} (astronomy:
{天|tiān}{文学|wén xué}, {天文台|tiān wén tái}), {轨道|guǐ dào} (an orbit; a track: {地铁|dì tiě}{的|de}{轨道|guǐ dào}), {运行|yùn xíng} (to move along a path; to run: {月球|yuè qiú}{绕|rào}{着|zhe}{地球|dì qiú}{运行|yùn xíng};
{系统|xì tǒng}{运行|yùn xíng}{正常|zhèng cháng}), {航空|háng kōng} (aviation; by air: {航空|háng kōng}{公司|gōng sī}, {航空|háng kōng}{信|xìn}), {探索|tàn suǒ} (to explore: {探索|tàn suǒ}{太空|tài kōng}, {探索|tàn suǒ}{新|xīn}{的|de}{方法|fāng fǎ}), {落地|luò dì} (to land,
touch down: {飞机|fēi jī}{安全|ān quán}{落地|luò dì}{了|le}). {太空|tài kōng} is outer space; {天空|tiān kōng} (HSK 4) is the sky you see.

The poles: {北极|běi jí} (the North Pole, the Arctic), {南极洲|Nán jí zhōu} (Antarctica: the continent), {两极|liǎng jí} (the two poles;
also two extremes).

## Words for the sea and the coast

**The coast.** {海岸|hǎi àn} (the coast), {岸|àn} (a bank, a shore: {河|hé}{岸|àn}, {上|shàng}{岸|àn}), {两岸|liǎng àn} (both banks of a river:
{长江|Cháng Jiāng}{两岸|liǎng àn}), {沿海|yán hǎi} (coastal: {沿海|yán hǎi}{城市|chéng shì}, {沿海|yán hǎi}{一带|yí dài}), {一带|yí dài} (the area around: {这|zhè}{一带|yí dài}, {北京|Běi jīng}{一带|yí dài}), {港口|gǎng kǒu} (a port), {码头|mǎ tou}
(a pier, a wharf), {岛|dǎo} (an island), {海拔|hǎi bá} (height above sea level: {海拔|hǎi bá}{三千|sān qiān}{米|mǐ}), {风光|fēng guāng} (scenery: {海|hǎi}{边|biān}{风光|fēng guāng}).

**On the water.** {海面|hǎi miàn} / {水面|shuǐ miàn} (the surface of the sea / of the water), {海域|hǎi yù} (sea area, waters), {水流|shuǐ liú}
(a current: {水流|shuǐ liú}{很|hěn}{急|jí}, the current is strong), {轮船|lún chuán} (a steamship, a ship), {船只|chuán zhī} (shipping, vessels), {渡|dù} (to
cross water: {渡|dù}{河|hé}, {渡|dù}{海|hǎi}; also to get through a time: {过渡|guò dù}, lesson 21), {漂|piāo} (to float on or drift in
water: {一|yì}{只|zhī}{小|xiǎo}{船|chuán}{在|zài}{海面|hǎi miàn}{上|shàng}{漂|piāo}{着|zhe}), {浮|fú} (to float; to rise to the surface: {木头|mù tou}{会|huì}{浮|fú}{在|zài}{水|shuǐ}{上|shàng}), {飘|piāo} (to float in the
air, to flutter: {天上|tiān shàng}{飘|piāo}{着|zhe}{白|bái}{云|yún}). {漂|piāo} and {飘|piāo} are both piāo: {漂|piāo} has 氵 (water), {飘|piāo} has {风|fēng} (wind).

**Catching and carrying.** {捕|bǔ} (to catch: written: {捕|bǔ}{鱼|yú}, to fish), {捉|zhuō} (to catch, by hand: {捉|zhuō}{鱼|yú}, {捉|zhuō}{小|xiǎo}{鸟|niǎo}),
{牵|qiān} (to lead by the hand or a rope: {牵|qiān}{着|zhe}{孩子|hái zi}{的|de}{手|shǒu}, {牵|qiān}{着|zhe}{狗|gǒu}), {顶|dǐng} (the top: {山顶|shān dǐng}, the mountain top; to carry on the head),
{挖|wā} (to dig), {钻|zuān} (to drill; to get into: {钻|zuān}{进|jìn}{水|shuǐ}{里|lǐ}), {砍|kǎn} (to chop: {砍|kǎn}{树|shù}).

## Words for describing the natural world

**Weather.** {晴朗|qíng lǎng} (sunny and clear), {彩虹|cǎi hóng} (a rainbow), {干燥|gān zào} (dry: {北方|běi fāng}{的|de}{冬天|dōng tiān}{很|hěn}{干燥|gān zào}), {潮湿|cháo shī} (damp, humid),
{湿度|shī dù} (humidity), {常年|cháng nián} (all year round: {这里|zhè lǐ}{常年|cháng nián}{下雨|xià yǔ}).

**How things are.** {广阔|guǎng kuò} (vast, wide), {迷人|mí rén} (charming, enchanting), {神奇|shén qí} (magical, amazing), {天然|tiān rán} (natural:
{天然|tiān rán}{的|de}{湖|hú}), {万物|wàn wù} (all things), {物体|wù tǐ} (an object, a body), {元素|yuán sù} (an element), {形态|xíng tài} (form, shape), {构造|gòu zào} (structure;
how something is put together: {地球|dì qiú}{的|de}{构造|gòu zào}), {密度|mì dù} (density), {密|mì} (dense, close together; also secret: {这|zhè}{片|piàn}
{树林|shù lín}{很|hěn}{密|mì}), {清|qīng} (clear, clean: {水|shuǐ}{很|hěn}{清|qīng}), {坚硬|jiān yìng} (hard, solid), {化石|huà shí} (a fossil), {进化|jìn huà} (evolution; to evolve).

**Measuring.** {测量|cè liáng} (to measure, to survey), {精确|jīng què} (precise, exact: of numbers and measurements), {垂直|chuí zhí}
(vertical; perpendicular), {方位|fāng wèi} (a direction, a position), {弯曲|wān qū} (winding, bent), {延伸|yán shēn} (to extend, stretch:
{这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{路|lù}{一直|yì zhí}{延伸|yán shēn}{到|dào}{海|hǎi}{边|biān}), {覆盖|fù gài} (to cover: {雪|xuě}{覆盖|fù gài}{了|le}{整个|zhěng gè}{山顶|shān dǐng}).

{精确|jīng què} and {精准|jīng zhǔn} (lesson 16) are both "precise": {精确|jīng què} is of measurements and numbers ({精确|jīng què}{的|de}{数字|shù zì}), {精准|jīng zhǔn} of
hitting a target ({精准|jīng zhǔn}{定位|dìng wèi}). {天然|tiān rán} is "natural" as made by nature ({天然气|tiān rán qì}, natural gas: lesson 18); {自然|zì rán}
(HSK 3) is nature, or natural in manner ({说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{自然|zì rán}).

## Characters

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Traditional | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 岸 ✎ | bank, shore | àn | 山 | 8 | 岸 | {岸|àn}, {海岸|hǎi àn}, {两岸|liǎng àn} |
| 虹 | rainbow | hóng | 虫 | 9 | 虹 | {彩虹|cǎi hóng} |
| 捕 | catch | bǔ | 扌 | 10 | 捕 | {捕|bǔ} |
| 岛 ✎ | island | dǎo | 山 | 7 | 島 | {岛|dǎo} |
| 顶 ✎ | top | dǐng | 页 | 8 | 頂 | {顶|dǐng}, {山顶|shān dǐng} (lesson 18) |

| 港 | harbour | gǎng | 氵 | 12 | 港 | {港口|gǎng kǒu} |
| 轨 ✎ | track | guǐ | 车 | 6 | 軌 | {轨道|guǐ dào} |

| 拔 ✎ | pull out | bá | 扌 | 8 | 拔 | {海拔|hǎi bá}, {选拔|xuǎn bá} (lesson 29) |

In traditional, {岛|dǎo} is 島 (10 strokes: the top of 鳥, a bird, over {山|shān}), {顶|dǐng} 頂 (11, with 頁), {轨|guǐ} 軌 (9,

  drifted. {虹|hóng} hóng is {虫|chóng} + {工|gōng}, the hóng of {红|hóng}. {顶|dǐng} dǐng is {丁|dīng} dīng + {页|yè}: {丁|dīng} also gives {订|dìng} dìng ({预订|yù dìng}) and
  {灯|dēng} dēng (a lamp). {燥|zào} zào has {火|huǒ} (fire: dry heat) and the sound part of {澡|zǎo} zǎo ({洗澡|xǐ zǎo}). {朗|lǎng} lǎng is {良|liáng} liáng + {月|yuè}:

- **{顶|dǐng}** (8): {丁|dīng} on the left, then {页|yè} (six strokes).

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Why we always see only one side of the moon (the title).
2. Because the moon takes about 27 days both to go round the Earth and to turn once on its axis:
   the two times are equal ({两|liǎng}{个|gè}{时间|shí jiān}{相等|xiāng děng}).
3. Because there's no wind on the moon ({因为|yīn wèi}{没有|méi yǒu}{风|fēng}).

   it still has much to discover: a conclusion that looks forward.

"**Why do we only ever see one side of the moon?** On a clear night, look up and the moon is always
so enchanting. But have you ever noticed that whether you're in Beijing or Shanghai, this year or ten
years ago, the pattern on the moon's surface always seems the same? It isn't an illusion. The moon
always turns the same face towards the Earth.

The moon is the Earth's only natural satellite. It's on average about 380,000 kilometres from the
Earth, and takes about twenty-seven days to go round it once. At the same time it turns on its own
axis, and one turn also takes about twenty-seven days. The two times are equal, so the side facing
the Earth is always the same. Scientists think this is no accident: long ago the moon turned much
faster than now, and the Earth's gravity gradually slowed it down until it became what it is today.

The other side of the moon, the 'far side', can't be seen from the ground. Not until 1959, when a
probe flew behind the moon and took photographs, did people see what it looked like for the first
time. In 2019 a Chinese probe landed successfully on the far side: the first time a probe had made a
soft landing there.

Conditions on the moon are very different from the Earth's. There's almost no air and no flowing
water or wind, so there's no weather, still less a rainbow. Because there's no air, the sky on the moon is always
black, and you can see the stars even in the daytime. There, a person weighs only about a sixth of what they weigh
on the Earth, and a gentle jump takes you a long way up. In the daytime, in sunlight, the
temperature can reach more than 120 degrees; at night it can fall to below minus 170. The surface is
covered with a layer of fine grey dust and stones of every size; because there's no wind, the
footprints astronauts left many years ago may still be there today.

Although the moon is far away, it affects our lives every day. The sea rises and falls regularly
every day: that's the tide, and it's caused mainly by the moon's gravity. People living along the
coast learned long ago to judge from the moon's changes when it was safest to go out to sea.

Interestingly, the moon is moving away from the Earth year by year, by a few centimetres each year.
Of course the change is tiny: it takes a very, very long time before there's any obvious difference.

From ancient times to today, people have always explored the moon. People long ago looked at it, wrote
poems and told many beautiful stories about it; in 1969 astronauts set foot on the moon for the
first time; today scientists are still studying its structure and form, wanting to know how it came
into being. In recent years more probes have flown to the moon, and some have brought back its rocks and
soil. Scientists hope that one day people will be able to live and work on the moon for long periods. We know more and more about the moon, but it still has many amazing things waiting to be
discovered."

(The figures are NASA's: an average distance of 384,400 km, and about 127 °C in sunlight and −173 °C
in the dark.)

- {漂|piāo} piāo, {飘|piāo} piāo, {票|piào} piào: the same syllable, two tones.
- {一同|yì tóng} yì tóng, {一带|yí dài} yí dài: {一|yī} changes before the second tone (yì) and the fourth (yí).
- {潮湿|cháo shī} cháo shī, {湿度|shī dù} shī dù: sh; {垂直|chuí zhí} chuí zhí: ch, then zh.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{三|sān}{个|gè}{船只|chuán zhī}~~: {船只|chuán zhī} is collective and never takes {个|gè}. Say {三|sān}{艘|sōu}{船|chuán} / {三|sān}{条|tiáo}{船|chuán} (in news, {三|sān}{艘|sōu}{船只|chuán zhī}), or {船只|chuán zhī}{很|hěn}{多|duō}.
- {太空|tài kōng} (outer space) is not {天空|tiān kōng} (the sky): {天空|tiān kōng}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{卫星|wèi xīng} is less accurate than {太空|tài kōng}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{卫星|wèi xīng}.
- {漂|piāo} is on water, {飘|piāo} in the air: {白|bái}{云|yún}{在|zài}{天上|tiān shàng}{飘|piāo}, {树|shù}{叶|yè}{在|zài}{水|shuǐ}{上|shàng}{漂|piāo}.
- {一同|yì tóng} is written: in a chat, {我们|wǒ men}{一同|yì tóng}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba} sounds stiff; {一起|yì qǐ} is usual.
- {精确|jīng què} is for numbers and measurements: {精确|jīng què}{的|de}{时间|shí jiān}, {精确|jīng què}{地|de}{测量|cè liáng}; for a translation, {准确|zhǔn què}{的|de}{翻译|fān yì} is the usual word.
