## Key points

- {一同|yì tóng} (written {一起|yì qǐ}): {一同|yì tóng}{出发|chū fā}. {一时|yì shí}…{一时|yì shí}… (now…, now…): {一时|yì shí}{晴|qíng}{一时|yì shí}{雨|yǔ}; in speech {一会儿|yí huìr}…{一会儿|yí huìr}….
- Measure words {艘|sōu} (ships) and {株|zhū} (plants, written); {船只|chuán zhī} never takes {个|gè}.
- {结|jiē} jiē / {结果|jiē guǒ} jiē guǒ (to bear fruit); {结果|jié guǒ} jié guǒ (a result). {露|lù} lù: dew; to show ({露|lù}{了|le}{出来|chū lái}).
- Space: {太空|tài kōng}, {月球|yuè qiú}, {天文|tiān wén}, {轨道|guǐ dào}, {运行|yùn xíng}, {航空|háng kōng}, {探索|tàn suǒ}, {落地|luò dì}; the coast: {海岸|hǎi àn}, {岸|àn}, {两岸|liǎng àn}, {沿海|yán hǎi}, {一带|yí dài}, {港口|gǎng kǒu}, {码头|mǎ tou}, {岛|dǎo}, {海拔|hǎi bá};
  water: {海面|hǎi miàn}, {水面|shuǐ miàn}, {海域|hǎi yù}, {水流|shuǐ liú}, {渡|dù}, {漂|piāo}, {浮|fú}; weather: {晴朗|qíng lǎng}, {彩虹|cǎi hóng}, {干燥|gān zào}, {潮湿|cháo shī}, {湿度|shī dù}; describing: {广阔|guǎng kuò}, {神奇|shén qí}, {形态|xíng tài},
  {构造|gòu zào}, {密度|mì dù}, {垂直|chuí zhí}, {弯曲|wān qū}, {延伸|yán shēn}, {覆盖|fù gài}.
- New characters: {岸|àn}✎ {虹|hóng} {捕|bǔ} {岛|dǎo}✎ {顶|dǐng}✎ {垂|chuí} {渡|dù} {浮|fú} {港|gǎng} {轨|guǐ}✎ {拔|bá}✎ {覆|fù} {燥|zào} {阔|kuò} {砍|kǎn} {飘|piāo} {牵|qiān} {朗|lǎng} {探|tàn} {挖|wā}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Energy, ecology and the land
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is a heavy word lesson: about eighty words for energy, the environment and the land. {大卫|Dà wèi}
(David) and {白涛|Bái Tāo} (Bai Tao) plan a "new energy" study trip for British students, and the reading is a
report on a solar power station on a high plateau, where sheep graze under the panels. It's also the
base of the module's "sentence for the gap" question. You'll learn:

- no new grammar, but a review of the ways to say **purpose** ({为了|wèi le}, {以便|yǐ biàn}) and **cause** ({由于|yóu yú}…{因此|yīn cǐ}), which
  reports on energy and the environment use all the time, and the adverb **{净|jìng}** (nothing but);
- the words of energy ({能源|néng yuán}, {新能源|xīn néng yuán}, {太阳能|tài yáng néng}, {风力|fēng lì}, {发电|fā diàn}, {石油|shí yóu}, {煤|méi}, {天然气|tiān rán qì}, {二氧化碳|èr yǎng huà tàn}, {低碳|dī tàn}, {节能|jié néng}, {排放|pái fàng}), of water
  and heating ({自来水|zì lái shuǐ}, {饮用水|yǐn yòng shuǐ}, {污水|wū shuǐ}, {水库|shuǐ kù}, {暖气|nuǎn qì}, {热水器|rè shuǐ qì}), of looking after the environment ({生态|shēng tài}, {治理|zhì lǐ}, {监测|jiān cè},
  {绿化|lǜ huà}, {循环|xún huán}, {再生|zài shēng}), of science ({固体|gù tǐ}, {液体|yè tǐ}, {气体|qì tǐ}, {氧气|yǎng qì}, {合成|hé chéng}, {混合|hùn hé}), and of the land and its animals ({草原|cǎo yuán}, {高原|gāo yuán},
  {山坡|shān pō}, {野生|yě shēng}, {狼|láng}, {蜜蜂|mì fēng}, {蚂蚁|mǎ yǐ}, {繁殖|fán zhí}).

The less central words (animals, the states of matter) are in tables: learn them for reading.

## Purpose: {为了|wèi le} and {以便|yǐ biàn}

Reports on energy explain why things are done. Two ways you'll see most:

- **{为了|wèi le}** (HSK 3) comes first and gives the aim; the main clause says what's done:
  {为了|wèi le}{减少|jiǎn shǎo}{排放|pái fàng}，{很|hěn}{多|duō}{城市|chéng shì}{开始|kāi shǐ}{发展|fā zhǎn}{新能源|xīn néng yuán}。 — To cut emissions, many cities have started developing new energy.
- **{以便|yǐ biàn}** (so that, in order to: written; lesson 27's word) comes in the second clause, after what's
  done:
  {发电站|fā diàn zhàn}{建|jiàn}{了|le}{储存|chǔ cún}{电能|diàn néng}{的|de}{设备|shè bèi}，{以便|yǐ biàn}{晚上|wǎn shang}{也|yě}{能|néng}{供应|gōng yìng}{电力|diàn lì}。 — The power station has built equipment to store electricity, so that it can supply power at night too.

{为了|wèi le} puts the aim first; {以便|yǐ biàn} adds it after, and belongs in written texts (reports, notices,
instructions). In speech you'd say …，{这样|zhè yàng}{晚上|wǎn shang}{也|yě}{能|néng}{用|yòng}{电|diàn}.

## Cause and result: {由于|yóu yú}…{因此|yīn cǐ}

{由于|yóu yú} (because of, written: HSK 4) gives the cause; {因此|yīn cǐ} (therefore) or {所以|suǒ yǐ} introduces the result:

{由于|yóu yú}{这里|zhè lǐ}{常年|cháng nián}{风|fēng}{大|dà}、{雨|yǔ}{少|shǎo}，{因此|yīn cǐ}{地|dì}{上|shàng}{的|de}{草|cǎo}{越|yuè}{来|lái}{越|yuè}{少|shǎo}。 — Because it's windy and dry here all year, the grass has been getting sparser and sparser.

{由于|yóu yú} can also come before a noun: {由于|yóu yú}{天气|tiān qì}{的|de}{原因|yuán yīn}，{发电量|fā diàn liàng}{减少|jiǎn shǎo}{了|le} (because of the weather, the power output
fell). Don't use {由于|yóu yú} with {因此|yīn cǐ} *and* {所以|suǒ yǐ} together; and in speech, {因为|yīn wèi}…{所以|suǒ yǐ}… is more natural.

## {净|jìng}: clean; net; nothing but

{净|jìng} is first an adjective, "clean" (the {净|jìng} of {干净|gān jìng}, HSK 2): {把|bǎ}{桌子|zhuō zi}{擦|cā}{净|jìng} (wipe the table clean; written).
It's also "net", after deductions: {净重|jìng zhòng} (net weight), {净|jìng}{收入|shōu rù} (net income). And in speech it's an adverb,
"nothing but, only": often a complaint:

{你|nǐ}{别|bié}{净说|jìng shuō}{废话|fèi huà}，{快|kuài}{说|shuō}{正事|zhèng shì}{吧|ba}！ — Stop talking nonsense and get to the point!

{这|zhè}{几|jǐ}{天|tiān}{净|jìng}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{衣服|yī fu}{都|dōu}{晾|liàng}{不|bu}{干|gān}。 — It's done nothing but rain these last few days: the washing won't dry.

{净|jìng} as an adverb is spoken and a little critical: compare {只是|zhǐ shì} (neutral) and {都|dōu} ({这|zhè}{几|jǐ}{天|tiān}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{下雨|xià yǔ}).

## Words for energy

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {能源|néng yuán} | energy (sources) | {新能源|xīn néng yuán} | new (renewable) energy |
| {太阳能|tài yáng néng} | solar energy | {风力|fēng lì} | wind power; wind force |
| {电力|diàn lì} | electric power | {发电|fā diàn} | to generate electricity |
| {电源|diàn yuán} | a power supply; a socket | {能量|néng liàng} | energy (physics; also a person's) |
| {动力|dòng lì} | motive power; motivation | {燃料|rán liào} | fuel |
| {石油|shí yóu} | oil, petroleum | {煤|méi} | coal |
| {天然气|tiān rán qì} | natural gas | {二氧化碳|èr yǎng huà tàn} | carbon dioxide |
| {低碳|dī tàn} | low-carbon | {节能|jié néng} | to save energy; energy-saving |
| {排放|pái fàng} | to emit; emissions | {消耗|xiāo hào} | to consume, use up |
| {短缺|duǎn quē} | a shortage; to be short of | {供应|gōng yìng} / {供给|gōng jǐ} | to supply; supply |
| {输送|shū sòng} | to transport, deliver (power, oil) | {管道|guǎn dào} | a pipe, a pipeline |
| {储存|chǔ cún} | to store (goods, energy, water) | {持久|chí jiǔ} | lasting |

- {能源|néng yuán} is energy as a resource ({能源|néng yuán}{短缺|duǎn quē}, an energy shortage); {能量|néng liàng} is energy as an amount (in physics,
  in food, or a person's: {他|tā}{总是|zǒng shì}{充满|chōng mǎn}{能量|néng liàng}, he's always full of energy).
- {供应|gōng yìng} and {供给|gōng jǐ} are close: {供应|gōng yìng} is the everyday one ({供应|gōng yìng}{电力|diàn lì}, {供应|gōng yìng}{热|rè}{水|shuǐ}); {供给|gōng jǐ} is more formal and economic
  ({供给|gōng jǐ}{不足|bù zú}, supply falls short). {供给|gōng jǐ} is gōng jǐ: {给|jǐ} is jǐ here, not gěi.
- {储存|chǔ cún} and {存储|cún chǔ} (lesson 16): {储存|chǔ cún} is to store things ({粮食|liáng shi}, {能源|néng yuán}, {水|shuǐ}); {存储|cún chǔ} is mostly for data.

## Water, heating and light

{自来水|zì lái shuǐ} (tap water), {饮用水|yǐn yòng shuǐ} (drinking water), {污水|wū shuǐ} (waste water, sewage), {水库|shuǐ kù} (a reservoir), {暖气|nuǎn qì} (central
heating; a radiator), {暖|nuǎn} (warm: {天气|tiān qì}{暖|nuǎn}{了|le}, {暖和|nuǎn huo} is HSK 3), {热水器|rè shuǐ qì} (a water heater), {照明|zhào míng} (lighting), {发光|fā guāng}
(to give off light, to shine), {发电|fā diàn} (to generate electricity), {调节|tiáo jié} (to regulate, adjust: {调节|tiáo jié}{温度|wēn dù}), {喷|pēn} (to
spray, to spout: {喷|pēn}{水|shuǐ}), {散发|sàn fā} (to give off: a smell, heat: {散发|sàn fā}{出|chū}{香|xiāng}{味|wèi}), {融化|róng huà} (to melt: {雪|xuě}{融化|róng huà}{了|le}), {灰尘|huī chén}
(dust), {清理|qīng lǐ} (to clear up, clean out), {清洁|qīng jié} (clean; to clean: {清洁|qīng jié}{工|gōng}, a cleaner), {净|jìng} (clean; net; only).

## Looking after the environment

{生态|shēng tài} (ecology: {生态|shēng tài}{环境|huán jìng}), {治理|zhì lǐ} (to bring under control, to manage: {治理|zhì lǐ}{污染|wū rǎn}, {治理|zhì lǐ}{河流|hé liú}), {监测|jiān cè} (to monitor:
{监测|jiān cè}{空气|kōng qì}{质量|zhì liàng}), {绿化|lǜ huà} (to plant trees and grass, greening: {城市|chéng shì}{绿化|lǜ huà}), {循环|xún huán} (a cycle; to circulate: {循环|xún huán}{使用|shǐ yòng},
to reuse), {再生|zài shēng} (to regenerate; recycled: {再生|zài shēng}{纸|zhǐ}, recycled paper; {可|kě}{再生|zài shēng}{能源|néng yuán}, renewable energy), {有机|yǒu jī}
(organic: {有机|yǒu jī}{蔬菜|shū cài}), {周期|zhōu qī} (a cycle, a period: {生长|shēng zhǎng}{周期|zhōu qī}), {减弱|jiǎn ruò} (to weaken: {风力|fēng lì}{减弱|jiǎn ruò}{了|le}), {遍地|biàn dì} (all over the
place: {遍地|biàn dì}{是|shì}{垃圾|lā jī}).

{治理|zhì lǐ} and {管理|guǎn lǐ} (HSK 4): {治理|zhì lǐ} is to tackle a problem (a polluted river, desertification); {管理|guǎn lǐ} is to run
something (a company, a park).

## The science of matter

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {固体|gù tǐ} | a solid | {液体|yè tǐ} | a liquid |
| {气体|qì tǐ} | a gas | {氧气|yǎng qì} | oxygen |
| {合成|hé chéng} | to synthesise; synthetic, composite | {混合|hùn hé} | to mix; a mixture |
| {还原|huán yuán} | to restore (to the original state); reduction (chemistry) | | |

{冰|bīng}{融化|róng huà}{以后|yǐ hòu}{变成|biàn chéng}{液体|yè tǐ}，{水|shuǐ}{烧开|shāo kāi}{以后|yǐ hòu}{变成|biàn chéng}{气体|qì tǐ}。 — Ice melts into a liquid, and boiling water turns into a gas.
{还原|huán yuán} is huán yuán ({还|hái} huán, to return). {合成|hé chéng} is also "composite" ({合成|hé chéng}{照片|zhào piàn}, a composite photo).

## The land and its animals

**The land.** {草原|cǎo yuán} (grassland), {高原|gāo yuán} (a plateau), {大地|dà dì} (the earth, the land), {地形|dì xíng} (terrain, landform),
{地质|dì zhì} (geology), {坡|pō} / {山坡|shān pō} (a slope / a hillside), {山顶|shān dǐng} (a mountaintop), {山峰|shān fēng} (a mountain peak), {沟|gōu} (a ditch, a
gully), {井|jǐng} (a well: {一|yì}{口|kǒu}{井|jǐng}), {泥|ní} (mud), {野外|yě wài} (the open country, the wild: {野外|yě wài}{活动|huó dòng}), {野生|yě shēng} (wild: {野生|yě shēng}{动物|dòng wù}), {野|yě}
(wild; untamed: {野|yě}{花|huā}, wild flowers; {这|zhè}{孩子|hái zi}{太|tài}{野|yě}{了|le}, this child is too wild).

| Animal | Meaning | Animal | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {狼|láng} | a wolf | {狮子|shī zi} | a lion |
| {老鼠|lǎo shǔ} | a mouse, a rat | {鲨鱼|shā yú} | a shark |
| {乌龟|wū guī} | a tortoise, a turtle | {蜜蜂|mì fēng} | a bee |
| {蚂蚁|mǎ yǐ} | an ant | {繁殖|fán zhí} | to breed, reproduce |

{野生|yě shēng} and {天然|tiān rán} (lesson 17): {野生|yě shēng} is of living things that grow or live without people ({野生|yě shēng}{动物|dòng wù}, {野生|yě shēng}{的|de}{花|huā});
{天然|tiān rán} is of anything made by nature ({天然气|tiān rán qì}, {天然|tiān rán}{的|de}{湖|hú}).

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Traditional | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 艘 | (for ships) | sōu | 舟 | 15 | 艘 | {艘|sōu} |
| 捉 | catch | zhuō | 扌 | 10 | 捉 | {捉|zhuō} |
| 钻 | drill; get into | zuān | 钅 | 10 | 鑽 | {钻|zuān} |
| 株 | (for plants) | zhū | 木 | 10 | 株 | {株|zhū} |
| 氧 | oxygen | yǎng | 气 | 10 | 氧 | {二氧化碳|èr yǎng huà tàn}, {氧气|yǎng qì} |
| 碳 | carbon | tàn | 石 | 14 | 碳 | {二氧化碳|èr yǎng huà tàn}, {低碳|dī tàn} |
| 殖 | breed | zhí | 歹 | 12 | 殖 | {繁殖|fán zhí} |
| 尘 ✎ | dust | chén | 小 | 6 | 塵 | {灰尘|huī chén} |
| 混 | mix | hùn | 氵 | 11 | 混 | {混合|hùn hé}, {混乱|hùn luàn} (lesson 19) |
| 井 ✎ | well | jǐng | 二 | 4 | 井 | {井|jǐng} |

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Traditional | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 狼 | wolf | láng | 犭 | 10 | 狼 | {狼|láng} |
| 蚂 | (ant) | mǎ | 虫 | 9 | 螞 | {蚂蚁|mǎ yǐ} |
| 蚁 | ant | yǐ | 虫 | 9 | 蟻 | {蚂蚁|mǎ yǐ} |
| 煤 | coal | méi | 火 | 13 | 煤 | {煤|méi} |
| 蜜 | honey | mì | 虫 | 14 | 蜜 | {蜜蜂|mì fēng} |
| 蜂 | bee | fēng | 虫 | 13 | 蜂 | {蜜蜂|mì fēng} |
| 泥 ✎ | mud | ní | 氵 | 8 | 泥 | {泥|ní}, {水泥|shuǐ ní} (lesson 20) |
| 喷 | spray | pēn | 口 | 12 | 噴 | {喷|pēn} |
| 坡 ✎ | slope | pō | 土 | 8 | 坡 | {坡|pō}, {山坡|shān pō} |
| 鲨 | shark | shā | 鱼 | 15 | 鯊 | {鲨鱼|shā yú} |

The first four ({艘|sōu} {捉|zhuō} {钻|zuān} {株|zhū}) were in lesson 17's words. Seven characters in this lesson's words are
taught in lesson 19: {乌|wū} {龟|guī} ({乌龟|wū guī}), {狮|shī} ({狮子|shī zi}), {洁|jié} ({清洁|qīng jié}), {耗|hào} ({消耗|xiāo hào}), {循|xún} ({循环|xún huán}) and {野|yě} ({野外|yě wài}, {野生|yě shēng}, {野|yě}).

In traditional, {钻|zuān} is 鑽 (26 strokes: {金|jīn} + 贊), {尘|chén} 塵 (14: 鹿 over {土|tǔ}), {蚂|mǎ} 螞 (16: {虫|chóng} + 馬), {蚁|yǐ} 蟻 (19:
{虫|chóng} + 義), {喷|pēn} 噴 (15) and {鲨|shā} 鯊 (18: {沙|shā} over 魚).

**A new radical: {鱼|yú} (fish).** At the bottom of {鲨|shā} shā ({沙|shā} over {鱼|yú}: the sound and "fish"), and on the
left of {鲜|xiān} xiān (fresh, HSK 4); and it's the character {鱼|yú} itself. In traditional it's 魚, with four dots.

- **Sound parts.** {艘|sōu} sōu is 舟 (a boat) + {叟|sǒu} sǒu, the sound part of {搜|sōu} sōu ({搜索|sōu suǒ}). {株|zhū} zhū is {木|mù} + {朱|zhū} zhū: the
  family of {珠|zhū} zhū ({珍珠|zhēn zhū}, a pearl, lesson 22). {氧|yǎng} yǎng is {气|qì} (gas) + {羊|yáng} yáng, the sound of {样|yàng} yàng and {洋|yáng}
  yáng. {碳|tàn} tàn is {石|shí} + {炭|tàn} tàn (charcoal): the same sound. {殖|zhí} zhí is 歹 + {直|zhí} zhí, as in {植|zhí} zhí ({植物|zhí wù}) and {值|zhí}
  zhí: {直|zhí} gives zhí to all three. {煤|méi} méi is {火|huǒ} (fire) + {某|mǒu} mǒu, sound drifted to méi. {蜂|fēng} fēng is {虫|chóng} + 夆, the
  sound part of {峰|fēng} fēng ({山峰|shān fēng}, this lesson): a bee and a peak, said the same. {泥|ní} ní is 氵 + {尼|ní} ní (the sound
  of {呢|ne} ne, too). {坡|pō} pō is {土|tǔ} + {皮|pí} pí, the family of {破|pò} pò, {披|pī} pī (lesson 11) and {被|bèi} bèi. {蚂|mǎ} mǎ is {虫|chóng} + {马|mǎ}
  mǎ, and {蚁|yǐ} yǐ is {虫|chóng} + {义|yì} yì, the sound part of {议|yì} yì and {仪|yí} yí.

"**Grass grows under the solar panels.** On a plateau in the north-west, row upon row of blue solar
panels stand in neat lines, stretching further than the eye can see. This is a large solar power
station. Go closer and you'll notice something interesting: the ground under the panels is covered
in green grass, and flocks of sheep are slowly grazing on it.

A few years ago this place looked completely different. Because it's windy and dry here all year
round, the grass got sparser and sparser and much of the land turned to sand. Whenever the wind
blew there was sand and dust everywhere, and people nearby didn't even dare open their doors.

Then people realised that the sunshine here was plentiful and the land flat, ideal for solar power,
and they started building a power station. (1) Within a few years, tens of thousands of panels went up
over dozens of square kilometres. At the time many people worried: would such a big power station
make an ecology that was already poor even worse?

The result surprised everyone. The panels block some of the sun and wind, so moisture doesn't
evaporate so easily and the soil has become a little damper. To clear the dust off the panels, staff
wash them down regularly, and the water running onto the ground gives the grass more water too. (2)
Gradually the grass under the panels grew, and grew taller and taller. In some places people have
even planted vegetables under the panels.

But then a new problem came up: grass that grows too tall not only shades the panels and lowers
output, but when it dries out in autumn it catches fire very easily. Cutting it by machine would use
a lot of energy and labour. (3) How could the problem be solved cheaply and without wasting energy?
The station came up with an idea: ask the people nearby to drive their sheep under the panels to
graze. That way the grass doesn't grow too tall, the sheep eat well, and local incomes have risen.
People joke that the sheep 'go to work' at the power station every day. An old man who lives nearby
says: 'It used to be that whenever the wind blew, nothing would grow, and keeping sheep meant spending
a lot on fodder. Now the sheep graze under the panels every day and grow fast and healthy, and life's
much better for our family.'

Of course, it isn't all easy. Solar power depends heavily on the weather: at night and on cloudy days
output falls. (4) In winter, heavy snow covering the panels affects it too. So that people in the
cities have a steady supply, the station has built equipment to store electricity and sends it along
long power lines to cities in the east thousands of kilometres away. Besides, solar panels generally
last only twenty-odd years, and how to collect and recycle the old ones later is another problem to
be solved.

Experts think this example shows that developing new energy and protecting the ecology need not be
at odds. As long as it's well planned, one piece of land can generate power, grow grass and raise
sheep at the same time. (5) What this plateau has brought is not just electricity, but green."

  {供应|gōng yìng}, {输送|shū sòng}, {储存|chǔ cún}; water and heat: {自来水|zì lái shuǐ}, {饮用水|yǐn yòng shuǐ}, {污水|wū shuǐ}, {水库|shuǐ kù}, {暖气|nuǎn qì}, {热水器|rè shuǐ qì}; the environment: {生态|shēng tài}, {治理|zhì lǐ}, {监测|jiān cè}, {绿化|lǜ huà},
  {循环|xún huán}, {再生|zài shēng}, {有机|yǒu jī}; matter: {固体|gù tǐ}, {液体|yè tǐ}, {气体|qì tǐ}, {氧气|yǎng qì}, {合成|hé chéng}, {混合|hùn hé}; the land: {草原|cǎo yuán}, {高原|gāo yuán}, {山坡|shān pō}, {山峰|shān fēng}, {野外|yě wài}, {野生|yě shēng}.
- New characters: {艘|sōu} {捉|zhuō} {钻|zuān} {株|zhū} {氧|yǎng} {碳|tàn} {殖|zhí} {尘|chén}✎ {混|hùn} {井|jǐng}✎ {狼|láng} {蚂|mǎ} {蚁|yǐ} {煤|méi} {蜜|mì} {蜂|fēng} {泥|ní}✎ {喷|pēn} {坡|pō}✎ {鲨|shā}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Disasters and rescue
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about floods, storms, fires and the people who help. The reading is a news report on
a flood in a county town, and the dialogue is an interview with a volunteer who was there: the same
events told twice, once in the written style of the news and once in everyday speech. You'll learn:

- the adverbs of sudden change and of what's about to happen: **{顿时|dùn shí}** (at once: written), **{眼看|yǎn kàn}** (any
  moment now; to look on helplessly), **{接连|jiē lián}** (one after another), the measure word **{一阵|yí zhèn}** (a spell, a
  burst), and **{炸|zhà}** zhà (to explode) beside HSK 5's {炸|zhá} zhá (to deep-fry);
- the words of disasters ({灾害|zāi hài}, {灾难|zāi nàn}, {洪水|hóng shuǐ}, {旱灾|hàn zāi}, {火灾|huǒ zāi}, {台风|tái fēng}, {打雷|dǎ léi}, {闪电|shǎn diàn}), of rescue ({救援|jiù yuán}, {急救|jí jiù}, {消防|xiāo fáng}, {转移|zhuǎn yí}, {运送|yùn sòng},
  {重建|chóng jiàn}) and of suffering and fear ({遭受|zāo shòu}, {遭遇|zāo yù}, {伤亡|shāng wáng}, {恐惧|kǒng jù}, {吓|xià}, {饥饿|jī è}, {艰难|jiān nán});
- how the **same content** sounds in the two registers: {顿时|dùn shí} / {一下|yí xià}{子|zi}, {遭受|zāo shòu} / {受到|shòu dào}, {转移|zhuǎn yí} / {搬|bān}{到|dào}, {凌晨|líng chén} / {半夜|bàn yè}.

The module's four-photo story is near the end.

## {顿时|dùn shí}: at once, suddenly (written)

{顿时|dùn shí} says that a situation changed immediately, as a result of what came before. It describes the
past, mostly in written narrative:

{一|yì}{声|shēng}{巨响|jù xiǎng}，{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{顿时|dùn shí}{黑|hēi}{了|le}{下来|xià lái}。 — There was a huge bang, and the room went dark at once.

{听|tīng}{到|dào}{这个|zhè ge}{消息|xiāo xi}，{大家|dà jiā}{顿时|dùn shí}{安静|ān jìng}{了|le}。 — When they heard the news, everyone fell silent.

- {顿时|dùn shí} is for a change that happens *to* a situation or to people's feelings, not for an action you
  choose: ~~{我|wǒ}{顿时|dùn shí}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}~~ is wrong. For actions, use {立刻|lì kè} or {马上|mǎ shàng} ({我|wǒ}{立刻|lì kè}{去|qù}{了|le}{医院|yī yuàn}).
- It's never used for the future or in orders: ~~{你|nǐ}{顿时|dùn shí}{过来|guò lái}~~. Say {马上|mǎ shàng}{过来|guò lái}.
- In speech, {一下|yí xià}{子|zi} does the same job: {灯|dēng}{一下|yí xià}{子|zi}{全|quán}{灭|miè}{了|le}.

## {眼看|yǎn kàn}: any moment now; to look on helplessly

{眼看|yǎn kàn} has two uses, both with a sense of something that can't be stopped:

1. **About to happen** (+ {就|jiù} / {快|kuài} … {了|le}): {眼看|yǎn kàn}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{赶快|gǎn kuài}{回去|huí qù}{吧|ba}。 (It's about to rain any minute:
   let's hurry back.) {眼看|yǎn kàn}{天|tiān}{就|jiù}{黑|hēi}{了|le}。 (It'll be dark any moment.)
2. **Watching something happen and being unable to help** ({眼看|yǎn kàn}{着|zhe} + what happens): {他|tā}{眼看|yǎn kàn}{着|zhe}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{房子|fáng zi}{被|bèi}
   {大|dà}{水|shuǐ}{淹没|yān mò}，{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{办法|bàn fǎ}{也|yě}{没有|méi yǒu}。 (He watched his house disappear under the flood, with nothing he could do.)

## {接连|jiē lián} and {一阵|yí zhèn}

**{接连|jiē lián}** (one after another, in a row) goes before the verb, often with a number of times or days:

{这个|zhè ge}{月|yuè}，{南方|nán fāng}{接连|jiē lián}{下|xià}{了|le}{十|shí}{几|jǐ}{天|tiān}{的|de}{大雨|dà yǔ}。 — This month it rained heavily in the south for over ten days in a row.

{那|nà}{年|nián}{夏天|xià tiān}，{这|zhè}{一带|yí dài}{接连|jiē lián}{遭遇|zāo yù}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}{台风|tái fēng}。 — That summer the area was hit by two typhoons one after the other.

**{一阵|yí zhèn}** is a spell of something that comes and goes: {一|yí}{阵雨|zhèn yǔ} (a shower), {一阵|yí zhèn}{风|fēng} (a gust), {一阵|yí zhèn}{掌声|zhǎng shēng} (a burst of
applause), {一阵|yí zhèn}{恐惧|kǒng jù} (a wave of fear). It can also go after a verb for a while: {他们|tā men}{聊|liáo}{了|le}{一阵|yí zhèn} (they chatted
for a while). {一|yī} is yí: {一阵|yí zhèn} yí zhèn. {阵雨|zhèn yǔ} is a shower in a weather forecast: {明天|míng tiān}{有|yǒu}{阵雨|zhèn yǔ}.

## {炸|zhà} zhà: to explode

{炸|zhà} has two readings. HSK 5's {炸|zhá} zhá is to deep-fry ({炸鸡|zhá jī}, fried chicken). {炸|zhà} zhà is to explode, to blow up,
or to burst:

{气球|qì qiú}{炸|zhà}{了|le}，{把|bǎ}{孩子|hái zi}{吓了一跳|xià le yí tiào}。 — The balloon burst and gave the child a fright.

{爆炸|bào zhà} bào zhà is an explosion, to explode; {爆|bào} bào is to burst ({爆|bào}{了|le}, of a tyre or a pipe), and {爆发|bào fā} bào
fā is to break out (of a war, a disease, a volcano: {火山|huǒ shān}{爆发|bào fā}).

## The same event in two registers

News reports, notices and official statements use written words; a person telling what happened
uses everyday ones. Here are pairs you'll meet in this lesson's two texts:

| Written (the report) | Spoken (the volunteer) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {顿时|dùn shí} | {一下|yí xià}{子|zi} | at once |
| {遭受|zāo shòu} / {遭到|zāo dào} | {受到|shòu dào} / {被|bèi}… | to suffer (a disaster) |
| {转移|zhuǎn yí} | {搬|bān}{到|dào} / {送|sòng}{到|dào} | to move (people) |
| {凌晨|líng chén} | {半夜|bàn yè} / {天|tiān}{还|hái}{没|méi}{亮|liàng} | the small hours |
| {突发|tū fā} | {突然|tū rán}{发生|fā shēng} | sudden |
| {伤亡|shāng wáng} | {有|yǒu}{人|rén}{受伤|shòu shāng}、{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{死|sǐ}{了|le} | casualties |
| {罕见|hǎn jiàn} | {很|hěn}{少见|shǎo jiàn} | rare |
| {赶忙|gǎn máng} | {赶紧|gǎn jǐn} | hurriedly |
| {淹没|yān mò} | {被|bèi}{水|shuǐ}{淹|yān}{了|le} | to be under water |
| {日夜|rì yè} | {白天|bái tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang} | day and night |

The report: {凌晨|líng chén}{两|liǎng}{点|diǎn}，{洪水|hóng shuǐ}{突然|tū rán}{冲|chōng}{进|jìn}{县城|xiàn chéng}，{低处|dī chù}{的|de}{房屋|fáng wū}{顿时|dùn shí}{被|bèi}{淹没|yān mò}。 The volunteer: {半夜|bàn yè}{两|liǎng}{点|diǎn}，{水|shuǐ}{一下|yí xià}{子|zi}{就|jiù}{进来|jìn lái}{了|le}，
{低|dī}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{的|de}{房子|fáng zi}{全|quán}{淹|yān}{了|le}。 Same facts; different words, different sentence length.

## Words for disasters

**Kinds of disaster.** {灾|zāi} (a disaster: {受灾|shòu zāi}, {救灾|jiù zāi}, {灾区|zāi qū}), {灾害|zāi hài} (a natural disaster: {自然|zì rán}{灾害|zāi hài}), {灾难|zāi nàn} (a
catastrophe), {洪水|hóng shuǐ} (a flood), {旱灾|hàn zāi} (a drought), {干旱|gān hàn} (drought; arid), {火灾|huǒ zāi} (a fire), {台风|tái fēng} (a typhoon), {雷|léi} /
{打雷|dǎ léi} (thunder / to thunder), {闪电|shǎn diàn} (lightning), {阵雨|zhèn yǔ} (a shower), {严寒|yán hán} (bitter cold), {寒冬|hán dōng} (a severe winter),
{炎热|yán rè} (scorching hot), {中暑|zhòng shǔ} (heatstroke: {中|zhòng} is zhòng here, "to be hit by").

**Describing them.** {恶劣|è liè} (very bad, harsh: {恶劣|è liè}{的|de}{天气|tiān qì}), {极端|jí duān} (extreme: {极端|jí duān}{天气|tiān qì}), {异常|yì cháng} (unusual;
extremely: {异常|yì cháng}{炎热|yán rè}), {罕见|hǎn jiàn} (rare: {百|bǎi}{年|nián}{罕见|hǎn jiàn}{的|de}{大雨|dà yǔ}), {惊人|jīng rén} (astonishing), {剧烈|jù liè} (violent, acute: {剧烈|jù liè}{的|de}
{疼痛|téng tòng}), {突发|tū fā} (sudden: {突发|tū fā}{事件|shì jiàn}), {人为|rén wéi} (man-made: {人为|rén wéi}{的|de}{原因|yuán yīn}), {加剧|jiā jù} (to get worse, intensify), {引发|yǐn fā} (to
trigger, set off), {爆发|bào fā} (to break out), {冒|mào} (to give off: {冒|mào}{烟|yān}, smoke rising; to brave: {冒雨|mào yǔ}, to go out in the
rain), {闪|shǎn} (to flash; to dodge), {淋|lín} (to drench: {被|bèi}{雨|yǔ}{淋|lín}{湿|shī}{了|le}), {淹|yān} / {淹没|yān mò} (to flood, to submerge), {险|xiǎn} (dangerous;
nearly: {好险|hǎo xiǎn}！, that was close).

**The scene.** {景象|jǐng xiàng} (a scene, a sight), {局面|jú miàn} (a situation: {混乱|hùn luàn}{的|de}{局面|jú miàn}), {混乱|hùn luàn} (chaos; chaotic), {艰难|jiān nán} (hard,
difficult), {饥饿|jī è} (hunger), {恐惧|kǒng jù} (fear: written), {吓|xià} (to frighten: {吓了一跳|xià le yí tiào}, to get a fright).

## Words for rescue

{救命|jiù mìng} (to save a life; "Help!"), {求救|qiú jiù} (to call for help), {救援|jiù yuán} (rescue; to rescue), {救灾|jiù zāi} (disaster relief),
{急救|jí jiù} (first aid; emergency treatment), {伤员|shāng yuán} (the injured), {伤亡|shāng wáng} (casualties), {死亡|sǐ wáng} (death; to die:
written), {消防|xiāo fáng} (firefighting: {消防员|xiāo fáng yuán}, a firefighter), {扑灭|pū miè} / {灭|miè} (to put out a fire), {消灭|xiāo miè} (to wipe out: of
pests, of a disease), {避|bì} / {躲避|duǒ bì} (to avoid; to shelter from: {避|bì}{雨|yǔ}, {躲避|duǒ bì}{洪水|hóng shuǐ}), {阻挡|zǔ dǎng} (to block, hold back), {转移|zhuǎn yí} (to
move, evacuate: {转移|zhuǎn yí}{群众|qún zhòng}), {运送|yùn sòng} (to transport: {运送|yùn sòng}{物资|wù zī}), {日夜|rì yè} (day and night), {赶忙|gǎn máng} (hurriedly: written),
{凌晨|líng chén} (the small hours), {重建|chóng jiàn} (to rebuild: {重|chóng} is chóng here), {遭到|zāo dào} / {遭受|zāo shòu} / {遭遇|zāo yù} (to suffer, to meet with).

{遭到|zāo dào}, {遭受|zāo shòu} and {遭遇|zāo yù} are all "to suffer, meet with" something bad:

- {遭到|zāo dào} + an action done to you: {遭到|zāo dào}{批评|pī píng}, {遭到|zāo dào}{破坏|pò huài} (to be damaged).
- {遭受|zāo shòu} + a loss or a disaster: {遭受|zāo shòu}{损失|sǔn shī}, {遭受|zāo shòu}{洪水|hóng shuǐ}.
- {遭遇|zāo yù} + an event you run into: {遭遇|zāo yù}{台风|tái fēng}; as a noun, one's misfortunes ({他|tā}{的|de}{遭遇|zāo yù}).

## Characters

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Traditional | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 狮 | lion | shī | 犭 | 9 | 獅 | {狮子|shī zi} |
| 洁 | clean | jié | 氵 | 9 | 潔 | {清洁|qīng jié} |
| 乌 ✎ | crow; black | wū | 丿 | 4 | 烏 | {乌龟|wū guī} |
| 龟 ✎ | tortoise | guī | 龟 | 7 | 龜 | {乌龟|wū guī} |
| 野 | wild | yě | 里 | 11 | 野 | {野外|yě wài}, {野生|yě shēng}, {野|yě} |

| 旱 ✎ | drought | hàn | 日 | 7 | 旱 | {旱灾|hàn zāi}, {干旱|gān hàn} |
| 灾 ✎ | disaster | zāi | 火 | 7 | 災 | {灾|zāi}, {灾害|zāi hài}, {救灾|jiù zāi}, {火灾|huǒ zāi} |

The first seven were in lesson 18's words. Five characters in this lesson's words are taught in
lesson 20: {扑|pū} ({扑灭|pū miè}), {亡|wáng} ({伤亡|shāng wáng}, {死亡|sǐ wáng}), {吓|xià} ({吓|xià}), {淹|yān} ({淹|yān}, {淹没|yān mò}) and {遭|zāo} ({遭到|zāo dào}, {遭受|zāo shòu}, {遭遇|zāo yù}).

In traditional, {狮|shī} is 獅 (13 strokes, with 師), {洁|jié} 潔 (15), {乌|wū} 烏 (10), {龟|guī} 龜 (18 in the tracing data),
{饥|jī} 飢 (10, with {食|shí} on the left), {惧|jù} 懼 (21), {灭|miè} 滅 (13: 氵 + 烕) and {闪|shǎn} 閃 (10, with 門). {灾|zāi} is 災 in
traditional (7 strokes: 巛, a river, over {火|huǒ}); {灾|zāi} itself is an old variant that simplified chose.

- **Sound parts.** {狮|shī} shī is 犭 + {师|shī} shī: exact. {洁|jié} jié is 氵 + {吉|jí} jí, the jié of {结|jié}. {爆|bào} bào is {火|huǒ} + {暴|bào} bào
  ({暴力|bào lì}, lesson 09): exact. {洪|hóng} hóng is 氵 + {共|gòng} gòng (and {供|gōng} gōng): a sound that has drifted. {惧|jù} jù is 忄
  (the heart) + {具|jù} jù: exact. {淋|lín} lín is 氵 + {林|lín} lín: exact. {饥|jī} jī is 饣 (food) + {几|jǐ} jǐ, as in {机|jī} jī. {援|yuán} yuán
  is 扌 + 爰 yuán, which gives the sound exactly; in {暖|nuǎn} nuǎn and {缓|huǎn} huǎn the same part has drifted. {耗|hào} hào is 耒 (a plough)
  + {毛|máo} máo; {循|xún} xún is 彳 (a step) + {盾|dùn} dùn: both sounds have drifted.
- **Memory aids** (not histories): {旱|hàn} is {日|rì} (the sun) over {干|gān} (dry). {灾|zāi} is 宀 (a roof) over {火|huǒ} (fire): a house
  on fire. {灭|miè} is {一|yī} (a lid) on {火|huǒ}: smother a fire. {劣|liè} is {少|shǎo} (little) over {力|lì} (strength): poor quality. {闪|shǎn}
  is {人|rén} in {门|mén}: someone flashing past a door. {乌|wū} is {鸟|niǎo} (a bird) without the dot of its eye: the crow
  is so black you can't see it, people say. {雷|léi} is {雨|yǔ} (rain) over {田|tián}.
- **Look-alikes.** {乌|wū} wū and {鸟|niǎo} niǎo; {旱|hàn} hàn and {早|zǎo} zǎo; {灭|miè} miè and {灰|huī} huī ({灰尘|huī chén}, lesson 18); {闪|shǎn} shǎn and {问|wèn} wèn;
  {洪|hóng} hóng and {供|gōng} gōng.

### Stroke order

- **{乌|wū}** (4): left-falling, then the turning hook, then the vertical that turns twice and hooks, then the
  horizontal. There is no dot: that's the difference from {鸟|niǎo}.
- **{灾|zāi}** (7): 宀 first, then {火|huǒ} (the two short strokes, then left-falling and right-falling).
- **{灭|miè}** (5): the horizontal, then {火|huǒ}.
- **{闪|shǎn}** (5): {门|mén} (three strokes), then {人|rén}.
- **{饥|jī}** (5): 饣 (three strokes), then {几|jǐ}.

1. A long spell of very heavy rain ({接连|jiē lián}{出现|chū xiàn}{大|dà}{范围|fàn wéi}{降雨|jiàng yǔ}…{罕见|hǎn jiàn}{的|de}{极端|jí duān}{天气|tiān qì}) made the river rise until it went over
   its banks.
2. Because a flood warning had been issued beforehand ({事先|shì xiān}{已|yǐ}{发布|fā bù}{了|le}{洪水|hóng shuǐ}{预警|yù jǐng}), so they were on standby.
3. Nobody died; one rescuer was slightly hurt and recovered after first aid.
4. To give experts' advice: be prepared for disasters, learn how to save yourself, and get to high
   ground in a flood.

"**Heavy rain brings floods; county town residents moved to safety in time.** This website reports:
According to the weather service, since the start of this month a province in the south has had
widespread rain one spell after another; in some areas the rainfall is the highest since local
records began, rare extreme weather. As a result, the water level of a river flowing through a
county town has been rising steadily.

At about two in the morning on the 15th, the river overflowed its banks and poured into the town.
Low-lying streets and houses were flooded at once; some areas lost power, and communications were
cut for a time. Because a flood warning had been issued in advance, the county's rescue team,
firefighters and large numbers of volunteers were already standing by nearby. On receiving calls for
help, they hurried into the disaster area in small boats, searching house by house for people
trapped.

It was still raining at the time, with thunder and lightning from time to time, and the rescue was
very hard work. Following the order 'old people and children first, then everyone else', rescuers
moved the trapped residents to a school and a sports hall on higher ground. A woman in her eighties
was trapped on the first floor of her home, and rescuers carried her out on their backs through the
rain. By midday, more than three thousand people across the county had been moved, with no deaths.
One rescuer was slightly hurt during the rescue and was not seriously injured after first aid.

In the sports hall, a villager in their sixties told our reporter: 'The water came so fast. I'd only
just woken my grandson when the ground floor was completely flooded. We climbed onto the roof and
shouted for help, and waited over an hour before the rescue team's boat found us.' Talking about the
scene that night, the villager still seemed a little frightened. Nearby, several volunteers were handing
out hot food and drinking water. The hall was rather crowded, but very orderly.

To make sure the people affected had the basics, the local government transported food, drinking
water, medicine and other supplies day and night, and arranged for doctors at the temporary
shelters to prevent illness. Because of the heat, staff also reminded people to guard against
heatstroke. According to preliminary figures, more than two hundred houses were damaged in the flood
and some farmland was flooded; the exact losses are still being counted.

The rain has now eased, the river is starting to fall, and the town's power and communications are
largely back. Many shops have reopened and the schools have resumed classes. The county has also had experts
check the safety of the houses, and only once they're confirmed safe can people move back home. For days now, many
volunteers from elsewhere have come to the town of their own accord to help residents clear the mud
and rubbish from the streets.

Experts remind us that extreme weather has been happening more and more often in recent years;
every area should prepare well to prevent disasters and respond to emergencies, and people should
learn basic self-rescue: in a flood, don't panic, get to high ground as quickly as you can, and wait
for rescue. They also suggest every household keep an emergency kit with a torch, drinking water and
everyday medicines."
</details>

## Speaking: a story from four photos

The speaking test shows four numbered photos to tell a story about (as reported, about three minutes
to prepare and two to speak). The photos, in words:

1. After school, a girl walks home. The sky is very dark.
2. There's thunder and lightning and heavy rain; she shelters in a shop doorway, soaked.
3. The shop owner gives her a towel and lends her an umbrella.
4. The next day, she brings the umbrella back with a thank-you card.

Use time words ({那|nà}{天|tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}, {突然|tū rán}, {第|dì}{二|èr}{天|tiān}), the lesson's words ({打雷|dǎ léi}, {闪电|shǎn diàn}, {淋|lín}, {躲避|duǒ bì}, {吓了一跳|xià le yí tiào}) and one written
word for the change ({顿时|dùn shí}).

<details>
<summary>Model story</summary>

{那|nà}{天|tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{放学|fàng xué}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{小红|Xiǎo Hóng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{人|rén}{走路|zǒu lù}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。{走|zǒu}{到|dào}{半路|bàn lù}，{一阵|yí zhèn}{大|dà}{风|fēng}{吹|chuī}{过来|guò lái}，{天|tiān}{顿时|dùn shí}{黑|hēi}{了|le}{下来|xià lái}，{眼看|yǎn kàn}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。

{突然|tū rán}，{天上|tiān shàng}{打|dǎ}{起|qǐ}{雷|léi}{来|lái}，{一道|yí dào}{闪电|shǎn diàn}{把|bǎ}{她|tā}{吓了一跳|xià le yí tiào}。{紧接着|jǐn jiē zhe}，{大雨|dà yǔ}{就|jiù}{下来|xià lái}{了|le}。{小红|Xiǎo Hóng}{没|méi}{带|dài}{伞|sǎn}，{赶忙|gǎn máng}{跑|pǎo}{到|dào}{路边|lù biān}{一|yì}{家|jiā}{小|xiǎo}{商店|shāng diàn}{的|de}{门口|mén kǒu}{躲|duǒ}{雨|yǔ}，{可是|kě shì}{衣服|yī fu}{已经|yǐ jīng}{被|bèi}{淋|lín}{湿|shī}{了|le}。

{商店|shāng diàn}{的|de}{主人|zhǔ rén}{是|shì}{一|yí}{位|wèi}{老|lǎo}{奶奶|nǎi nai}。{她|tā}{看见|kàn jiàn}{小红|Xiǎo Hóng}{全身|quán shēn}{都|dōu}{湿|shī}{了|le}，{就|jiù}{把|bǎ}{她|tā}{叫|jiào}{进|jìn}{店|diàn}{里|lǐ}，{给|gěi}{了|le}{她|tā}{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{毛巾|máo jīn}，{还|hái}{借|jiè}{给|gěi}{她|tā}{一|yì}{把|bǎ}{雨伞|yǔ sǎn}，{让|ràng}{她|tā}{早|zǎo}{点儿|diǎnr}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。

{第|dì}{二|èr}{天|tiān}{放学|fàng xué}，{小红|Xiǎo Hóng}{拿|ná}{着|zhe}{雨伞|yǔ sǎn}{来|lái}{到|dào}{商店|shāng diàn}，{还|huán}{给|gěi}{老|lǎo}{奶奶|nǎi nai}，{还|hái}{送|sòng}{了|le}{她|tā}{一|yì}{张|zhāng}{自己|zì jǐ}{画|huà}{的|de}{卡片|kǎ piàn}，{上面|shàng miàn}{写|xiě}{着|zhe}：“{谢谢|xiè xie}{您|nín}，{奶奶|nǎi nai}！”{老|lǎo}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{看|kàn}{了|le}，{笑|xiào}{得|de}{特别|tè bié}{开心|kāi xīn}。

({半路|bàn lù}: halfway; {紧接着|jǐn jiē zhe}: right after; {毛巾|máo jīn}: a towel; {卡片|kǎ piàn}: a card, lesson 27.)
</details>

## Write it: a thank-you letter

Write a thank-you letter ({感谢信|gǎn xiè xìn}) of 150–200 characters from the residents of a street to the rescue
team that helped them in a flood. Say what happened, what the team did, how you feel, and close
politely.

<details>
<summary>Model letter</summary>

**{感谢信|gǎn xiè xìn}**

{县|xiàn}{救援队|jiù yuán duì}{全体|quán tǐ}{队员|duì yuán}：

{本|běn}{月|yuè}{十五|shí wǔ}{日|rì}{凌晨|líng chén}，{洪水|hóng shuǐ}{突然|tū rán}{冲|chōng}{进|jìn}{县城|xiàn chéng}，{我们|wǒ men}{街道|jiē dào}{的|de}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{房屋|fáng wū}{被|bèi}{淹|yān}，{不|bù}{少|shǎo}{老人|lǎo rén}{和|hé}{孩子|hái zi}{被困|bèi kùn}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{中|zhōng}。{危急|wēi jí}{时刻|shí kè}，{你们|nǐ men}{冒|mào}{着|zhe}{大雨|dà yǔ}，{开|kāi}{着|zhe}{小|xiǎo}{船|chuán}，{一|yì}{家|jiā}{一|yì}{家|jiā}{地|de}{寻找|xún zhǎo}{被困|bèi kùn}{群众|qún zhòng}，{把|bǎ}{我们|wǒ men}{安全|ān quán}{地|de}{转移|zhuǎn yí}{到|dào}{了|le}{学校|xué xiào}。{一|yí}{位|wèi}{队员|duì yuán}{在|zài}{救援|jiù yuán}{中|zhōng}{受|shòu}{了|le}{伤|shāng}，{却|què}{一直|yì zhí}{坚持|jiān chí}{到|dào}{天|tiān}{亮|liàng}。

{洪水|hóng shuǐ}{退|tuì}{了|le}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{你们|nǐ men}{又|yòu}{日夜|rì yè}{帮助|bāng zhù}{我们|wǒ men}{清理|qīng lǐ}{街道|jiē dào}，{运送|yùn sòng}{食品|shí pǐn}{和|hé}{饮用水|yǐn yòng shuǐ}，{让|ràng}{我们|wǒ men}{感到|gǎn dào}{了|le}{温暖|wēn nuǎn}。

{在此|zài cǐ}，{我们|wǒ men}{向|xiàng}{全体|quán tǐ}{队员|duì yuán}{表示|biǎo shì}{深|shēn}{深|shēn}{的|de}{感谢|gǎn xiè}！{祝|zhù}{你们|nǐ men}{工作|gōng zuò}{顺利|shùn lì}，{身体|shēn tǐ}{健康|jiàn kāng}！

{幸福|xìng fú}{街|jiē}{全体|quán tǐ}{居民|jū mín}
{七|qī}{月|yuè}{二十|èr shí}{日|rì}

({全体|quán tǐ}: all (the members); {危急|wēi jí}{时刻|shí kè}: at a critical moment; {在此|zài cǐ}: here, hereby: a formal opening for thanks.)
</details>

Checklist: {感谢信|gǎn xiè xìn} as the title; who it's to (…{全体|quán tǐ}{队员|duì yuán}：); what happened and what they did; your feelings;
{在此|zài cǐ}…{表示|biǎo shì}{深|shēn}{深|shēn}{的|de}{感谢|gǎn xiè}; a wish; who it's from and the date.

## Say it

```speak
# Disasters and rescue
{一|yì}{声|shēng}{巨响|jù xiǎng}，{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{顿时|dùn shí}{黑|hēi}{了|le}{下来|xià lái}。
= There was a huge bang, and the room went dark at once.
{眼看|yǎn kàn}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{赶快|gǎn kuài}{回去|huí qù}{吧|ba}。
= It's going to rain any minute: let's hurry back.
{这个|zhè ge}{月|yuè}，{南方|nán fāng}{接连|jiē lián}{下|xià}{了|le}{十|shí}{几|jǐ}{天|tiān}{的|de}{大雨|dà yǔ}。
= This month it rained heavily in the south for over ten days in a row.
{一阵|yí zhèn}{大|dà}{风|fēng}{吹|chuī}{过来|guò lái}，{树|shù}{叶|yè}{飘|piāo}{了|le}{一|yí}{地|dì}。
= A gust of wind blew, and leaves drifted all over the ground.
{气球|qì qiú}{炸|zhà}{了|le}，{把|bǎ}{孩子|hái zi}{吓了一跳|xià le yí tiào}。
= The balloon burst and gave the child a fright.
{救援|jiù yuán}{人员|rén yuán}{把|bǎ}{被困|bèi kùn}{群众|qún zhòng}{转移|zhuǎn yí}{到|dào}{了|le}{学校|xué xiào}。
= The rescuers moved the trapped residents to the school.
```

## Pronunciation

- {炸|zhà} zhà (to explode) and {炸|zhá} zhá (to deep-fry, HSK 5): only the tone differs.
- {中暑|zhòng shǔ} zhòng shǔ: {中|zhòng} is zhòng, "to be hit by" (as in {中奖|zhòng jiǎng}, lesson 13), not zhōng.
- {重建|chóng jiàn} chóng jiàn: {重|chóng} is chóng, "again" (HSK 4's {重新|chóng xīn}), not zhòng.
- {一阵|yí zhèn} yí zhèn ({一|yī} before a fourth tone); {阵雨|zhèn yǔ} zhèn yǔ.
- {灾|zāi} zāi, {灾害|zāi hài} zāi hài, {灾难|zāi nàn} zāi nàn (nàn: a disaster; {难|nán} nán is difficult).
- {恶劣|è liè} è liè; {饥饿|jī è} jī è; {罕见|hǎn jiàn} hǎn jiàn; {救援|jiù yuán} jiù yuán.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{顿时|dùn shí}{去|qù}~~: {顿时|dùn shí} is only for a sudden change in the past. For the future or for what someone
  decides to do: {马上|mǎ shàng} / {立刻|lì kè}.
- {眼看|yǎn kàn} needs {就|jiù}…{了|le} or {快|kuài}…{了|le} for "about to": {眼看|yǎn kàn}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}. ~~{眼看|yǎn kàn}{下雨|xià yǔ}~~ alone is incomplete.
- {遭受|zāo shòu} takes a loss or a disaster, not a good thing: ~~{遭受|zāo shòu}{表扬|biǎo yáng}~~. For good things, {受到|shòu dào} ({受到|shòu dào}{表扬|biǎo yáng}).
- {伤亡|shāng wáng} is a written collective noun (casualties): ~~{他|tā}{伤亡|shāng wáng}{了|le}~~ is wrong. Say {他|tā}{受伤|shòu shāng}{了|le} / {他|tā}{去世|qù shì}{了|le}, or {这|zhè}{次|cì}{事故|shì gù}
  {没有|méi yǒu}{人员|rén yuán}{伤亡|shāng wáng}.
- {死亡|sǐ wáng} is written and factual ({死亡|sǐ wáng}{人数|rén shù}); for a person you know, say {去世|qù shì} (HSK 4).

## Key points

- {顿时|dùn shí} (written: at once, a sudden change in the past); {眼看|yǎn kàn} ({就|jiù}…{了|le}: about to; {眼看|yǎn kàn}{着|zhe}: to look on helplessly);
  {接连|jiē lián} (in a row: {接连|jiē lián}{下|xià}{了|le}{十|shí}{几|jǐ}{天|tiān}); {一阵|yí zhèn} (a spell: {一|yí}{阵雨|zhèn yǔ}, {一阵|yí zhèn}{风|fēng}; {聊|liáo}{了|le}{一阵|yí zhèn}); {炸|zhà} zhà (to explode) / {爆炸|bào zhà} / {爆发|bào fā}.
- Registers: {顿时|dùn shí} / {一下|yí xià}{子|zi}, {遭受|zāo shòu} / {受到|shòu dào}, {转移|zhuǎn yí} / {搬|bān}{到|dào}, {凌晨|líng chén} / {半夜|bàn yè}, {突发|tū fā} / {突然|tū rán}{发生|fā shēng}, {罕见|hǎn jiàn} / {很|hěn}{少见|shǎo jiàn}.
- Disasters: {灾害|zāi hài}, {灾难|zāi nàn}, {洪水|hóng shuǐ}, {旱灾|hàn zāi}, {干旱|gān hàn}, {火灾|huǒ zāi}, {台风|tái fēng}, {打雷|dǎ léi}, {闪电|shǎn diàn}, {阵雨|zhèn yǔ}, {严寒|yán hán}, {炎热|yán rè}, {中暑|zhòng shǔ}; describing: {恶劣|è liè}, {极端|jí duān}, {异常|yì cháng},
  {罕见|hǎn jiàn}, {剧烈|jù liè}, {加剧|jiā jù}, {引发|yǐn fā}, {淹没|yān mò}; rescue: {救命|jiù mìng}, {求救|qiú jiù}, {救援|jiù yuán}, {急救|jí jiù}, {伤员|shāng yuán}, {伤亡|shāng wáng}, {消防|xiāo fáng}, {扑灭|pū miè}, {转移|zhuǎn yí}, {运送|yùn sòng}, {重建|chóng jiàn}, {遭到|zāo dào} / {遭受|zāo shòu} / {遭遇|zāo yù}.
- New characters: {狮|shī} {洁|jié} {乌|wū}✎ {龟|guī}✎ {野|yě} {耗|hào} {循|xún} {爆|bào} {雷|léi}✎ {劣|liè}✎ {旱|hàn}✎ {灾|zāi}✎ {洪|hóng} {罕|hǎn}✎ {援|yuán} {饥|jī}✎ {惧|jù} {淋|lín} {灭|miè}✎ {闪|shǎn}✎.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Products, design and innovation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about making things: materials, machines, testing and new ideas. {大卫|Dà wèi} and {白涛|Bái Tāo} have
designed a suitcase for the students on their study trips, and they go to the factory of {石经理|Shí jīng lǐ}, the
bag manufacturer they ordered backpacks from (lesson 02), to test the first sample. The reading asks
a question about invention: people had wheels for thousands of years, so why did suitcases get them
so late? You'll learn:

- the degree pattern **verb / adjective + {透|tòu}{了|le}** (soaked through; terrible, fed up: {湿|shī}{透|tòu}{了|le}, {糟|zāo}{透|tòu}{了|le}, {烦|fán}{透|tòu}{了|le});
- **{率先|shuài xiān}** (to be the first to: written), with {率|shuài} shuài;
- the words of innovation ({专利|zhuān lì}, {商标|shāng biāo}, {突破|tū pò}, {创意|chuàng yì}, {新颖|xīn yǐng}, {涌现|yǒng xiàn}, {取代|qǔ dài}, {畅销|chàng xiāo}, {高端|gāo duān}), of what a product is like
  ({性能|xìng néng}, {特性|tè xìng}, {结实|jiē shi}, {坚固|jiān gù}, {弹性|tán xìng}, {透明|tòu míng}, {缺陷|quē xiàn}, {故障|gù zhàng}, {损坏|sǔn huài}), of materials ({材质|cái zhì}, {金属|jīn shǔ}, {棉|mián}, {木材|mù cái}, {水泥|shuǐ ní}, {砖|zhuān}, {胶水|jiāo shuǐ}) and of
  machines and measurements ({仪器|yí qì}, {机械|jī xiè}, {轮子|lún zi}, {旋转|xuán zhuǎn}, {转|zhuàn}, {开关|kāi guān}, {插座|chā zuò}, {尺寸|chǐ cun}, {体积|tǐ jī}, {毫米|háo mǐ}, {尺|chǐ}, {寸|cùn}).

The module's last writing task, a complaint, is near the end.

## Verb / adjective + {透|tòu}{了|le}: through and through; utterly

{透|tòu} (lesson 12) is "to go through; thorough". After a verb or an adjective, with {了|le}, it says that
something has gone all the way:

1. **A result, all the way through.** {雨|yǔ}{下|xià}{得|de}{太|tài}{大|dà}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{全身|quán shēn}{都|dōu}{湿|shī}{透|tòu}{了|le}。 (The rain was so heavy I was soaked
   through.) {这些|zhè xiē}{苹果|píng guǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{熟|shú}{透|tòu}{了|le}。 (These apples are fully ripe.)
2. **Degree: utterly, extremely**, mostly for bad things and bad feelings. {第|dì}{一|yī}{个|gè}{样品|yàng pǐn}{糟|zāo}{透|tòu}{了|le}，{轮子|lún zi}{一|yì}{推|tuī}{就|jiù}{掉|diào}{了|le}。
   (The first sample was dreadful: the wheels came off as soon as you pushed it.) {等|děng}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}，{他|tā}{心里|xīn li}{烦|fán}{透|tòu}{了|le}。
   (After waiting two hours he was thoroughly fed up.) {这个|zhè ge}{主意|zhǔ yi}{坏|huài}{透|tòu}{了|le}。 (That idea is just terrible.)

{透|tòu}{了|le} is spoken and strong. It goes with {湿|shī}, {熟|shú}, {糟|zāo}, {坏|huài}, {烦|fán}, {累|lèi} and the like; it isn't
used for good things: for "extremely good", say {好|hǎo}{极|jí}{了|le} or {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le} (~~{好|hǎo}{透|tòu}{了|le}~~ isn't said). Compare the
degree complements of HSK 4–5: {累|lèi}{死|sǐ}{了|le}, {好|hǎo}{极|jí}{了|le}, {高兴|gāo xìng}{得|de}{不得了|bù dé liǎo}.

## {率先|shuài xiān}: to be the first to (written)

{率先|shuài xiān} (shuài xiān) goes before a verb and says that someone did something before anyone else, leading
the way:

{这|zhè}{家|jiā}{工厂|gōng chǎng}{率先|shuài xiān}{使用|shǐ yòng}{了|le}{新|xīn}{技术|jì shù}。 — This factory was the first to use the new technology.

{在|zài}{这个|zhè ge}{领域|lǐng yù}，{他们|tā men}{率先|shuài xiān}{取得|qǔ dé}{了|le}{突破|tū pò}。 — In this field, they were the first to make a breakthrough.

### Stroke order

- **{亡|wáng}** (3): the dot, the horizontal, then the vertical that turns right.
- **{寸|cùn}** (3): the horizontal, the vertical hook, then the dot.
- **{仓|cāng}** (4): {人|rén} (left-falling, right-falling), then the stroke that turns down, then the last stroke that
  turns and hooks up.
- **{启|qǐ}** (7): {户|hù} (dot, horizontal-turn, horizontal, left-falling), then {口|kǒu}.
- **{吓|xià}** (6): {口|kǒu}, then {下|xià} (horizontal, vertical, dot).

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Why, when people had had wheels for about five thousand years, it took so long to put them on
   suitcases.
2. People were used to carrying their cases, there were porters at stations and piers, the roads
   were uneven and small wheels broke easily.
3. The case stood upright on two wheels with a handle that pulled out: sturdier, better-looking and
   easier to push.

   changing habits, and good ideas come from noticing what's inconvenient in daily life.

"**Putting wheels on a suitcase: why did it take so long?** Today, at airports and stations alike,
almost every traveller pulls a suitcase on wheels. But you may not realise that something so simple
only really became common in the second half of the twentieth century. People have used wheels for
about five thousand years; carts, cars and trains all depend on them. So why did nobody think of
putting wheels on a suitcase? The question sounds simple, but the answer is interesting.

In fact, people had thought of it long before. According to records, in the first half of the
twentieth century some people had already made suitcases with wheels and even applied for patents,
but none of them caught on. At the time people were used to carrying their cases and didn't find it
inconvenient; there were porters at stations and piers, the roads were uneven, and small wheels
broke easily. So those inventions never caught on.

The real breakthrough is generally thought to have come around 1970. An American businessman at an
airport saw a worker pushing a machine on wheels along with no effort, and at once had an idea: why
not put wheels on suitcases too? He fixed four wheels under a case, pulled it along with a strap, and
was the first to apply for a patent on the design. At first, though, the cases didn't sell well:
shops were worried nobody would want them. And the case was pulled lying flat, so it tipped over
easily and wasn't very steady.

Over ten years later, at the end of the eighties, a pilot improved it: he stood the case upright, with
two wheels at the bottom and a handle on top that pulled out. This kind of case was sturdy and
good-looking, and easy to push. At first he only made them for his colleagues, but to his surprise
they soon caught on among travellers and gradually replaced the old-style cases. It's said
the pilot never set out to start a business: flying between airports every day, he found his case
heavy and awkward, so he rebuilt an old one himself. When his colleagues saw it, they all asked him
to make one for them too. And so a small improvement made to solve his own problem became a product
that sells all over the world. Later, new designs
kept coming: spinner wheels that all turn, lighter materials, combination locks and more.

The story shows that many important inventions don't use any new principle. Wheels had long existed,
and so had suitcases: the hard part was putting them together, and harder still was changing
people's habits. A good idea often comes from looking carefully at everyday life: the place where
other people think 'it's always been like this' may be exactly where a product falls short.

So next time something strikes you as awkward to use, don't complain straight away: it may be the
start of a new invention. Good inventions are often hidden in small inconveniences like these."

(The facts: Bernard Sadow's wheeled suitcase of 1970, patented in 1972, and the upright case with a
pull-out handle made by the pilot Robert Plath in 1987; there were earlier wheeled cases that didn't
catch on.)
</details>

- {结实|jiē shi} jiē shi: {结|jiē} is jiē (as in {结果|jié guǒ} jiē guǒ, lesson 17) and {实|shí} is light.

- {率先|shuài xiān} is written: in a chat, {我|wǒ}{率先|shuài xiān}{到|dào}{了|le} sounds odd; say {我|wǒ}{第|dì}{一|yī}{个|gè}{到|dào}{的|de}.

lessons.title: Shen Kuo's notebooks
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

{沈括|Shěn Kuò} (Shěn Kuò, Shen Kuo) was an official of the Northern Song dynasty and one of the most curious
minds in Chinese history. Late in life he wrote 《{梦溪笔谈|Mèng xī Bǐ tán}》 (*Mèngxī Bǐtán*, the "Dream Brook Essays"), a
book of short notes on almost everything: mathematics, the stars, maps, medicine, music, and the
inventions of ordinary craftsmen. This honors lesson tells what the book records, using the words of
lesson 16 to 20: movable type, the compass needle, fossils and changing coastlines, and the oil he called
{石油|shí yóu}. HSK 3's honors lesson on the four great inventions (05h2) met printing and the
compass; here is the man who wrote the earliest account of both.

Dates are as most sources give them; where they differ, the lesson says so.

## Who he was

{沈括|Shěn Kuò} was born in 1031 in what is now Hangzhou, and died in 1095 (some sources give a year either side).
He spent his career as an official: he ran the office of
astronomy ({天文|tiān wén}), worked on water works ({水利|shuǐ lì}) and maps, went as an envoy (his diplomatic reports survive), and commanded troops on the
north-western frontier, where a defeat ended his career. In 1088 he retired to a garden he had bought
near {镇江|Zhèn jiāng} (Zhenjiang) and named {梦溪|Mèng xī} (Dream Brook). There he wrote the book he is remembered for.

《{梦溪笔谈|Mèng xī Bǐ tán}》 is a {笔记|bǐ jì} (bǐjì): a "notebook" of separate entries, about five hundred of them (nearly six hundred with his later
supplements), in no strict order. {笔|bǐ}{谈|tán} is "talking with the brush": in his preface he explains that
at Dream Brook he had only his brush and his inkstone to talk to.

## What the book records

**Movable type.** The book's best-known entry describes how a commoner ({平民|píng mín}) named {毕昇|Bì Shēng} (Bì Shēng) made
movable type in the Qingli years (1041–1048). Each character was shaped in clay ({胶泥|jiāo ní}), baked hard in
a fire, then set in an iron frame to print a page; afterwards the type could be taken apart and used
again. {沈括|Shěn Kuò} noted that for two or three copies this was no quicker than carving a whole wooden block,
but for hundreds or thousands it was extremely fast.

**The compass needle.** He describes a needle rubbed on a lodestone that points south, and notes that
it doesn't point due south but a little to the east. This is generally taken to be the world's
earliest written record of magnetic declination: the difference between magnetic north and true
north.

**Fossils and changing land.** In the Taihang mountains ({太行山|Tài háng shān}) he saw bands of shells and round stones in
a cliff, far from the sea, and concluded that the coast had once been there and had moved east as
rivers laid down silt. Near {延州|Yán zhōu} (Yánzhōu, in the north-west) a collapsed river bank uncovered hundreds of
bamboo stems turned to stone; bamboo didn't grow there, so he reasoned the climate had once been
much damper.

**Oil.** In the same region he described a black liquid that came out of the ground with spring water
and burned like hemp oil. He called it {石油|shí yóu} ("rock oil"), made ink from its soot, and wrote that it
would one day be widely used: {此|cǐ}{物|wù}{后|hòu}{必|bì}{大|dà}{行|xíng}{于|yú}{世|shì} ("this substance will surely be used widely in the
world in future"). The sentence comes straight after his account of the ink, so "this substance" may mean the ink
made from the oil's soot rather than the oil itself; the next sentence explains that oil is plentiful in the
ground, unlike the pine wood that ink was usually made from.

## Reading: a book that wrote down everything

Our own account in Chinese, using the module's words.

> **{一|yì}{本|běn}{什么|shén me}{都|dōu}{写|xiě}{的|de}{书|shū}**

work.

The line in quotation marks is classical Chinese ({文言|wén yán}), checked against a transcription of the original
(chapter 24 of the book's 26): {此|cǐ} (this),
{物|wù} (thing), {后|hòu} (later), {必|bì} (surely), {大|dà}{行|xíng} (be widely used), {于|yú}{世|shì} (in the world). In the original it follows his account of making ink from the soot, so {此|cǐ}{物|wù} may mean
that ink rather than the oil itself.

1. Why do people remember {沈括|Shěn Kuò} today?
2. Why was movable type better than carving a whole block?
3. What did the bamboo fossils at {延州|Yán zhōu} tell {沈括|Shěn Kuò}?
4. How does the writer describe 《{梦溪笔谈|Mèng xī Bǐ tán}》 in the last paragraph?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Mainly for the book he wrote late in life, 《{梦溪笔谈|Mèng xī Bǐ tán}》.
2. With a carved block, one wrong character ruined the whole block; clay type could be rearranged and
   reused, and for hundreds or thousands of copies it was much faster.
3. That the climate there must once have been much damper, because bamboo didn't grow there in his
   day.
4. Not a specialised scientific work but a curious person's notebook: yet because he wanted to know
   and write down everything, we know about many ancient inventions and discoveries.

"**A book that wrote down everything.** Shen Kuo lived in the Northern Song; he is generally
thought to have been born in 1031 and to have died in 1095. He became an official when young and
did many different jobs: he ran astronomy, worked on water works, drew maps, and led troops in the
north-west. But today people remember him mainly for a book he wrote late in life: the *Dream Brook
Essays*.

Around 1088 Shen Kuo left official life and moved into a garden in Zhenjiang. He named it 'Dream
Brook', and there he wrote down, one entry at a time, the things he had seen, heard and thought about
in his life. The book has more than five hundred entries, on a very wide range of subjects:
mathematics, astronomy, geography, medicine, music, literature, and many inventions by ordinary
craftsmen.

The most famous entry records movable-type printing, invented by a commoner named Bi Sheng. Before
this, to print a book you first carved every character of a page on a wooden block; carve one
character wrong and the whole block was useless. Bi Sheng made characters one by one from clay and
baked them hard in a fire. To print, the characters needed were set in order, and after printing
they could be taken apart and used again. Shen Kuo wrote that for only two or three copies the method
saved no trouble, but for hundreds or thousands it was much faster.

Shen Kuo also left an important record about the compass. He said that a needle rubbed with a stone
that attracts iron could point south, but that it didn't point due south: it pointed a little to the
east. This is generally taken to be the earliest written record of the phenomenon in the world.

Shen Kuo was also a keen observer of nature. Passing through the Taihang mountains, he saw fossils of
many small sea creatures in the rocks. He inferred that long ago this had been the seashore, and
that the land had slowly extended eastwards as the silt brought by rivers piled up. At Yanzhou, once
when a river bank collapsed, many bamboos turned to stone were exposed underground. But Yanzhou's climate was dry
and bamboo didn't grow there. He concluded that long ago the climate there must have been damper
than in his own time. In today's terms, he saw that both landforms and climate change over time.

It was also in the Yanzhou area that Shen Kuo noticed a black liquid flowing out of the ground,
which gave off very thick smoke when it burned. He called it 'rock oil' and used the black smoke from burning
it to make ink for writing. In his book he wrote: 'This substance will surely be used widely in the
world in future.' Over nine hundred years later, oil really has become one of the world's most
important sources of energy.

The *Dream Brook Essays* isn't a specialised scientific work: it's more like a curious person's
notebook. But precisely because Shen Kuo wanted to know about everything and was willing to write
everything down, we can learn today about so many ancient inventions and discoveries."
</details>

## Key points

- {沈括|Shěn Kuò} (1031–1095, dates as usually given), an official of the Northern Song; 《{梦溪笔谈|Mèng xī Bǐ tán}》 (about 1088), a
  notebook of about five hundred entries, written at his Dream Brook garden near {镇江|Zhèn jiāng}.
- It records {毕昇|Bì Shēng}'s clay movable type (1040s), the compass needle that points a little east of south
  (the earliest record of magnetic declination), shell fossils in the Taihang mountains and stone
  bamboo at {延州|Yán zhōu} (the land and the climate change), and {石油|shí yóu}, with {此|cǐ}{物|wù}{后|hòu}{必|bì}{大|dà}{行|xíng}{于|yú}{世|shì}.

lessons.title: Guo Shoujing's calendar
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

{郭守敬|Guō Shǒu jìng} (Guō Shǒujìng, Guo Shoujing) was an astronomer, mathematician and engineer of the Yuan dynasty.
With a team of astronomers he made a calendar, the {授时历|Shòu shí lì} (*Shòushí lì*, "the Season-Granting
Calendar"), that came into use in 1281 and set the length of the year at 365.2425 days: the same
figure as the Gregorian calendar adopted in Europe three hundred years later. This honors lesson
tells how he measured the sun's shadow, what instruments he built, and why a calendar mattered so
much. It uses the words of lessons 16 to 20: {测量|cè liáng}, {精确|jīng què}, {仪器|yí qì}, {垂直|chuí zhí}, {运行|yùn xíng}, {轨道|guǐ dào}, {天文|tiān wén}, {误差|wù chā}.

HSK 5's honors lesson on {祖冲之|Zǔ Chōng zhī} (Zu Chongzhi, 10h2) met an earlier calendar maker; this is the next
great step.

## Who he was

{郭守敬|Guō Shǒu jìng} was born in 1231 in what is now Hebei province, and died in 1316 (some sources give 1314).
His grandfather taught him mathematics and water engineering, and as a young man he worked on canals
and rivers. After the Yuan dynasty's emperor {忽必烈|Hū bì liè} (Kublai Khan) ordered a new calendar in the 1270s,
{郭守敬|Guō Shǒu jìng} was given the job of making the instruments and the observations, working with other
astronomers. The calendar was finished in 1280 and used from 1281.

He later ran the empire's water works, and brought water to the capital, {大都|Dà dū} (Dàdū: today's Beijing),
by a long channel from springs in the hills.

## Why a calendar mattered

In an agricultural country the calendar told farmers when to plough, sow and harvest. The Chinese
calendar follows both the moon (the months) and the sun (the year and its {二十四|èr shí sì}{节气|jié qi}, the twenty-four
solar terms such as {夏至|xià zhì}, the summer solstice, and {冬至|dōng zhì}, the winter solstice). If the length of the year
is slightly wrong, the error grows every year, and after a century the solar terms no longer fall
when they should. Each dynasty therefore tried to measure the year more precisely.

## How he measured

The length of the year can be found from the sun's noon shadow. On {冬至|dōng zhì} the sun is lowest and the shadow
of an upright pole (a gnomon) is longest; count the days from one longest shadow to the next, over many
years, and divide. The longer the pole, the longer the shadow, and the smaller the error in reading
it.

- **A taller gnomon.** The traditional gnomon was a short pole; {郭守敬|Guō Shǒu jìng} had towers built with a much
  taller one. The one that survives is the {观星台|Guān xīng tái} (*Guānxīng tái*, the Star-Observing
  Tower) at {登封|Dēng fēng} (Dēngfēng) in Henan, built in 1276: a brick tower about nine and a half metres high, with
  a stone "ruler" over thirty metres long laid on the ground to its north to measure the shadow. It's
  part of a UNESCO World Heritage site listed in 2010.
- **Sharper readings.** He added a small device with a pinhole that focused the sun's image on the
  ruler, so that the edge of the shadow could be read precisely.
- **New instruments.** His {简仪|jiǎn yí} (jiǎnyí, the "simplified armilla") split the many rings of the old
  armillary sphere into separate, simpler instruments, so that almost the whole sky could be seen.
- **Many stations.** Observations were made at twenty-seven places across the empire, from the far
  south to the far north.

The result was a year of 365.2425 days, which is 365 days 5 hours 49 minutes 12 seconds: about
twenty-six seconds longer than the modern figure for the solar year. The Gregorian calendar, adopted
in 1582, has the same average year. Under the next dynasty, the Ming, the {授时历|Shòu shí lì} was used in a lightly
revised form, so that in all it served for over three hundred and sixty years.

## Reading: a shadow that measured the year

Our own account in Chinese, using the module's words.

>
> {郭守敬|Guō Shǒu jìng}{想|xiǎng}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{办法|bàn fǎ}。{第|dì}{一|yī}，{把|bǎ}{杆子|gān zi}{做|zuò}{得|de}{更|gèng}{高|gāo}。{以前|yǐ qián}{的|de}{杆子|gān zi}{比较|bǐ jiào}{矮|ǎi}，{他|tā}{建造|jiàn zào}{的|de}{观测台|guān cè tái}{要|yào}{高|gāo}{得|de}{多|duō}，{影子|yǐng zi}{也|yě}{就|jiù}{长|cháng}{得|de}{多|duō}，{同样|tóng yàng}{的|de}{误差|wù chā}，{对|duì}{结果|jié guǒ}{的|de}{影响|yǐng xiǎng}{就|jiù}{小|xiǎo}{了|le}。{今天|jīn tiān}{在|zài}{河南|Hé nán}{登封|Dēng fēng}，{还|hái}{能|néng}{看|kàn}{到|dào}{一|yí}{座|zuò}{元朝|Yuán cháo}{建造|jiàn zào}{的|de}{观星台|Guān xīng tái}。{它|tā}{用|yòng}{砖|zhuān}{建|jiàn}{成|chéng}，{高|gāo}{九|jiǔ}{米|mǐ}{多|duō}，{北|běi}{面|miàn}{的|de}{地|dì}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{三十|sān shí}{多|duō}{米|mǐ}{长|cháng}{的|de}{石头|shí tou}“{尺子|chǐ zi}”，{专门|zhuān mén}{用来|yòng lái}{测量|cè liáng}{影子|yǐng zi}。{第|dì}{二|èr}，{他|tā}{发明|fā míng}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小|xiǎo}{工具|gōng jù}，{利用|lì yòng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小孔|xiǎo kǒng}，{让|ràng}{太阳|tài yang}{的|de}{光|guāng}{在|zài}“{尺子|chǐ zi}”{上|shàng}{形成|xíng chéng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{清晰|qīng xī}{的|de}{小|xiǎo}{亮点|liàng diǎn}，{这样|zhè yàng}{就|jiù}{能|néng}{把|bǎ}{影子|yǐng zi}{的|de}{长度|cháng dù}{读|dú}{得|de}{更|gèng}{准确|zhǔn què}。
>
> {除了|chú le}{这些|zhè xiē}，{郭守敬|Guō Shǒu jìng}{还|hái}{和|hé}{同事|tóng shì}{们|men}{在|zài}{全|quán}{国|guó}{二十七|èr shí qī}{个|gè}{地方|dì fang}{进行|jìn xíng}{了|le}{观测|guān cè}。{经过|jīng guò}{几|jǐ}{年|nián}{的|de}{努力|nǔ lì}，{他们|tā men}{算|suàn}{出|chū}{一|yì}{年|nián}{的|de}{长度|cháng dù}{是|shì}365.2425{天|tiān}。{这个|zhè ge}{数字|shù zì}{跟|gēn}{今天|jīn tiān}{科学家|kē xué jiā}{测量|cè liáng}{的|de}{结果|jié guǒ}{只|zhǐ}{相差|xiāng chà}{二十|èr shí}{多|duō}{秒|miǎo}。{三百|sān bǎi}{年|nián}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{欧洲|Ōu zhōu}{开始|kāi shǐ}{使用|shǐ yòng}{的|de}{公历|gōng lì}，{一|yì}{年|nián}{的|de}{平均|píng jūn}{长度|cháng dù}{也|yě}{正|zhèng}{是|shì}365.2425{天|tiān}。
>
> {新|xīn}{的|de}{历法|lì fǎ}{叫作|jiào zuò}“{授时历|Shòu shí lì}”，{从|cóng}1281{年|nián}{开始|kāi shǐ}{使用|shǐ yòng}。{后来|hòu lái}{的|de}{明朝|Míng cháo}{基本上|jī běn shang}{继续|jì xù}{使用|shǐ yòng}{它|tā}，{只是|zhǐ shì}{换|huàn}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{名字|míng zi}。{这样|zhè yàng}{算|suàn}{起来|qǐ lái}，{它|tā}{一共|yí gòng}{用|yòng}{了|le}{三百六十|sān bǎi liù shí}{多|duō}{年|nián}，{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{历史|lì shǐ}{上|shàng}{使用|shǐ yòng}{时间|shí jiān}{最|zuì}{长|cháng}{的|de}{历法|lì fǎ}。
>
> {今天|jīn tiān}，{我们|wǒ men}{打开|dǎ kāi}{手机|shǒu jī}{就|jiù}{能|néng}{知道|zhī dào}{日期|rì qī}{和|hé}{节气|jié qi}，{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{会|huì}{想|xiǎng}{到|dào}，{这|zhè}{背后|bèi hòu}{有|yǒu}{过|guo}{多少|duō shao}{人|rén}{一|yì}{年|nián}{又|yòu}{一|yì}{年|nián}{地|de}{观测|guān cè}{太阳|tài yang}{和|hé}{星星|xīng xing}。{郭守敬|Guō Shǒu jìng}{的|de}{故事|gù shi}{告诉|gào su}{我们|wǒ men}，{精确|jīng què}{的|de}{科学|kē xué}，{往往|wǎng wǎng}{是|shì}{从|cóng}{一|yì}{根|gēn}{杆子|gān zi}、{一|yí}{个|gè}{影子|yǐng zi}{开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de}。

{影子|yǐng zi} (lesson 25): a shadow. {历法|lì fǎ}: a calendar (as a system). {节气|jié qi}: the solar terms. {生|shēng}{于|yú} ({于|yú}, lesson 27): born in. {对不上|duì bu shàng}: no longer match. {制定|zhì dìng} (HSK 5): to draw up.
{天文学家|tiān wén xué jiā}: an astronomer. {祖父|zǔ fù}: a grandfather (written). {立|lì}: to stand up (lesson 24). {杆子|gān zi}: a pole. {冬至|dōng zhì}: the
winter solstice. {观测台|guān cè tái} / {观星台|Guān xīng tái}: an observatory tower. {小孔|xiǎo kǒng}: a small hole. {公历|gōng lì}: the Gregorian calendar.

1. Why did a precise calendar matter so much in ancient China?
2. Why did a taller pole give a more precise result?
3. How close was the {授时历|Shòu shí lì}'s year to today's figure?
4. What does the writer want us to take from the story?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Farming depended on it: if the calendar's year is a little wrong, the error adds up and the solar
   terms no longer match the seasons.
2. A taller pole casts a longer shadow, so the same error in reading it has a smaller effect on the
   result.
3. Only about twenty-odd seconds different ({只|zhǐ}{相差|xiāng chà}{二十|èr shí}{多|duō}{秒|miǎo}).
4. That precise science often starts from something very simple: a pole and its shadow.

"**Measuring the length of a year with a shadow.** How many days are there in a year? The question
sounds simple, but it's very hard to answer. Ancient China was a farming country: when to sow and when
to harvest all depended on the calendar. If the calendar's year was a little longer or shorter than
the real one, the error would add up year after year, and after a few decades or a century the solar
terms would no longer match. So almost every dynasty wanted to measure the length of the year a little
more precisely.

Early in the Yuan dynasty, the emperor Kublai Khan decided to draw up a new calendar. The work was
given to a few astronomers, the most famous of whom was Guo Shoujing. Born in 1231, Guo Shoujing
learned mathematics and water engineering from his grandfather as a child. He could not only
calculate but was very good with his hands, and made many new astronomical instruments.

How can you find out how long a year is? People long ago used a simple method: stand a vertical pole
in the ground and measure the length of its shadow at noon. On the winter solstice the sun is at its
lowest and the shadow at its longest. From one winter solstice to the next is a year. But the edge of
the shadow is never very clear, so it's hard to measure precisely.

Guo Shoujing thought of two solutions. First, make the pole taller. Earlier poles were fairly short; the
observation towers he built were much taller, so the shadow was much longer, and
the same error had a smaller effect on the result. Today, at Dengfeng in Henan, you can still see a
Star-Observing Tower built in the Yuan dynasty. It's built of brick, more than nine metres high, and on
the ground to its north there's a stone 'ruler' over thirty metres long, made specially to measure the
shadow. Second, he invented a small device that used a tiny hole to make the sunlight form a sharp
bright spot on the 'ruler', so that the length of the shadow could be read more accurately.

Besides this, Guo Shoujing and his colleagues made observations at twenty-seven places across the
country. After several years' work they calculated the length of the year as 365.2425 days. This
figure differs from what scientists measure today by only about twenty seconds. Three hundred years
later, the Gregorian calendar that Europe began to use also had an average year of exactly 365.2425
days.

The new calendar was called the Shoushi calendar, and it came into use in 1281. The Ming dynasty
that followed went on using it more or less as it was, only under another name. Counted like this, it
was used for more than three hundred and sixty years in all, the longest-used calendar in Chinese
history.

Today we can open our phones and see the date and the solar term, and few people think how many
people, year after year, watched the sun and the stars to make it possible. Guo Shoujing's story
shows that precise science often begins with a pole and a shadow."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Guo Shoujing
{古代|gǔ dài}{中国|Zhōng guó}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{农业|nóng yè}{国家|guó jiā}，{种地|zhòng dì}{要|yào}{看|kàn}{历法|lì fǎ}。
= Ancient China was a farming country, and farming went by the calendar.
{冬至|dōng zhì}{那|nà}{一|yì}{天|tiān}，{太阳|tài yang}{最|zuì}{低|dī}，{影子|yǐng zi}{最|zuì}{长|cháng}。
= On the winter solstice the sun is at its lowest and the shadow at its longest.
{杆子|gān zi}{越|yuè}{高|gāo}，{影子|yǐng zi}{越|yuè}{长|cháng}，{测量|cè liáng}{的|de}{误差|wù chā}{就|jiù}{越|yuè}{小|xiǎo}。
= The taller the pole, the longer the shadow, and the smaller the error in measuring it.
{他们|tā men}{算|suàn}{出|chū}{一|yì}{年|nián}{的|de}{长度|cháng dù}{是|shì}365.2425{天|tiān}。
= They calculated the length of the year as 365.2425 days.
{授时历|Shòu shí lì}{一共|yí gòng}{用|yòng}{了|le}{三百六十|sān bǎi liù shí}{多|duō}{年|nián}。
= The Shoushi calendar was used for more than three hundred and sixty years in all.
```

## Key points

- {郭守敬|Guō Shǒu jìng} (1231–1316; some sources give 1314), astronomer and engineer of the Yuan; the {授时历|Shòu shí lì}, finished in
  1280 and used from 1281, with a year of 365.2425 days (the Gregorian calendar's average year, 1582).
- His methods: a much taller gnomon (the {观星台|Guān xīng tái} at {登封|Dēng fēng}, 1276, with a ruler over thirty metres long), a
  pinhole device for a sharp reading, the {简仪|jiǎn yí}, and observations at twenty-seven places.
- The calendar was used, under the Ming in a revised form, for over three hundred and sixty years.
- Module words in use: {测量|cè liáng}, {精确|jīng què}, {误差|wù chā}, {垂直|chuí zhí}, {仪器|yí qì}, {天文|tiān wén}, {相差|xiāng chà}, {清晰|qīng xī}, {砖|zhuān}, {尺|chǐ}.

lessons.title: Growing up and education
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 5 is about people: growing up, marrying, quarrelling, what we admire and what we remember.
It opens with childhood and school. Wang Fang visits her {舅舅|jiù jiu} (her mother's brother: next
lesson's word, with the other names for relatives), whose
grandson {豆豆|Dòu dou} has just started primary school, and the family argues over whether a seven-year-old
needs extra classes at the weekend. Afterwards she writes a commentary for the website comparing two
generations' schoolbags.

The grammar:

- {一向|yí xiàng}: "always, all along", for a habit or a character that has held for a long time;
- {下功夫|xià gōng fu}: to put effort into something ({在|zài}…{上|shàng}{下功夫|xià gōng fu});
- {伴随|bàn suí}: to go along with, to accompany (written);
- **{把|bǎ} with a non-living subject**: {这么|zhè me}{多|duō}{作业|zuò yè}{把|bǎ}{孩子|hái zi}{累|lèi}{坏|huài}{了|le}, where a thing or an event, not a person,
  is what causes the result.

The words cover the stages of life from the {婴儿|yīng ér} to the {未成年人|wèi chéng nián rén}, children's characters, the school
system from {初等|chū děng} to {高等|gāo děng} education, and studying, with its {难点|nán diǎn} and its {补习|bǔ xí}.

## {一向|yí xiàng}: always, all along

{一向|yí xiàng} says that something has been true for a long time and still is: a habit, a way of behaving, a
character. It goes before the verb or adjective:

{他|tā}{一向|yí xiàng}{很|hěn}{用功|yòng gōng}。 — He has always worked hard.

{舅舅|jiù jiu}{一向|yí xiàng}{对|duì}{孩子|hái zi}{很|hěn}{严|yán}。 — My uncle has always been strict with children.

{我|wǒ}{一向|yí xiàng}{不|bú}{太|tài}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{早|zǎo}{起|qǐ}。 — I've never much liked getting up early.

{一向|yí xiàng} and {一直|yì zhí} both translate "always", but they look at time differently:

| | What it covers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {一向|yí xiàng} | a habit or a quality, true as far back as you can see | {她|tā}{一向|yí xiàng}{很|hěn}{准时|zhǔn shí}。 She's always punctual. |
| {一直|yì zhí} | a continuous action or state over a stretch of time; also "straight on" | {雨|yǔ}{一直|yì zhí}{下|xià}{到|dào}{晚上|wǎn shang}。 It rained right through to the evening. |

So {一向|yí xiàng} doesn't take a single stretch of action: {我|wǒ}{一直|yì zhí}{等|děng}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí} (I waited two whole hours), never
~~{我|wǒ}{一向|yí xiàng}{等|děng}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}~~. And {一直|yì zhí} can describe what happened over one afternoon ({他|tā}{一直|yì zhí}{没|méi}{说话|shuō huà}, he didn't
say a word the whole time), which {一向|yí xiàng} can't. {一向|yí xiàng} is common in speech and writing; lesson 24's {一贯|yí guàn}
is its more formal partner, for conduct and principles.

## {下功夫|xià gōng fu}: to put in the effort

{功夫|gōng fu} here is time and effort spent to get good at something, and {下功夫|xià gōng fu} is "to put it in". The area
goes in {在|zài}…{上|shàng}:

{学|xué}{汉字|hàn zì}{要|yào}{下功夫|xià gōng fu}。 — Learning characters takes real effort.

{她|tā}{在|zài}{发音|fā yīn}{上|shàng}{下|xià}{了|le}{很|hěn}{大|dà}{的|de}{功夫|gōng fu}。 — She put a lot of work into her pronunciation.

The phrase splits like a verb and its object: {下|xià}{了|le}{不|bù}{少|shǎo}{功夫|gōng fu}, {下|xià}{过|guo}{功夫|gōng fu}, {下|xià}{点儿|diǎnr}{功夫|gōng fu}. {功夫|gōng fu} is also
"kung fu", the martial art; lesson 25's {工夫|gōng fu}, written with {工|gōng}, is free time ("{有|yǒu}{工夫|gōng fu}{吗|ma}?"). In
{下功夫|xià gōng fu} the usual form is {功夫|gōng fu}.

## {伴随|bàn suí}: to go along with

{伴随|bàn suí} is a written verb: one thing goes along with another, often with {着|zhe}:

{伴随|bàn suí}{着|zhe}{音乐|yīn yuè}，{孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{走|zǒu}{上|shàng}{了|le}{台|tái}。 — The children walked onto the stage to music.

{这|zhè}{首|shǒu}{歌|gē}{伴随|bàn suí}{了|le}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{整个|zhěng gè}{青春|qīng chūn}。 — This song was with me all through my youth.

{成长|chéng zhǎng}{总是|zǒng shì}{伴随|bàn suí}{着|zhe}{烦恼|fán nǎo}。 — Growing up always comes with its worries.

For a person keeping someone company, use HSK 5's {陪伴|péi bàn} or plain {陪|péi} ({妈妈|mā ma}{陪|péi}{着|zhe}{孩子|hái zi}). {伴随|bàn suí} is for things,
feelings and processes: music, a song, worries, change ({伴随|bàn suí}{着|zhe}{经济|jīng jì}{的|de}{发展|fā zhǎn}, as the economy develops).

## {把|bǎ} with a non-living subject

You know the {把|bǎ} sentence with a person as the doer: {我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{作业|zuò yè}{写|xiě}{完|wán}{了|le}. At HSK 6 the subject can be a
thing or an event, the cause, and {把|bǎ} brings in the person (or thing) it affects. The verb then
describes what happened to them, usually with a result or a degree:

{这么|zhè me}{多|duō}{作业|zuò yè}{把|bǎ}{孩子|hái zi}{累|lèi}{坏|huài}{了|le}。 — All this homework has worn the child out.

{这个|zhè ge}{消息|xiāo xi}{把|bǎ}{妈妈|mā ma}{高兴|gāo xìng}{得|de}{一|yì}{晚上|wǎn shang}{没|méi}{睡着|shuì zháo}。 — The news made Mum so happy she didn't sleep all night.

{那|nà}{次|cì}{考试|kǎo shì}{把|bǎ}{他|tā}{吓|xià}{坏|huài}{了|le}。 — That exam gave him a real fright.

{一|yì}{场|chǎng}{大|dà}{雨|yǔ}{把|bǎ}{我们|wǒ men}{淋|lín}{透|tòu}{了|le}。 — A downpour soaked us to the skin.

- The subject ({作业|zuò yè}, {消息|xiāo xi}, {考试|kǎo shì}, {大|dà}{雨|yǔ}) is not doing anything on purpose: it's what causes the feeling or
  the state. English often says "X made someone…" or "X wore / frightened / soaked someone".
- The verb is often an adjective used as a verb ({累|lèi}, {急|jí}, {高兴|gāo xìng}, {忙|máng}) or a verb of feeling ({吓|xià}), and it
  needs a result: {坏|huài}{了|le}, {得|de} + a description, {透|tòu}{了|le} (lesson 20), {死|sǐ}{了|le}.
- {让|ràng} says almost the same, more neutrally: {这么|zhè me}{多|duō}{作业|zuò yè}{让|ràng}{孩子|hái zi}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}. The {把|bǎ} version stresses the strong
  result: {累|lèi}{坏|huài}{了|le}.

This kind of sentence is the **{把|bǎ} with a non-living subject**. Its partner pattern, {看|kàn}{把|bǎ}{你|nǐ}{高兴|gāo xìng}{得|de}, is
lesson 22's.

## Growing up

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {婴儿|yīng ér} | baby (formal, written) | {婴儿|yīng ér}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{要|yào}{睡|shuì}{十|shí}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 Babies sleep over ten hours a day. |
| {娃娃|wá wa} | baby, small child (spoken); a doll | {他|tā}{还是|hái shi}{个|gè}{娃娃|wá wa}{呢|ne}。 He's only a little kid. |
| {少儿|shào ér} | children (in names of things for them) | {少儿|shào ér}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn} children's library; {少儿|shào ér}{频道|pín dào} children's channel |
| {未成年人|wèi chéng nián rén} | a minor (under eighteen: legal, written) | {商店|shāng diàn}{不|bù}{能|néng}{卖|mài}{烟|yān}{给|gěi}{未成年人|wèi chéng nián rén}。 Shops may not sell cigarettes to minors. |
