Yet one small bookshop holds a "handwritten letter" event every year. During the event, the shop provides customers with letter paper, envelopes and fountain pens; customers can write to anyone they like, and the shop posts the letters free of charge.
```speak
{书店|shū diàn}{老板|lǎo bǎn}{说|shuō}，{之所以|zhī suǒ yǐ}{举办|jǔ bàn}{这个|zhè ge}{活动|huó dòng}，{是|shì}{因为|yīn wèi}{他|tā}{发现|fā xiàn}，{人们|rén men}{打字|dǎ zì}{越来越|yuè lái yuè}{快|kuài}，{却|què}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{再|zài}{认真|rèn zhēn}{地|de}{想|xiǎng}{一|yi}{想|xiǎng}{自己|zì jǐ}{要|yào}{说|shuō}{什么|shén me}。{一|yì}{封|fēng}{手写|shǒu xiě}{的|de}{信|xìn}，{从|cóng}{开头|kāi tóu}{到|dào}{结尾|jié wěi}，{每|měi}{一|yí}{个|gè}{字|zì}{都|dōu}{得|děi}{慢慢|màn màn}{写|xiě}，{写|xiě}{错|cuò}{了|le}{还|hái}{要|yào}{重新|chóng xīn}{抄|chāo}{一|yí}{遍|biàn}。{正|zhèng}{是|shì}{这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}"{慢|màn}"，{让|ràng}{人|rén}{把|bǎ}{心里话|xīn li huà}{说|shuō}{清楚|qīng chu}。
= The owner says he holds the event because he noticed that people type faster and faster, yet seldom stop to think carefully about what they want to say. In a handwritten letter, every character from beginning to end has to be written slowly, and if you make a mistake you have to copy it out again. It's exactly this slowness that lets people say clearly what's in their hearts.
{第|dì}{一|yī}{年|nián}，{来|lái}{写信|xiě xìn}{的|de}{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{几|jǐ}{十|shí}{个|gè}{人|rén}；{到|dào}{了|le}{第|dì}{五|wǔ}{年|nián}，{已经|yǐ jīng}{有|yǒu}{一千|yì qiān}{多|duō}{人|rén}{参加|cān jiā}。{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{给|gěi}{远方|yuǎn fāng}{的|de}{父母|fù mǔ}{写|xiě}，{有的|yǒu de}{人|rén}{给|gěi}{十|shí}{年|nián}{后|hòu}{的|de}{自己|zì jǐ}{写|xiě}。{很|hěn}{多|duō}{收到|shōu dào}{信|xìn}{的|de}{人|rén}{说|shuō}，{他们|tā men}{把|bǎ}{信|xìn}{一一|yī yī}{收好|shōu hǎo}，{犹如|yóu rú}{收好|shōu hǎo}{了|le}{一|yí}{段|duàn}{时光|shí guāng}。
= In the first year only a few dozen people came to write; by the fifth, over a thousand took part. Some wrote to parents far away, some to themselves ten years on. Many who received letters said they kept them carefully, one by one, as if keeping a stretch of time.
```

<details>
<summary>A model retelling (about 150 characters)</summary>

{现在|xiàn zài}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}{觉得|jué de}{写信|xiě xìn}{已经|yǐ jīng}{过时|guò shí}{了|le}，{可是|kě shì}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{家|jiā}{小|xiǎo}{书店|shū diàn}{每|měi}{年|nián}{都|dōu}{办|bàn}{一|yí}{次|cì}"{手写信|shǒu xiě xìn}"{活动|huó dòng}：{店|diàn}{里|lǐ}{准备|zhǔn bèi}{好|hǎo}{信纸|xìn zhǐ}{和|hé}{钢笔|gāng bǐ}，{顾客|gù kè}{可以|kě yǐ}{给|gěi}{任何|rèn hé}{人|rén}{写信|xiě xìn}，{书店|shū diàn}{免费|miǎn fèi}{寄|jì}{出|chū}。{老板|lǎo bǎn}{说|shuō}，{他|tā}{办|bàn}{这个|zhè ge}{活动|huó dòng}，{是|shì}{因为|yīn wèi}{人们|rén men}{打字|dǎ zì}{很|hěn}{快|kuài}，{却|què}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{认真|rèn zhēn}{想|xiǎng}{要|yào}{说|shuō}{什么|shén me}，{而|ér}{手写信|shǒu xiě xìn}{要|yào}{一|yí}{个|gè}{字|zì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{字|zì}{慢|màn}{慢|màn}{写|xiě}，{能|néng}{让|ràng}{人|rén}{把|bǎ}{心里话|xīn li huà}{说|shuō}{清楚|qīng chu}。{活动|huó dòng}{越|yuè}{来|lái}{越|yuè}{受|shòu}{欢迎|huān yíng}，{从|cóng}{几|jǐ}{十|shí}{个|gè}{人|rén}{发展|fā zhǎn}{到|dào}{一千|yì qiān}{多|duō}{人|rén}。{很|hěn}{多|duō}{收到|shōu dào}{信|xìn}{的|de}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{把|bǎ}{信|xìn}{好好|hǎo hǎo}{地|de}{保存|bǎo cún}{下来|xià lái}。
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Formal phrases
{请|qǐng}{出示|chū shì}{您|nín}{的|de}{证件|zhèng jiàn}。
= Please show your identity document.
{未经|wèi jīng}{许可|xǔ kě}，{不得|bù dé}{拍照|pāi zhào}。
= No photographs without permission.
{报名|bào míng}{截止|jié zhǐ}{日期|rì qī}{是|shì}{本|běn}{月|yuè}{下旬|xià xún}。
= Registration closes in the last ten days of this month.
{请|qǐng}{保管|bǎo guǎn}{好|hǎo}{贵重|guì zhòng}{物品|wù pǐn}，{以免|yǐ miǎn}{丢失|diū shī}。
= Please look after your valuables so they aren't lost.
{上述|shàng shù}{问题|wèn tí}{我们|wǒ men}{将|jiāng}{尽快|jǐn kuài}{加以|jiā yǐ}{解决|jiě jué}。
= We will resolve the above problems as soon as possible.
{他|tā}{之所以|zhī suǒ yǐ}{迟到|chí dào}，{是|shì}{因为|yīn wèi}{路上|lù shang}{堵车|dǔ chē}。
= The reason he was late is that the traffic was bad.
```

## Pronunciation

- {该|gāi} gāi, the written "this", sounds exactly like HSK 3's {该|gāi} "should": only the grammar tells them
  apart ({该|gāi}{公司|gōng sī} vs {你|nǐ}{该|gāi}{走|zǒu}{了|le}).
- {一一|yī yī} yī yī keeps both first tones; {一律|yí lǜ} yí lǜ changes as usual (before a fourth tone).
- {不得|bù dé} bù dé (must not) is not {不得不|bù dé bù} bù dé bù (have to); and {得|dé} is dé, not de or děi.
- {为何|wèi hé} wèi hé, {为此|wèi cǐ} wèi cǐ: wèi, as in {为什么|wèi shén me}. {之所以|zhī suǒ yǐ} zhī suǒ yǐ: {所以|suǒ yǐ} joined to {之|zhī}, with 3+3 sandhi on {所以|suǒ yǐ} as
  usual (said suó yǐ).
- {={卷|juàn}=} juàn, a volume, fourth tone; {={卷|juǎn}=} juǎn (traditional {=捲=}), to roll, third (lesson 12).
- {截至|jié zhì} jié zhì and {截止|jié zhǐ} jié zhǐ differ only in the tone of the second syllable: fourth for "up to", third
  for "stop".

## Common mistakes

- ~~{该|gāi}{一|yí}{个|gè}{公司|gōng sī}~~: the written {该|gāi} takes no number or measure word: {该|gāi}{公司|gōng sī}.
- ~~{加以|jiā yǐ}{研究|yán jiū}{这个|zhè ge}{问题|wèn tí}~~: {加以|jiā yǐ} takes the verb as its object, and the thing goes before it, usually with {对|duì}: {对|duì}{这个|zhè ge}
  {问题|wèn tí}{加以|jiā yǐ}{研究|yán jiū}.
- ~~{他|tā}{之所以|zhī suǒ yǐ}{成功|chéng gōng}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}…~~: {之所以|zhī suǒ yǐ} pairs with {是|shì}{因为|yīn wèi} (or {是|shì}{由于|yóu yú}), not with {所以|suǒ yǐ}: {他|tā}{之所以|zhī suǒ yǐ}{成功|chéng gōng}，{是|shì}{因为|yīn wèi}….
- {截止|jié zhǐ}{十|shí}{月|yuè}{底|dǐ}，{已|yǐ}{有|yǒu}{三千|sān qiān}{人|rén}{报名|bào míng} is common, and you'll see it, but careful writers use {截至|jié zhì} before a date
  ("up to"): {截至|jié zhì}{十|shí}{月|yuè}{底|dǐ}.
- ~~{以便|yǐ biàn}{丢失|diū shī}~~: with something you want to avoid, use {以免|yǐ miǎn}: {以免|yǐ miǎn}{丢失|diū shī}. {以便|yǐ biàn} is for what you want to make
  possible.
- A notice in chatty language isn't wrong, but it looks careless; a chat in notice language sounds
  cold or comic. Match the register to the text.

## Key points

- {于|yú}: written "in, at, from, than, to": {建|jiàn}{于|yú}, {于|yú}{本|běn}{周五|zhōu wǔ}, {多|duō}{于|yú}, {适用|shì yòng}{于|yú}; the {于|yú} verbs: {位于|wèi yú}, {用于|yòng yú}, {源于|yuán yú}, {出于|chū yú}, {限于|xiàn yú},
  {易于|yì yú}, {处于|chǔ yú}, {便于|biàn yú}. {至于|zhì yú}: as for.
- {因|yīn} (because of: {因|yīn}{病|bìng}, {因|yīn}{雨|yǔ}); {之所以|zhī suǒ yǐ}…{是|shì}{因为|yīn wèi} (result first); {为此|wèi cǐ} (for this reason); {为何|wèi hé} (why).
- {以便|yǐ biàn} (so that) and {以免|yǐ miǎn} (so as not to) start the second clause.
- {该|gāi} (the said) + noun, {上述|shàng shù}, {诸多|zhū duō}, {极为|jí wéi} / {较为|jiào wéi}, {特|tè} ({特此|tè cǐ}), {未|wèi} ({未经|wèi jīng}{许可|xǔ kě}), {虽|suī}, {犹如|yóu rú}, {一律|yí lǜ}, {一一|yī yī} (yī yī), {加以|jiā yǐ} + verb,
  {其间|qí jiān}.
- Rules: {不宜|bù yí} < {不许|bù xǔ} < {不得|bù dé} < {严禁|yán jìn}; {许可|xǔ kě}. Dates: {截至|jié zhì} + date; {截止|jié zhǐ}{日期|rì qī}; {上旬|shàng xún} / {中旬|zhōng xún} / {下旬|xià xún}.
- Practical texts: title or greeting, reason, details, request, closing ({特此|tè cǐ}{公告|gōng gào}, name and date).
- Reports: {前者|qián zhě} / {后者|hòu zhě}, {本身|běn shēn}, {层次|céng cì} / {层面|céng miàn}, {典型|diǎn xíng}, {定义|dìng yì}, {要素|yào sù}, {效应|xiào yìng}, {限度|xiàn dù}, {实质|shí zhì}, {类别|lèi bié}.
- New characters: {抄|chāo} {截|jié} {旬|xún} {携|xié} {叙|xù} {诸|zhū} (✎ {抄|chāo} {旬|xún}).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Dialects, idioms and set phrases
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You started {成语|chéng yǔ} (idioms) in HSK 5 with {丰富多彩|fēng fù duō cǎi}, {各行各业|gè háng gè yè} and {五颜六色|wǔ yán liù sè}. HSK 6 has thirteen more idioms and
set phrases, and they're among the most useful in the language: you'll hear {众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī} in speeches, {人|rén}{山|shān}
{人|rén}{海|hǎi} in every holiday news report, {一模一样|yì mú yí yàng} between friends. This lesson teaches them as a set: what
each one is made of, where it goes in a sentence, and the mistakes learners make with them.

It also gives you the words to talk about language itself: {方言|fāng yán} (dialect), {母语|mǔ yǔ} (mother tongue), {声调|shēng diào}
(tone), {音节|yīn jié} (syllable), {符号|fú hào} (symbol), {含义|hán yì} (meaning) and the stroke names {横|héng} and {竖|shù}. The reading is an
essay by a translator who grew up speaking a southern dialect and learned Putonghua at university.

The story: {李明|Lǐ Míng} (Li Ming), now a translator at a company in Beijing, has a colleague, {邱晓峰|Qiū Xiǎo fēng} (Qiu
Xiaofeng), whose Putonghua is so good that nobody guesses where he's from.

## What a {成语|chéng yǔ} is

A **{成语|chéng yǔ}** (chéng yǔ, an idiom) is a fixed phrase, almost always of four characters, that the language
has kept for centuries: you can't change its words or their order, and its meaning is often more than
its parts. A **[[set phrase]]** ({固定说法|gù dìng shuō fǎ}) is looser: a fixed expression, like {方方面面|fāng fāng miàn miàn}, that isn't a classical
idiom but is used as one. The thirteen of this level:

| Idiom | Literally | Meaning | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| {成千上万|chéng qiān shàng wàn} | become thousands, reach ten thousands | thousands upon thousands | parallel pair |
| {千家万户|qiān jiā wàn hù} | thousand families, ten thousand households | every household, everyone | parallel pair |
| {家家户户|jiā jiā hù hù} | family family household household | every single household | doubled (AABB) |
| {方方面面|fāng fāng miàn miàn} | side side aspect aspect | every aspect | doubled (AABB) |
| {人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi} | people mountain, people sea | a huge crowd | parallel pair |
| {自言自语|zì yán zì yǔ} | self speak, self talk | to talk to oneself | parallel pair ({自|zì}A{自|zì}B) |
| {多才多艺|duō cái duō yì} | much talent, much art | talented in many ways | parallel pair ({多|duō}A{多|duō}B) |
| {衣食住行|yī shí zhù xíng} | clothes, food, housing, travel | the basic needs of life | four nouns |
| {一模一样|yì mú yí yàng} yì mú yí yàng | one mould, one shape | exactly alike | {一|yī}A{一|yī}B |
| {一帆风顺|yì fān fēng shùn} | one sail, the wind fair | plain sailing | subject + predicate |
| {众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī} | what everyone knows thoroughly | as everyone knows | subject + {所|suǒ} + verb |
| {至关重要|zhì guān zhòng yào} | extremely important | of vital importance | adverb + adjective |
| {大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng} | greatly eat one shock | to get a great shock | verb phrase |

Many four-character idioms are built as **two parallel halves** (A-B + A-B: {人|rén}{山|shān} / {人|rén}{海|hǎi}, {自|zì}{言|yán} / {自|zì}{语|yǔ}), and
knowing this helps you remember them: the halves repeat a pattern and often mean nearly the same thing.
Some, like {一帆风顺|yì fān fēng shùn}, are a small sentence: {风|fēng}{顺|shùn} is "the wind is favourable", a subject and a predicate.
{众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī} uses the {所|suǒ} of lesson 27: {众|zhòng} (the crowd, everyone) + {所|suǒ} + {周|zhōu}{知|zhī} (to know completely).

## Where an idiom goes in a sentence

An idiom behaves like a single word, and each one has its own job.

**As a predicate**, after the subject, like an adjective:

- {节日|jié rì}{期间|qī jiān}，{公园|gōng yuán}{里|lǐ}{人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi}。 — During the holiday the park is packed with people.
- {他|tā}{多才多艺|duō cái duō yì}，{会|huì}{画|huà}{画|huà}，{会|huì}{弹|tán}{钢琴|gāng qín}，{还|hái}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{诗|shī}。 — He's talented in all sorts of ways: he paints, plays the piano and even writes poems.
- {这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{张|zhāng}{照片|zhào piàn}{一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}。 — These two photos are exactly the same.

**As an attributive**, before a noun, with {的|de}:

- {一|yí}{个|gè}{多才多艺|duō cái duō yì}{的|de}{人|rén} — a many-talented person
- {成千上万|chéng qiān shàng wàn}{的|de}{游客|yóu kè} — tens of thousands of tourists
- {一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}{的|de}{裙子|qún zi} — exactly the same skirt

**As an adverbial**, before a verb, with {地|de}:

- {他|tā}{一边|yì biān}{走|zǒu}，{一边|yì biān}{自言自语|zì yán zì yǔ}{地|de}{说|shuō}{着|zhe}{什么|shén me}。 — As he walked, he was muttering something to himself.

**As an object or a subject**:

- {我们|wǒ men}{要|yào}{考虑|kǎo lǜ}{到|dào}{方方面面|fāng fāng miàn miàn}。 — We need to think about every aspect.
- {衣食住行|yī shí zhù xíng}{都|dōu}{离|lí}{不|bu}{开|kāi}{钱|qián}。 — Food, clothes, housing and transport all take money.

**At the start of a sentence**, with a comma, for the whole statement:

- {众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī}，{健康|jiàn kāng}{至关重要|zhì guān zhòng yào}。 — As everyone knows, health is of vital importance.

## The thirteen, one by one

- **{成千上万|chéng qiān shàng wàn}** goes before a noun ({成千上万|chéng qiān shàng wàn}{的|de}{人|rén}) or after {有|yǒu} ({每|měi}{天|tiān}{有|yǒu}{成千上万|chéng qiān shàng wàn}{的|de}{人|rén}{经过|jīng guò}{这里|zhè lǐ}). It's "thousands and
  thousands", not an exact figure.
- **{千家万户|qiān jiā wàn hù}** and **{家家户户|jiā jiā hù hù}** both mean every household, but they're used differently. {千家万户|qiān jiā wàn hù} is "all the
  homes of a whole country or city", often as an object: {网络|wǎng luò}{已经|yǐ jīng}{走|zǒu}{进|jìn}{了|le}{千家万户|qiān jiā wàn hù}。 (The internet has reached
  every home.) {家家户户|jiā jiā hù hù} is "each and every household" in one place, often as a subject with {都|dōu}: {过年|guò nián}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，
  {家家户户|jiā jiā hù hù}{都|dōu}{贴|tiē}{春联|chūn lián}。 (At New Year every household puts up couplets. {春联|chūn lián}, glossed.)
- **{方方面面|fāng fāng miàn miàn}** is every aspect: {生活|shēng huó}{的|de}{方方面面|fāng fāng miàn miàn} (every aspect of life), {考虑|kǎo lǜ}{到|dào}{方方面面|fāng fāng miàn miàn}.
- **{人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi}** is the predicate of a crowded place: {车站|chē zhàn}{里|lǐ}{人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi}。 It can't take a measure: ~~{一|yí}{个|gè}{人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi}~~.
- **{自言自语|zì yán zì yǔ}** is "to talk to oneself", as a verb ({他|tā}{常常|cháng cháng}{自言自语|zì yán zì yǔ}) or with {地|de}.
- **{多才多艺|duō cái duō yì}** describes a person: {她|tā}{多才多艺|duō cái duō yì}。 {一|yí}{位|wèi}{多才多艺|duō cái duō yì}{的|de}{演员|yǎn yuán}.
- **{衣食住行|yī shí zhù xíng}** names the four basic needs, as a subject or object: {衣食住行|yī shí zhù xíng}{的|de}{变化|biàn huà} (changes in daily life).
- **{一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}** (yì mú yí yàng: {模|mú} is mú here, as in {模样|mú yàng}, not mó) is "exactly alike": A {和|hé} B {一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}, A {跟|gēn} B
  {长|zhǎng}{得|de}{一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}.
- **{一帆风顺|yì fān fēng shùn}** is plain sailing, and very often a wish: {祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{一帆风顺|yì fān fēng shùn}！ (I wish you every success.) Or with {不|bú}{是|shì}:
  {人生|rén shēng}{不|bù}{可能|kě néng}{总是|zǒng shì}{一帆风顺|yì fān fēng shùn}。 (Life can't always be plain sailing.)
- **{众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī}** starts a sentence: {众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī}，… Use it for what really is common knowledge.
- **{至关重要|zhì guān zhòng yào}** is "of vital importance", usually with {对|duì}: {睡眠|shuì mián}{对|duì}{健康|jiàn kāng}{至关重要|zhì guān zhòng yào}。 (Sleep is vital to health.)
- **{大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng}** is to be astonished: {听|tīng}{到|dào}{这个|zhè ge}{消息|xiāo xi}，{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng}。 To say what caused it, put the cause first, or
  use {让|ràng} / {使|shǐ}: {他|tā}{的|de}{回答|huí dá}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng}。

## Common mistakes with idioms

- ~~{很|hěn}{众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī}~~, ~~{非常|fēi cháng}{至关重要|zhì guān zhòng yào}~~, ~~{十分|shí fēn}{一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}~~: an idiom already has its degree built in. Don't add {很|hěn}, {非常|fēi cháng} or
  {十分|shí fēn}. ({至|zhì}{关|guān} already means "extremely".)
- ~~{大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng}{这个|zhè ge}{消息|xiāo xi}~~: {大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng} takes no object. Say {这个|zhè ge}{消息|xiāo xi}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng} or {听|tīng}{到|dào}{这个|zhè ge}{消息|xiāo xi}，{我|wǒ}{大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng}.
- {这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}{书|shū}{一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}{的|de} is heard in speech, but in writing say {这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}{书|shū}{一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}: as a predicate, no {的|de} is needed (with {是|shì}…{的|de} it's
  fine: {这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}{书|shū}{是|shì}{一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}{的|de}).
- {一|yí}{个|gè}{人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi}{的|de}{地方|dì fang} is fine, but {一|yí}{个|gè}{人|rén}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{的|de}{地方|dì fang} or {人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi} as a predicate is more usual.
- **[[Register]]**: most idioms are neutral or a little formal. A speech or an essay can take several;
  a chat with a friend, one at most, or it sounds like a textbook. Lesson 26's essay checklist
  applies: one well-placed idiom does more than five.

  {你|nǐ}{的|de}{字|zì}{写|xiě}{歪|wāi}{了|le}。 (Your characters are crooked.)

Strokes have names, and you can now say them in Chinese: {横|héng} (héng, horizontal), {竖|shù} (shù, vertical), {撇|piě} (piě,
left-falling), {点|diǎn} (diǎn, dot), {捺|nà} (nà, right-falling) and {折|zhé} (zhé, a turn). A teacher might say: {先|xiān}{写|xiě}{横|héng}，{再|zài}{写|xiě}{竖|shù}。

**{外来词|wài lái cí}** (loanwords) take one of three routes into Chinese. Some copy the sound: {沙发|shā fā} (sofa), {咖啡|kā fēi} (coffee),
{巧克力|qiǎo kè lì} (chocolate), {模特儿|mó tèr} (model). Some translate the meaning: {电脑|diàn nǎo} (electric brain, a computer), {热狗|rè gǒu} (hot dog).
And some do both, sound and meaning at once: {幽默|yōu mò} (yōu mò, "humour") sounds like the English word and its
characters suggest something quiet and subtle. Naming a new thing well is an art: a good name is {巧妙|qiǎo miào},
and a clumsy one sounds {歪|wāi}.

### Stroke order

- **{横|héng}**: {木|mù} first (horizontal, vertical, left-falling, dot), then {黄|huáng}: a short horizontal, the two short
  verticals and the long horizontal, then {由|yóu}, then a left-falling stroke and a dot at the bottom.
- **{竖|shù}**: the two short verticals on the top left, then {又|yòu}, then {立|lì}: dot, horizontal, the dot and the
  left-falling stroke, the long horizontal last.
- **{帆|fān}**: {巾|jīn} first (vertical, horizontal-turn-hook, the long vertical through the middle), then {凡|fán}: the
  left-falling stroke, the horizontal-turn-slanting hook, the dot inside.

1. His Putonghua wasn't standard: he said {四|sì} for {是|shì} and {私人|sī rén} ("private") for {诗人|shī rén} ("poet"), and couldn't tell zh, ch, sh

"**My two 'mother tongues'.** I was born in a small town in the south. There, every household
speaks the dialect, and every aspect of life, from food and clothes to every feeling, depends on it.
Our dialect has its own tones and syllables, very different from Putonghua's; some words can't even
be written in characters. The old people at home speak only the dialect, and can hardly follow the
Putonghua on television. As a child I thought everyone in the world talked like this.

The year I turned eighteen I got into a university in Beijing. The first day, walking into the
dorm, I greeted my roommates in what I thought was standard Putonghua, and to my surprise they just
stared. Later I found out I'd said sì for shì, and sīrén ("private") for shīrén ("poet"). Once, answering a question in class, I'd said only two sentences when someone
laughed out loud. For a while I
was nervous whenever I opened my mouth, and sometimes I'd rather say nothing than let people hear my
accent.

I made up my mind to learn Putonghua properly. A teacher told me that to learn pronunciation you
first have to listen: only when you hear clearly can you speak clearly. So every morning I went to
the sports ground to read texts aloud, and in the evenings I listened to the radio, imitated the
presenters' tones and intonation, and recorded my own voice to compare with the radio sentence by
sentence. What gave me the biggest headache was zh, ch, sh and z, c, s: in my dialect there's no
difference between the two sets. To get them right I copied the words I tended to say wrong onto
cards and took them everywhere. My roommates laughed that I talked to myself all day, but a year later,
listening to me, they couldn't tell where I was from. Of course I still slip now and then: when I'm in a hurry, {是|shì}
turns into {四|sì} again. But I'm not afraid any more: if I get it wrong, I just say it again.

Now I'm a translator, working in Putonghua and English every day. People ask me: after all these
years of Putonghua, is there any point keeping a dialect? My answer is: of course there is.
Putonghua is the language used throughout the country; with it, people from different regions can
communicate smoothly, and that's vital. But a dialect has things Putonghua can't replace. Our dialect
has a word for the feeling after rain when the air is damp and cool and very pleasant, and I can never
find a suitable word in Putonghua to translate it. Behind a word like that lie centuries of a place's
life and culture: it has real depth. A few years ago I even took part in a project to protect
the dialect, helping to record the stories old people told and write them down.

So, as I see it, Putonghua and dialect aren't in conflict: it's like one person having two mother
tongues. The former took me out of my home town; the latter reminds me where I come from. Last year my
child was born. When he's a bit older, I plan to teach him both standard Putonghua and our home
dialect."

people speak it at school, and can't do without it online or watching TV. So some worry that
dialects will slowly disappear. I think the use of dialects will certainly decline, but they won't
necessarily disappear. First, a dialect is part of a place's life and culture. Many old people
speak only the dialect, and children who go back to their home town need a little of it to talk with
their grandparents. Second, dialects have many words and expressions Putonghua can't replace, and some
local operas can only be sung in dialect. These things are vital to a place, and people won't give them
up lightly. Of course, we must also see that if nobody uses a dialect, it may grow weaker and weaker.
Even so, we needn't set Putonghua and dialects against each other. Putonghua lets us talk with people
across the country; a dialect lets us remember our home. So rather than worrying that dialects will
disappear, it's better to let children learn both from an early age."

```speak
{从|cóng}{那|nà}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{他|tā}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{花|huā}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{练习|liàn xí}{声调|shēng diào}。{他|tā}{把|bǎ}{容易|róng yì}{说|shuō}{错|cuò}{的|de}{词|cí}{写|xiě}{在|zài}{卡片|kǎ piàn}{上|shàng}，{一边|yì biān}{朗读|lǎng dú}，{一边|yì biān}{用|yòng}{手势|shǒu shì}{帮|bāng}{自己|zì jǐ}{记|jì}{住|zhù}{声调|shēng diào}{的|de}{方向|fāng xiàng}：{第|dì}{一|yī}{声|shēng}{手|shǒu}{平|píng}{着|zhe}{走|zǒu}，{第|dì}{四|sì}{声|shēng}{手|shǒu}{往|wǎng}{下|xià}。{同学|tóng xué}{们|men}{觉得|jué de}{他|tā}{的|de}{样子|yàng zi}{很|hěn}{好笑|hǎo xiào}，{他|tā}{却|què}{说|shuō}，{这个|zhè ge}{办法|bàn fǎ}{很|hěn}{妙|miào}。
= From then on he spent half an hour every day practising tones. He wrote words he tended to get wrong on cards, and as he read them aloud he used gestures to help himself remember which way each tone went: for the first tone his hand moved level, for the fourth it went down. His classmates thought he looked funny, but he said the method worked wonderfully.
{一|yì}{年|nián}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{他|tā}{参加|cān jiā}{了|le}{学校|xué xiào}{的|de}{朗读|lǎng dú}{比赛|bǐ sài}，{得|dé}{了|le}{第|dì}{一|yī}{名|míng}。{他|tā}{说|shuō}，{学|xué}{语言|yǔ yán}{没有|méi yǒu}{什么|shén me}{巧妙|qiǎo miào}{的|de}{办法|bàn fǎ}，{最|zuì}{重要|zhòng yào}{的|de}{是|shì}{不|bú}{怕|pà}{说|shuō}{错|cuò}，{每|měi}{天|tiān}{坚持|jiān chí}。
= A year later he entered the school's reading-aloud competition and came first. He said there's no clever trick to learning a language: the main thing is not to be afraid of mistakes and to keep at it every day.
```

<details>
<summary>A model retelling (about 140 characters)</summary>

{一|yí}{个|gè}{外国|wài guó}{留学生|liú xué shēng}{刚|gāng}{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}{时|shí}，{觉得|jué de}{声调|shēng diào}{最|zuì}{难|nán}。{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{次|cì}{他|tā}{想|xiǎng}{要|yào}{一|yì}{碗|wǎn}{汤|tāng}，{却|què}{说|shuō}{成|chéng}{了|le}"{一|yì}{碗|wǎn}{糖|táng}"，{让|ràng}{服务|fú wù}{员|yuán}{大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng}。{后来|hòu lái}，{他|tā}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{练习|liàn xí}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}，{把|bǎ}{容易|róng yì}{错|cuò}{的|de}{词|cí}{写|xiě}{在|zài}{卡片|kǎ piàn}{上|shàng}，{一边|yì biān}{读|dú}{一边|yì biān}{用|yòng}{手势|shǒu shì}{记|jì}{声调|shēng diào}。{同学|tóng xué}{们|men}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{好笑|hǎo xiào}，{他|tā}{却|què}{觉得|jué de}{这个|zhè ge}{办法|bàn fǎ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。{一|yì}{年|nián}{后|hòu}，{他|tā}{在|zài}{朗读|lǎng dú}{比赛|bǐ sài}{中|zhōng}{得|dé}{了|le}{第|dì}{一|yī}{名|míng}。{他|tā}{认为|rèn wéi}，{学|xué}{语言|yǔ yán}{最|zuì}{重要|zhòng yào}{的|de}{是|shì}{不|bú}{怕|pà}{说|shuō}{错|cuò}，{坚持|jiān chí}{练习|liàn xí}。
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Idioms in use
{众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī}，{坚持|jiān chí}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{对|duì}{健康|jiàn kāng}{至关重要|zhì guān zhòng yào}。
= As everyone knows, regular exercise is vital to health.
{春节|Chūn jié}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{火车站|huǒ chē zhàn}{里|lǐ}{人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi}。
= At the Spring Festival the railway stations are packed with people.
{这|zhè}{对|duì}{双胞胎|shuāng bāo tāi}{长|zhǎng}{得|de}{一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}。
= These twins look exactly alike.
{祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{新|xīn}{的|de}{工作|gōng zuò}{一帆风顺|yì fān fēng shùn}！
= I wish you plain sailing in your new job!
{听|tīng}{到|dào}{这个|zhè ge}{消息|xiāo xi}，{我|wǒ}{大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng}。
= I was astonished to hear the news.
{这个|zhè ge}{主意|zhǔ yi}{真|zhēn}{妙|miào}！
= What a brilliant idea!
```

{双胞胎|shuāng bāo tāi} (shuāng bāo tāi): twins.

## Pronunciation

- {一模一样|yì mú yí yàng} yì mú yí yàng: {模|mú} is mú (as in {模样|mú yàng}, lesson 22), not the mó of {模仿|mó fǎng} and {模特儿|mó tèr}. The first {一|yī} is yì
  (before mú, a second tone), the second yí (before yàng, a fourth).
- {一帆风顺|yì fān fēng shùn} yì fān fēng shùn: {一|yī} before a first tone, so yì.
- {成千上万|chéng qiān shàng wàn} chéng qiān shàng wàn (2-1-4-4); {众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī} zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī (4-3-1-1). Say
  each idiom as one unit, without a pause inside it.
- {横|héng} héng and {竖|shù} shù: as stroke names; {横|héng} is also hèng (rude, unreasonable) in a few words you'll meet later.
- {识|shí} shí (to know), second tone, as in {认识|rèn shi} rèn shi (where it's light) and {知识|zhī shi} zhī shi.
- {方言|fāng yán} fāng yán, {母语|mǔ yǔ} mǔ yǔ: {母语|mǔ yǔ} is two third tones, said mú yǔ.

## Key points

- A {成语|chéng yǔ} is a fixed phrase, usually four characters; you can't change its words. Many are two parallel
  halves ({人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi}, {自言自语|zì yán zì yǔ}, {多才多艺|duō cái duō yì}); some double their characters ({家家户户|jiā jiā hù hù}, {方方面面|fāng fāng miàn miàn}); some are small
  sentences ({一帆风顺|yì fān fēng shùn}, {众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī}).
- Each has a job: predicate ({人山人海|rén shān rén hǎi}, {一模一样|yì mú yí yàng}, {多才多艺|duō cái duō yì}), attributive with {的|de} ({成千上万|chéng qiān shàng wàn}{的|de}), adverbial with {地|de}
  ({自言自语|zì yán zì yǔ}{地|de}), object ({方方面面|fāng fāng miàn miàn}, {千家万户|qiān jiā wàn hù}), sentence opener ({众所周知|zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī}，…).
- Never {很|hěn} / {非常|fēi cháng} before an idiom; {大吃一惊|dà chī yì jīng} takes no object; {至关重要|zhì guān zhòng yào} goes with {对|duì}.
- Language words: {方言|fāng yán}, {母语|mǔ yǔ}, {地域|dì yù}, {声调|shēng diào}, {音节|yīn jié}, {符号|fú hào}, {含义|hán yì}, {内涵|nèi hán}, {手势|shǒu shì}, {外来词|wài lái cí}; {精通|jīng tōng}, {入门|rù mén}, {朗读|lǎng dú}, {模仿|mó fǎng}, {命名|mìng míng},
  {称作|chēng zuò}, {简化|jiǎn huà}, {通用|tōng yòng}; {横|héng} and {竖|shù} as strokes.
- New characters: {横|héng} {涵|hán} {妙|miào} {竖|shù} {歪|wāi} {帆|fān} (✎ {妙|miào} {帆|fān}).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Sport and competition: writing and speaking practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last lesson with new words. It has two halves:

- **Sport and competition**: the words for contests and results ({选拔|xuǎn bá}, {淘汰|táo tài}, {排名|pái míng}, {冠军|guàn jūn}, {亚军|yà jūn}, {季军|jì jūn}, {金牌|jīn pái}…),
  for sports ({田径|tián jìng}, {体操|tǐ cāo}, {跳水|tiào shuǐ}, {滑冰|huá bīng}, {滑雪|huá xuě}, {射击|shè jī}, {围棋|wéi qí}, {象棋|xiàng qí}…) and for what bodies do ({奔跑|bēn pǎo}, {踩|cǎi}, {蹲|dūn}, {扑|pū}, {抛|pāo}, {扭|niǔ}),
  with two colloquial formats in passing: {好|hǎo}{你|nǐ}{个|gè} X and X {到|dào} Y {头|tóu}{上|shàng}{来|lái}{了|le}.
- **The writing and speaking parts of the exam**, put together: the practical text and the argued
  essay, then the speaking tasks: retelling a passage, telling a story from four photos, and giving
  your opinion.

The story: {大卫|Dà wèi} (David) has decided to stay in Beijing. His company with {白涛|Bái Tāo} (Bai Tao) has grown, and
the staff have started a lunchtime chess habit and a team for the city's amateur games.

## Contests and results

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {竞赛|jìng sài} | a competition, contest (often of knowledge or skill) | {数学|shù xué}{竞赛|jìng sài} |
| {赛事|sài shì} | a sporting event | {今年|jīn nián}{的|de}{赛事|sài shì}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 |
| {选拔|xuǎn bá} | to select (by trials) | {选拔|xuǎn bá}{运动员|yùn dòng yuán} |
| {入选|rù xuǎn} | to be selected | {她|tā}{入选|rù xuǎn}{了|le}{国家|guó jiā}{队|duì}。 |
| {淘汰|táo tài} | to eliminate, knock out | {他|tā}{在|zài}{第|dì}{一|yī}{轮|lún}{就|jiù}{被|bèi}{淘汰|táo tài}{了|le}。 |
| {轮|lún} | a round (measure word: {第|dì}{二|èr}{轮|lún}) | {比赛|bǐ sài}{进入|jìn rù}{了|le}{第|dì}{三|sān}{轮|lún}。 |
| {局|jú} | a game, a set (measure word: {一|yì}{局|jú}{棋|qí}) | {三|sān}{局|jú}{两|liǎng}{胜|shèng} |
| {排名|pái míng} | a ranking; to rank | {他|tā}{的|de}{排名|pái míng}{升|shēng}{到|dào}{了|le}{第|dì}{五|wǔ}。 |
| {出场|chū chǎng} | to come on, appear (in a match, on stage) | {他|tā}{第|dì}{二|èr}{个|gè}{出场|chū chǎng}。 |
| {上台|shàng tái} | to go on stage, onto the podium | {冠军|guàn jūn}{上台|shàng tái}{领|lǐng}{奖|jiǎng}。 |
| {夺|duó}, {夺取|duó qǔ}, {争夺|zhēng duó} | to seize, win; to fight for | {夺冠|duó guàn} (to win the title), {夺取|duó qǔ}{金牌|jīn pái}, {争夺|zhēng duó}{第|dì}{一|yī}{名|míng} |
| {击败|jī bài}, {战胜|zhàn shèng}, {败|bài} | to defeat; to beat, overcome; to lose | {他|tā}{击败|jī bài}{了|le}{去年|qù nián}{的|de}{冠军|guàn jūn}。{我们|wǒ men}{败|bài}{了|le}。 |
| {亚军|yà jūn}, {季军|jì jūn} | runner-up, third place | {冠军|guàn jūn}、{亚军|yà jūn}、{季军|jì jūn} |
| {金牌|jīn pái}, {银牌|yín pái}, {铜牌|tóng pái}, {奖牌|jiǎng pái} | gold, silver, bronze medal; a medal | {一共|yí gòng}{拿|ná}{了|le}{三|sān}{块|kuài}{奖牌|jiǎng pái} |
| {团体|tuán tǐ} | a group, a team (as opposed to individual) | {团体|tuán tǐ}{比赛|bǐ sài}, {团体|tuán tǐ}{冠军|guàn jūn} |
| {高手|gāo shǒu}, {技巧|jì qiǎo}, {高超|gāo chāo} | an expert; a technique; superb | {他|tā}{是|shì}{象棋|xiàng qí}{高手|gāo shǒu}，{技巧|jì qiǎo}{高超|gāo chāo}。 |
| {俱乐部|jù lè bù}, {协会|xié huì} | a club; an association | {足球|zú qiú}{俱乐部|jù lè bù}, {围棋|wéi qí}{协会|xié huì} |
| {场地|chǎng dì}, {场馆|chǎng guǎn} | a ground, a venue; a stadium, a sports hall | {比赛|bǐ sài}{场地|chǎng dì}, {体育|tǐ yù}{场馆|chǎng guǎn} |
| {起点|qǐ diǎn}, {终点|zhōng diǎn}, {全程|quán chéng} | the start, the finish, the whole course | {全程|quán chéng}{十|shí}{公里|gōng lǐ} |
| {次数|cì shù} | the number of times | {训练|xùn liàn}{的|de}{次数|cì shù} |
| {解说|jiě shuō} | to commentate; a commentary | {他|tā}{在|zài}{电视|diàn shì}{上|shàng}{解说|jiě shuō}{足球|zú qiú}{比赛|bǐ sài}。 |

The pairs to watch:

- **{击败|jī bài}** and **{战胜|zhàn shèng}** are both "to defeat": {击败|jī bài} is the word of results ({击败|jī bài}{对手|duì shǒu}, to beat an opponent),
  {战胜|zhàn shèng} is also "to overcome" ({战胜|zhàn shèng}{困难|kùn nan}, {战胜|zhàn shèng}{自己|zì jǐ}). **{败|bài}** alone is "to lose, be defeated" (written; spoken
  {输|shū}): {甲|jiǎ}{队|duì}{以|yǐ}{二|èr}{比|bǐ}{三|sān}{败|bài}{给|gěi}{了|le}{乙|yǐ}{队|duì}。 (Team A lost 2–3 to Team B.)
- **{夺|duó}** is "to seize": {夺冠|duó guàn} (to win the championship), {夺得|duó dé}{金牌|jīn pái}; {夺取|duó qǔ} and {争夺|zhēng duó} are two-syllable verbs for the
  same: {两|liǎng}{队|duì}{争夺|zhēng duó}{冠军|guàn jūn}。
- **{轮|lún}** (a round of a competition) and **{局|jú}** (a game or set within a match: chess, table tennis,
  tennis): {第|dì}{一|yī}{轮|lún}{比赛|bǐ sài}, {一|yì}{局|jú}{棋|qí}, {三|sān}{局|jú}{两|liǎng}{胜|shèng} (best of three games).
- **{中|zhòng}** (zhòng, to hit a target): {射中|shè zhòng} (to hit), {打中|dǎ zhòng}, {猜中|cāi zhòng} (to guess right). It's the zhòng of {中奖|zhòng jiǎng} (to win
  a prize, lesson 13). **{射|shè}** is "to shoot": {射门|shè mén} (to shoot at goal), {射箭|shè jiàn} (archery), and **{射击|shè jī}** is the
  sport of shooting.

## Sports

| Sport | | Sport | |
|---|---|---|---|
| {田径|tián jìng} | athletics, track and field | {体操|tǐ cāo} | gymnastics |
| {跳水|tiào shuǐ} | diving | {射击|shè jī} | shooting |
| {滑冰|huá bīng} | ice skating | {滑雪|huá xuě} | skiing |
| {棒球|bàng qiú} | baseball | {台球|tái qiú} | billiards, snooker |
| {围棋|wéi qí} | go | {象棋|xiàng qí} | Chinese chess |

{滑|huá} is "to slide": {滑冰|huá bīng}, {滑雪|huá xuě} and {滑行|huá xíng} (to glide, as a skater or a plane on the runway). {围棋|wéi qí} and {象棋|xiàng qí} are
played with {棋子|qí zǐ} (pieces): {围棋|wéi qí} with black and white stones on a board of lines, {象棋|xiàng qí} with round pieces
marked with characters. In Chinese you {下棋|xià qí} (play chess: {下|xià} is the verb); children may say {玩|wán}{棋|qí}, but players say {下|xià}.

## The body in action

- **{奔跑|bēn pǎo}** (to run fast, race along): {孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{在|zài}{草地|cǎo dì}{上|shàng}{奔跑|bēn pǎo}。 It's written; in speech, {跑|pǎo}.
- **{踩|cǎi}** (to step on, tread): {你|nǐ}{踩|cǎi}{到|dào}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{脚|jiǎo}{了|le}！ **{蹲|dūn}** (to squat): {蹲|dūn}{下来|xià lái}. **{扑|pū}** (to throw oneself at, pounce):
  {守门员|shǒu mén yuán}{向|xiàng}{左|zuǒ}{一|yì}{扑|pū}，{把|bǎ}{球|qiú}{扑|pū}{了|le}{出去|chū qù}。 (The goalkeeper dived left and pushed the ball out.) **{抛|pāo}** (to throw, toss):
  {把|bǎ}{球|qiú}{抛|pāo}{起来|qǐ lái}. **{扭|niǔ}** (to twist, sprain): {扭|niǔ}{伤|shāng}{了|le}{脚|jiǎo} (to sprain an ankle).
- **{后退|hòu tuì}** (to step back, retreat): {往|wǎng}{后退|hòu tuì}{一|yí}{步|bù}. **{棍|gùn}** (a stick): {一|yì}{根|gēn}{木|mù}{棍|gùn}.
- **{使劲|shǐ jìn}** (to put effort in, push hard): {使劲|shǐ jìn}{推|tuī}; **{有劲|yǒu jìn}** (to be strong, energetic: {他|tā}{很|hěn}{有劲|yǒu jìn}); **{强壮|qiáng zhuàng}** (strong,
  sturdy); **{一口气|yì kǒu qì}** (in one breath, without stopping): {他|tā}{一口气|yì kǒu qì}{跑|pǎo}{了|le}{十|shí}{公里|gōng lǐ}。
- **{足|zú}** (full, sufficient: {信心|xìn xīn}{十足|shí zú}, lesson 24's {十足|shí zú}; {准备|zhǔn bèi}{得|de}{很|hěn}{足|zú}) and **{酷|kù}** (cool: spoken, from English:
  {这个|zhè ge}{动作|dòng zuò}{太|tài}{酷|kù}{了|le}！).

## Two colloquial formats

**{好|hǎo}{你|nǐ}{个|gè} X** (well, you X!) is a teasing or mock-angry exclamation when someone has surprised you,
usually with a person's name or a description:

- {好|hǎo}{你|nǐ}{个|gè}{大卫|Dà wèi}，{居然|jū rán}{赢|yíng}{了|le}{我|wǒ}！ — Well, David, you sly one: you've beaten me!
- {好|hǎo}{你|nǐ}{个|gè}{小王|Xiǎo Wáng}，{这么|zhè me}{大|dà}{的|de}{事|shì}{都|dōu}{不|bú}{告诉|gào su}{我|wǒ}。 — Honestly, Xiao Wang: something this big and you didn't tell me.

**X {到|dào} Y {头|tóu}{上|shàng}{来|lái}{了|le}** (it's come as far as Y: now even Y is affected) says that something unwelcome has
reached someone it shouldn't, often the speaker: {管|guǎn}{到|dào}{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{上|shàng}{来|lái}{了|le} (now you're bossing even me about), {欺负|qī fu}{到|dào}
{我们|wǒ men}{头|tóu}{上|shàng}{来|lái}{了|le} (now they're even picking on us).

- {你|nǐ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{新|xīn}{来|lái}{的|de}，{倒|dào}{管|guǎn}{到|dào}{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{上|shàng}{来|lái}{了|le}？ — You've only just arrived, and you're telling me what to do?

Both are spoken and lively: never in an essay.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| {奔|bēn} ✎ | rush, run | bēn | {大|dà} | 8 | {奔跑|bēn pǎo} |
| {踩|cǎi} | step on | cǎi | {足|zú} | 15 | {踩|cǎi} |

"**From 'eliminated' to the podium.** At the national youth diving championships that ended last
week, seventeen-year-old Lu Hang won the bronze medal in the women's ten-metre platform. On the
podium she smiled and waved to the crowd. Few people know that five years ago she was judged 'unsuited'
to the sport.

Lu Hang did gymnastics from childhood. At seven she entered the city sports school and trained six
hours a day: up at six, a run, then basic moves, and strength training in the evening. Gymnastics is extremely demanding of the body: once you grow tall, many moves become
hard to do. At twelve she grew more than ten centimetres and was eliminated at a selection. 'I cried
for a long time that night,' she remembers. 'I thought I'd never compete again in my life.'

What changed her fate was a diving coach, who had watched her train in the gymnastics hall and thought
her moves in the air were special, and asked if she'd like to try diving. 'At first I didn't even dare
jump off the three-metre board,' Lu Hang laughs. 'Standing up there, my legs wouldn't stop shaking.' But
gymnastics had left her a foundation: plenty of strength, good body control, and she learned twists and
somersaults fast. Her coach often says diving tests not
just nerve but control of the body: from the take-off through the moves in the air to the entry, no
stage can go wrong. A year later she could already dive from the ten-metre platform.

Progress wasn't plain sailing, though. At fifteen she sprained her foot in training and couldn't go in
the water for three whole months. Watching her teammates go off to competitions one after another, she
was anxious. But her coach told her: 'Injury isn't frightening. What's frightening is giving up on
yourself first.' During that time she went to the side of the pool every day to watch the others train,
and noted in a notebook the main points of every move; she also drew each move in the notebook and 'practised' it
in her head again and again, so that when her foot healed she could practise them one by one. At her
first session after recovering she dived only from the three-metre board, but she wasn't in the least
impatient.

In this championship she was fifth after the first four rounds, five points behind third place before
the last dive. Before the competition, her coach said just one thing to her: 'Dive your own
dive; don't look at the scores.' She chose a very difficult dive and entered the water with almost no splash; the
commentator at the pool said excitedly, 'What a beautiful dive!' With that dive she overtook two
rivals and won her first medal at a national competition.

Asked what she'd like to say to children in training, Lu Hang thought for a moment and said: 'Being
eliminated isn't the same as failing. Take a different road, and it may be a new starting point.' Then she added with a smile: 'Of course, I
still want gold.'"
</details>

The exam's writing part has two tasks in about 45 minutes, as reported from the sample papers: a
practical text of at least 150 characters and an argued essay of at least 300. Spend about 15

### Task 2: an argued essay (at least 300 characters)

The task gives a topic or a short text and asks for your opinion. Plan in four parts (lesson 26):
thesis, two reasons with examples, a concession, a conclusion.

Try it: {比赛|bǐ sài}{的|de}{结果|jié guǒ}{和|hé}{过程|guò chéng}，{哪个|nǎ ge}{更|gèng}{重要|zhòng yào}？{请|qǐng}{谈谈|tán tan}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{看法|kàn fǎ}。 (In a competition, which matters more, the result or the
process? Give your view.)

Checklist when you've finished:

1. **[[Thesis]]** clear in the first paragraph? ({我|wǒ}{认为|rèn wéi}…; {在|zài}{我|wǒ}{看来|kàn lái}…)
2. **Two reasons**, each with an example ({首先|shǒu xiān}…{其次|qí cì}…; {一|yì}{方面|fāng miàn}…{另|lìng}{一|yì}{方面|fāng miàn}…)?
3. **A concession** ({当然|dāng rán}…; {即便|jí biàn}…{也|yě}…; {诚然|chéng rán} is fine in writing too)?
4. **A conclusion** that answers the question ({由此|yóu cǐ}{可见|kě jiàn}…; {总之|zǒng zhī}…)?
5. **Connectors** varied but not crowded: three or four is plenty.
6. **[[Register]]** written throughout: no {吧|ba}, {啊|a}, {嘛|ma}; idioms only where they fit (one or two).
7. **Length** counted: at least 300 characters; leave time to check characters you often get wrong.

"**Result or process: which matters more?** In a competition people tend to remember only the
champion; few care about the runner-up and third place, let alone the competitors knocked out in the
first round. Seen like that, the result seems to matter most. But in my view the process deserves
more attention. First, there's only one result, but everyone can gain from the process. An athlete
often trains for years for one competition. Even without a medal in the end, the skills learned and
habits formed in training will benefit them for life. Second, effort in the process is what a person
can really control. We can't decide the weather on the day or the opponent's form, but how many times
we practise each day and whether we keep at it is entirely up to us. Of course, I'm not saying the
result doesn't matter. Without aiming at a result, training loses its direction and it's hard to stay
motivated. But if you look only at results, one failure is enough to discourage you or even make you
give up. In short, the result is a test of the process, and the process itself is growth. Rather than
staring at the medals, it's better to take every training session seriously. Then, whatever the
result, we won't have regrets."

```speak
{从|cóng}{那|nà}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{男|nán}{孩|hái}{每|měi}{个|gè}{周末|zhōu mò}{都|dōu}{来|lái}。{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}{有时|yǒu shí}{下|xià}{一|yì}{整个|zhěng gè}{下午|xià wǔ}，{谁|shéi}{也|yě}{不|bù}{说话|shuō huà}。{后来|hòu lái}{男|nán}{孩|hái}{去|qù}{外地|wài dì}{上|shàng}{了|le}{大学|dà xué}，{还|hái}{常常|cháng cháng}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{跟|gēn}{吕大爷|Lǚ dà ye}{下棋|xià qí}。{吕大爷|Lǚ dà ye}{说|shuō}，{输|shū}{给|gěi}{这个|zhè ge}{孩子|hái zi}，{比|bǐ}{赢|yíng}{了|le}{别人|bié ren}{还|hái}{高兴|gāo xìng}。
= After that the boy came every weekend. Sometimes the two of them played a whole afternoon without a word. Later the boy went to university in another city, and still often played with Grandpa Lü online. Grandpa Lü says losing to this boy makes him happier than beating anyone else.
```

{不知道天高地厚|bù zhī dào tiān gāo dì hòu}: not to know how high the sky is (an idiom outside the course: to be naive and overconfident); {小家伙|xiǎo jiā huo}: little
one, young fellow.

<details>
<summary>A model retelling (about 160 characters)</summary>

{公园|gōng yuán}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{位|wèi}{七十|qī shí}{多|duō}{岁|suì}{的|de}{吕大爷|Lǚ dà ye}，{每|měi}{天|tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{树|shù}{下|xià}{等|děng}{人|rén}{下|xià}{象棋|xiàng qí}。{他|tā}{是|shì}{有名|yǒu míng}{的|de}{高手|gāo shǒu}，{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{输|shū}。{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{天|tiān}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{十|shí}{来|lái}{岁|suì}{的|de}{男|nán}{孩|hái}{要|yào}{跟|gēn}{他|tā}{下棋|xià qí}，{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{笑|xiào}{他|tā}，{没|méi}{想|xiǎng}{到|dào}{男|nán}{孩|hái}{第|dì}{一|yī}{局|jú}{就|jiù}{赢|yíng}{了|le}。{吕大爷|Lǚ dà ye}{不但|bú dàn}{没|méi}{生气|shēng qì}，{反而|fǎn ér}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}，{让|ràng}{他|tā}{再|zài}{来|lái}{一|yì}{局|jú}。{后来|hòu lái}，{男|nán}{孩|hái}{每|měi}{个|gè}{周末|zhōu mò}{都|dōu}{来|lái}，{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}{常常|cháng cháng}{一下|yí xià}{就是|jiù shì}{一|yí}{下午|xià wǔ}。{男|nán}{孩|hái}{上|shàng}{大学|dà xué}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{他们|tā men}{还|hái}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{下棋|xià qí}。{吕大爷|Lǚ dà ye}{觉得|jué de}，{输|shū}{给|gěi}{这个|zhè ge}{孩子|hái zi}{比|bǐ}{赢|yíng}{别人|bié ren}{还|hái}{开心|kāi xīn}。

### Tell a story from four photos

You see four numbered photos (described here in words) and have a few minutes to prepare, then tell
the story in about two minutes. Give the people names, connect the photos with time words ({一|yì}{开始|kāi shǐ}, {后来|hòu lái},
{没|méi}{想|xiǎng}{到|dào}, {最后|zuì hòu}), and say what people feel, not just what they do.

1. A girl of about eight in skates holds on to the side of an ice rink, her legs wide apart; other
   children glide past.
2. She falls on the ice. Her father squats down beside her and points to his own feet, showing how to
   stand.
3. Weeks later: she glides across the rink alone, arms out, smiling.
4. At a children's competition she stands on the podium with a silver medal; her father claps in the
   crowd.

<summary>A model (about 220 characters)</summary>

{小|xiǎo}{雪|xuě}{今年|jīn nián}{八|bā}{岁|suì}，{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{去|qù}{学|xué}{滑冰|huá bīng}。{一|yì}{开始|kāi shǐ}，{她|tā}{只|zhǐ}{敢|gǎn}{扶|fú}{着|zhe}{场|chǎng}{边|biān}，{两|liǎng}{条|tiáo}{腿|tuǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{也|yě}{站|zhàn}{不|bu}{稳|wěn}，{看|kàn}{着|zhe}{别的|bié de}{小朋友|xiǎo péng you}{从|cóng}{身边|shēn biān}{滑|huá}{过去|guò qù}，{她|tā}{很|hěn}{着急|zháo jí}。{没|méi}{走|zǒu}{几|jǐ}{步|bù}，{她|tā}{就|jiù}{摔倒|shuāi dǎo}{在|zài}{冰|bīng}{上|shàng}，{差点儿|chà diǎnr}{哭|kū}{了|le}。{爸爸|bà ba}{蹲|dūn}{下来|xià lái}，{指|zhǐ}{着|zhe}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{脚|jiǎo}{告诉|gào su}{她|tā}："{别|bié}{怕|pà}，{脚|jiǎo}{这样|zhè yàng}{踩|cǎi}，{身体|shēn tǐ}{往|wǎng}{前|qián}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。"{小|xiǎo}{雪|xuě}{擦干|cā gān}{眼泪|yǎn lèi}，{又|yòu}{站|zhàn}{了|le}{起来|qǐ lái}。{后来|hòu lái}，{她|tā}{每|měi}{个|gè}{周末|zhōu mò}{都|dōu}{去|qù}{练习|liàn xí}，{摔倒|shuāi dǎo}{的|de}{次数|cì shù}{越|yuè}{来|lái}{越|yuè}{少|shǎo}。{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{她|tā}{已经|yǐ jīng}{能|néng}{张开|zhāng kāi}{双手|shuāng shǒu}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{人|rén}{在|zài}{冰|bīng}{上|shàng}{滑行|huá xíng}{了|le}。{最后|zuì hòu}，{在|zài}{一|yí}{次|cì}{少儿|shào ér}{滑冰|huá bīng}{比赛|bǐ sài}{中|zhōng}，{小|xiǎo}{雪|xuě}{获得|huò dé}{了|le}{亚军|yà jūn}。{她|tā}{站|zhàn}{在|zài}{领奖台|lǐng jiǎng tái}{上|shàng}，{看|kàn}{到|dào}{爸爸|bà ba}{在|zài}{下面|xià miàn}{使劲|shǐ jìn}{地|de}{为|wèi}{她|tā}{鼓掌|gǔ zhǎng}，{心里|xīn li}{别提多高兴了|bié tí duō gāo xìng le}。

{扶|fú} (fú): to hold on to; {摔倒|shuāi dǎo} (shuāi dǎo): to fall over; {别提多高兴了|bié tí duō gāo xìng le}: happier than words can say.

### Give your opinion

Two questions, each with a few minutes to prepare and about two and a half minutes to answer (as
reported). Thesis, two reasons, a concession or an example, a conclusion: the essay's shape, spoken.

## Say it

```speak
# Sport talk
{他|tā}{在|zài}{第|dì}{一|yī}{轮|lún}{就|jiù}{被|bèi}{淘汰|táo tài}{了|le}。
= He was knocked out in the first round.
{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{队|duì}{正在|zhèng zài}{争夺|zhēng duó}{冠军|guàn jūn}。
= The two teams are fighting for the championship.
{她|tā}{一口气|yì kǒu qì}{跑|pǎo}{完|wán}{了|le}{全程|quán chéng}。
= She ran the whole course without stopping.
```

## Pronunciation

- {夺|duó} duó, {夺取|duó qǔ} duó qǔ, {争夺|zhēng duó} zhēng duó: second tone. Don't confuse it with {多|duō} duō.
- {局|jú} jú (a game) and {句|jù} jù (a sentence): different tones; {俱乐部|jù lè bù} jù lè bù: {乐|lè} is lè here, not yuè.
- {中|zhòng} zhòng (to hit) is fourth tone: {射中|shè zhòng} shè zhòng, {打中|dǎ zhòng}; {中|zhōng} zhōng (middle) is first.
- {台球|tái qiú} tái qiú and {上台|shàng tái} shàng tái: tái, second tone.
- {使劲|shǐ jìn} shǐ jìn, {有劲|yǒu jìn} yǒu jìn: jìn, as in {劲|jìn} "strength"; not jìng.
- {车|jū} jū: in Chinese chess the chariot is read jū, a reading used only for this piece; everywhere else {车|chē} is chē.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{他|tā}{击败|jī bài}{了|le}~~ alone is incomplete: {击败|jī bài} needs an object ({击败|jī bài}{了|le}{对手|duì shǒu}). For "he lost", {他|tā}{输|shū}{了|le} (or written {他|tā}{败|bài}{了|le}).
- {玩|wán}{围棋|wéi qí} is heard from children, but the standard verb for board games is {下|xià}: {下|xià}{围棋|wéi qí}, {下|xià}{象棋|xiàng qí}. {打|dǎ} goes with ball games played with the hands or a bat ({打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}, {打|dǎ}{台球|tái qiú},
  {打|dǎ}{棒球|bàng qiú}), {踢|tī} with football, {下|xià} with board games.
- {得到|dé dào}{了|le}{一|yí}{块|kuài}{铜牌|tóng pái} isn't wrong, but medals are {拿|ná} (spoken) or {获得|huò dé} / {夺得|duó dé} (written): {拿|ná}{到|dào}{了|le}{一|yí}{块|kuài}{铜牌|tóng pái}, {夺得|duó dé}{铜牌|tóng pái}.
- ~~{他|tā}{很|hěn}{一口气|yì kǒu qì}{跑|pǎo}{了|le}{十|shí}{公里|gōng lǐ}~~: {一口气|yì kǒu qì} is an adverb by itself: {他|tā}{一口气|yì kǒu qì}{跑|pǎo}{了|le}{十|shí}{公里|gōng lǐ}.
- {好|hǎo}{你|nǐ}{个|gè} X and X {到|dào} Y {头|tóu}{上|shàng}{来|lái}{了|le} are for friends and family; in a meeting or an essay they'd sound rude.

## Key points

- Results: {选拔|xuǎn bá} / {入选|rù xuǎn}, {淘汰|táo tài}, {轮|lún} / {局|jú}, {排名|pái míng}, {夺|duó} / {夺取|duó qǔ} / {争夺|zhēng duó}, {击败|jī bài} / {战胜|zhàn shèng} / {败|bài}, {冠军|guàn jūn} / {亚军|yà jūn} / {季军|jì jūn}, {金牌|jīn pái} / {银牌|yín pái} /
  {铜牌|tóng pái} / {奖牌|jiǎng pái}, {团体|tuán tǐ}.
- Sports: {田径|tián jìng}, {体操|tǐ cāo}, {跳水|tiào shuǐ}, {射击|shè jī}, {滑冰|huá bīng}, {滑雪|huá xuě}, {棒球|bàng qiú}, {台球|tái qiú}, {围棋|wéi qí}, {象棋|xiàng qí} ({下棋|xià qí}).
- Bodies: {奔跑|bēn pǎo}, {踩|cǎi}, {蹲|dūn}, {扑|pū}, {抛|pāo}, {扭|niǔ}, {后退|hòu tuì}, {使劲|shǐ jìn}, {有劲|yǒu jìn}, {强壮|qiáng zhuàng}, {一口气|yì kǒu qì}.
- {好|hǎo}{你|nǐ}{个|gè} X (teasing surprise); X {到|dào} Y {头|tóu}{上|shàng}{来|lái}{了|le} (it's reached even Y): spoken only.
- Writing: a practical text (frame: title, reason, details, request, closing) and an argued essay
  (thesis, two reasons, concession, conclusion). Speaking: retell, four photos, two opinions.
- New characters: {奔|bēn} {踩|cǎi} {蹲|dūn} {夺|duó} {棍|gùn} {俱|jù} {酷|kù} {扭|niǔ} {抛|pāo} {棋|qí} {射|shè} {劲|jìn} {壮|zhuàng} {汰|tài} (✎ {奔|bēn} {夺|duó} {扭|niǔ} {抛|pāo} {劲|jìn} {壮|zhuàng} {汰|tài}).

lessons.title: The HSK 6 exam
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You now know the 5,400 words and 1,940 characters that the new HSK 6 covers, 700 of them to write
by hand, and the grammar of the level: the complex sentences ({要么|yào me}…{要么|yào me}, {除非|chú fēi}…{才|cái}, {凡是|fán shì}…{都|dōu}, {就算|jiù suàn}…{也|yě}, {与其|yǔ qí}…{不如|bù rú},
{虽|suī}…{却|què}, {以便|yǐ biàn}), the word-forming prefixes and suffixes, the written prepositions and the colloquial formats.
HSK 6 is the top of the intermediate band. This last lesson is about the exam: how it's built, what
each task asks, how to prepare in the last month, and what comes after.

It adds no new words or characters. It ends with a page of the 150 handwriting characters of this
course, and with a letter from {安娜|Ān nà} (Anna), who is taking the exam this winter.

## How the new HSK 6 is built

| Part | Questions | Time | Tasks, as reported |
|---|---|---|---|
| Listening | 40 (8 + 20 + 12) | about 30 minutes | choose the statement that matches what you hear; questions on dialogues and on longer talks, four choices each |
| Reading | 40 (10 + 10 + 20) | 40 minutes | a word for each gap in a passage (four choices); a sentence for each gap in a passage, from a list with one sentence left over; passages with four-choice questions |
| Writing | 2 | 45 minutes | a practical text of at least 150 characters; an argued essay of at least 300 characters giving your opinion |
| **Written exam** | **82** | **about 125 minutes**, with time to transfer answers and fill in your details | |
| Speaking | 5 | about 23 minutes, including about 10 minutes' preparation | retell a passage (2, about 1½ minutes each); tell a story from four numbered photos (1); give your opinion on two questions (2) |

The counts and times agree across the reports we found, which are based on the sample papers of
the new exam; treat the details of each task as a guide, and check the official site before you
register. The level-6 standard describes the listening as up to about 600 characters at 220 to 240
characters a minute, with the aim of grasping the speaker's real intent, and the reading as texts of
up to about 900 characters read at 180 characters a minute or more, analysing their structure and inferring what
isn't said.

### Listening

- **Matching statements** (the first part): you hear a short passage and choose the sentence that
  agrees with it. The wrong choices usually change one detail: a number, a time, who did it, or {一定|yí dìng}
  for {可能|kě néng}.
- **Dialogues**: the question is often about what one speaker **means**, not what they say: a
  suggestion behind a question ({你|nǐ}{不|bù}{觉得|jué de}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{贵|guì}{吗|ma}？ = don't buy it), a refusal behind politeness ({我|wǒ}{再|zài}
  {考虑|kǎo lǜ}{考虑|kǎo lǜ} = probably not), a feeling behind a format ({早|zǎo}{不|bù}{来|lái}{晚|wǎn}{不|bù}{来|lái} = annoyed at the timing).
- **Talks**: a few minutes of a lecture, an interview or a news report, with several questions.
  Listen for the structure ({首先|shǒu xiān}, {另外|lìng wài}, {总之|zǒng zhī}) and for the speaker's view ({我|wǒ}{认为|rèn wéi}, {在|zài}{我|wǒ}{看来|kàn lái}, {未必|wèi bì}).

### Reading

- **Words for gaps** (the first part): a passage with gaps and four choices for each. The four are
  usually near-synonyms or words of the same kind ({依旧|yī jiù} / {仍旧|réng jiù} / {依然|yī rán} / {仍然|réng rán}; {截至|jié zhì} / {截止|jié zhǐ}; {以便|yǐ biàn} / {以免|yǐ miǎn}).
  Decide by **[[collocation]]** (which words go together: {采取|cǎi qǔ}{措施|cuò shī}, {发挥|fā huī}{作用|zuò yòng}, {毫无|háo wú}{疑问|yí wèn}), by grammar ({毫不|háo bù} + verb, {毫无|háo wú} +
  noun), and by register (a notice takes {须|xū}, a chat {得|děi}).
- **[[Sentences for gaps]]** (the second part): a passage with five gaps and a list of six sentences; one
  is left over. Use **[[reference]]** (a sentence that starts {这|zhè} or {该|gāi} needs something before it to point
  to) and **connectors** (a sentence that starts {然而|rán ér} turns against what came before; one that starts {因此|yīn cǐ}
  draws a result). Check the leftover sentence: it should really fit nowhere.
- **Passages with questions** (the third part): longer texts, up to about 900 characters, with
  questions on the main idea, details, word meanings in context and the writer's attitude. Read the
  questions first, then the passage.

### Writing

- **A practical text** of at least 150 characters, such as a notice looking for a flatmate (lesson
  27). Follow the frame: title or greeting, reason, details in order, what you ask, closing.
- **An argued essay** of at least 300 characters giving your opinion on a topic (lessons 26 and 29).
  Thesis, two reasons with examples, a concession, a conclusion.

### Speaking

Registered with the written exam, as at levels 4 and 5 (reports differ on whether it's the same
session).

- **Retell two passages** you hear, about a minute and a half each, in your own words.
- **Tell a story from four numbered photos** (four in the level-6 sample paper as reported; three at levels 4 and 5), after a
  few minutes' preparation.
- **Give your opinion on two questions**, with preparation time for each.

## Scoring

The pass mark of the new HSK 6 hadn't been published when this course was written. (The old HSK 6,
of the 2.0 exam, was passed with 180 of 300 points.) Check the official site for the current rules,
and aim well above any pass mark: the level's words and grammar, not the cut-off, are what you'll
use afterwards.

## Strategies

### Before the exam

- Do at least one complete sample paper from the official site under exam conditions, with the
  times above.
- Make a list of the near-synonym sets you mix up (lesson 26's {未必|wèi bì} / {不|bù}{一定|yí dìng}, lesson 27's {截至|jié zhì} / {截止|jié zhǐ}, {以便|yǐ biàn}
  / {以免|yǐ miǎn}) and review one set a day.
- Write two practical texts and two essays by hand, and count the characters: you'll learn how much
  300 characters is on a grid.
- Practise speaking with a timer: retell a passage in ninety seconds, give an opinion in two and a
  half minutes.

### During the exam

- **Gap-fill by collocation and register**: say the phrase to yourself ({采取|cǎi qǔ}…{措施|cuò shī}? {发挥|fā huī}…{作用|zuò yòng}?); if the text is a
  notice, choose the written word.
- **Sentence insertion by reference and connectors**: look at the first word of each sentence ({这|zhè}, {该|gāi},
  {此外|cǐ wài}, {然而|rán ér}, {因此|yīn cǐ}, {不过|bú guò}) and at what the gap needs before and after.
- **Reading for the writer's attitude**: look at the evaluative words ({看似|kàn sì}, {未必|wèi bì}, {毫无|háo wú}{疑问|yí wèn}, {难免|nán miǎn}, {恰恰|qià qià}), at the
  concession ({当然|dāng rán}…), and at the last paragraph, where the view is usually stated.
- **Listening for the real intent**: when a speaker answers a question with a question, or uses {倒是|dào shi}, {还是|hái shi},
  {算了|suàn le} or {明明|míng míng}, the meaning is usually not the literal one.
- **Don't leave a blank**: an answer chosen by elimination can still be right.

> {您|nín}{的|de}{学生|xué sheng} {安娜|Ān nà}
> {十一|shí yī}{月|yuè}{八|bā}{日|rì}

1. Why did Anna hesitate to register, and what changed her mind?
2. What did Wang Fang say about Anna's essays, and what did Anna do about it?
3. How did Anna improve at the sentence-insertion task?
4. What is the tone of the letter's last paragraph?

{美术馆|měi shù guǎn}: an art museum; {议论文|yì lùn wén} (yì lùn wén): an argued essay; {凭感觉|píng gǎn jué} (píng gǎn jué): by feel; {正确率|zhèng què lǜ}: the rate of
correct answers; {婚礼|hūn lǐ} (hūn lǐ): a wedding.

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. She worried that with so much work she'd have no time to revise; David said that rather than wait
   until she "had time" she should start now, since nobody is ever fully ready ({与其|yǔ qí}{等到|děng dào}"{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}"，{不如|bù rú}{现在|xiàn zài}{就|jiù}{开始|kāi shǐ}).
2. Her content was good but she used too many spoken words: it read like a chat, not an argued essay.
   She practised the written register for several weeks ({因此|yīn cǐ}, {此外|cǐ wài}, {由此|yóu cǐ}{可见|kě jiàn}).
3. She stopped choosing by feel and looked first at the word each sentence begins with, then at what comes
   before and after the gap.
4. Warm and looking forward: she's glad they'll all be together with Teacher Wang again at the wedding,
   as in her class.

"Dear Teacher Wang, Hello! It's been a long time since I wrote. My work at the art museum is going well;
lately I've been preparing an exhibition on the gardens of Suzhou, and next month I'm going there on a
research trip. Some news: I've registered for the HSK 6 exam in December. To be honest, I hesitated a long
time before registering. With so much work, I was worried I'd have no time to revise. But David said that
rather than wait until I 'had time', I should start now, because the day when you're completely ready
never comes. I think he has a point. Oh, and David has decided to stay in Beijing: his company is doing
better and better, and he says Beijing is his second home now. These days I get up an hour early every
morning, do twenty minutes of listening, then write a paragraph. At weekends Wang Fang corrects my essays.
She says my content is good, but I use too many spoken words: it reads like a chat, not an argued essay. Only
then did I notice that the way I speak and the way I write are almost the same. For the last few weeks I've
practised written Chinese specially, and words like {因此|yīn cǐ}, {此外|cǐ wài} and {由此|yóu cǐ}{可见|kě jiàn} come much more naturally now. The
hardest thing is still the second reading part, putting sentences back into a text. At first I always chose
by feel and got lots wrong. Then I learned to look first at the word each sentence begins with, and then at
what comes before and after the gap, and my score went up a good deal. Wang Fang and Li Ming are getting
ready for their wedding next autumn, and they say you must come. Then the four of us will be with you again, just like in
your class. Wishing you good health and every success in your work! Your student, Anna. 8 November."
</details>

### E. Writing

1. **[[Practical text]]** (at least 150 characters): {你|nǐ}{的|de}{公司|gōng sī}{下|xià}{个|gè}{月|yuè}{要|yào}{组织|zǔ zhī}{员工|yuán gōng}{去|qù}{郊外|jiāo wài}{徒步|tú bù}。{请|qǐng}{写|xiě}{一|yí}{份|fèn}{通知|tōng zhī}，{说明|shuō míng}{时间|shí jiān}、
   {路线|lù xiàn}、{需要|xū yào}{带|dài}{的|de}{东西|dōng xi}{和|hé}{注意|zhù yì}{事项|shì xiàng}。 (Your company is organising a hike for staff next month. Write a notice giving the
   time, the route, what to bring and points to note.)
2. **Essay** (at least 300 characters): {有|yǒu}{人|rén}{说|shuō}："{工作|gōng zuò}{以后|yǐ hòu}{就|jiù}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}{学习|xué xí}{了|le}。"{你|nǐ}{同意|tóng yì}{吗|ma}？{请|qǐng}{谈谈|tán tan}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{看法|kàn fǎ}。 (Some say:
   "Once you're working there's no time to study." Do you agree? Give your view.)

Use lesson 27's frame for the first and lesson 26's four parts for the second; the checklist in lesson
29 applies to both.

### F. Speaking

Retell A3 in about a minute; then answer this in two minutes: {你|nǐ}{觉得|jué de}{年轻|nián qīng}{人|rén}{周末|zhōu mò}{应该|yīng gāi}{多|duō}{去|qù}{郊外|jiāo wài}，{还是|hái shi}{在|zài}{城市|chéng shì}{里|lǐ}{休息|xiū xi}？
{为什么|wèi shén me}？ (Should young people get out into the countryside at weekends, or rest in the city? Why?)

## What comes after HSK 6

HSK 6 is the last of the six levels, each with its own exam. Above it, levels 7, 8 and 9 (the
advanced band) are tested together in **one combined exam**, which reports a level from 7 to 9 by your
score, and which, as reported, adds **translation** to listening, reading, writing and speaking. The
advanced levels add several thousand more words and about 1,200 more characters (by the 2021 standard's count),
with far more written and literary Chinese, classical phrases and specialised vocabulary. The
honors lessons of this course (Lu Xun, the Laozi, Tao Yuanming) are a first taste of that.

Whatever you do next, keep reading: graded readers at their highest levels, then real books and
news, a little every day. The course's reading list has suggestions.

## A study plan for the last month

| Week | Focus |
|---|---|
| 1 | a full sample paper, timed; list your weak points; review lessons 26–27 (argument and register) |
| 2 | listening every day (talks and interviews); the near-synonym sets; two practical texts |
| 3 | reading: one long passage a day, timed; sentence insertion; two essays by hand |
| 4 | a second full sample paper; speaking with a timer; rest the day before |

## Can you do this?

- Follow a talk of a few minutes and say what the speaker really thinks.
- Read a commentary of 900 characters and give its thesis, its grounds and its concession.
- Choose between near-synonyms by collocation and register ({截至|jié zhì} / {截止|jié zhǐ}, {以便|yǐ biàn} / {以免|yǐ miǎn}, {毫不|háo bù} / {毫无|háo wú}).
- Write a notice, a request and a complaint of 150–200 characters, and an essay of 300–400.
- Retell a passage, tell a story from four photos and defend an opinion, out loud, in time.
- Use the level's idioms where they fit, and never with {很|hěn}.

## Common mistakes in the exam

- Spending too long on one gap: mark it and come back.
- Choosing a sentence for a gap because its topic matches, without checking its first word ({这|zhè}, {然而|rán ér}, {因此|yīn cǐ}).
- Writing a practical text with no frame (no greeting, no closing, no date), or an essay with no thesis.
- Writing the essay in spoken style ({吧|ba}, {啊|a}, {我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de} in every sentence), or crowding it with idioms.
- Retelling a passage word for word from memory and stopping when a sentence is forgotten: retell in your
  own words, and keep going.

## Key points

- The new HSK 6: listening 40, reading 40, writing 2: 82 questions in about 125 minutes; speaking 5
  tasks in about 23 minutes; pass mark not yet published (as reported).
- Reading: words for gaps (collocation, grammar, register), sentences for gaps (reference and
  connectors, one left over), passages (main idea, details, attitude).
- Writing: a practical text (frame) and an argued essay (thesis, reasons, concession, conclusion).
- Speaking: retell two passages, a four-photo story, two opinions.
- After HSK 6: levels 7–9 in one combined exam, with translation (as reported).

lessons.title: Laozi's sayings
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Three short sentences from the 《{道德经|Dào dé jīng}》 (*Dào dé jīng*, the *Daodejing* or *Tao Te Ching*) are among the
most quoted lines in Chinese: you'll find them on calligraphy scrolls, in school essays, in speeches
and on the walls of offices. This honors lesson reads each one in the original, word by word, with a
modern Chinese paraphrase and our own translation, and then looks at how they're used today. It's
history of ideas, not advice: what the lines meant, and what people make of them now.

The classical Chinese of the 《{道德经|Dào dé jīng}》 is very compressed: one character often does the work of a
modern two-character word ({善|shàn} for {善于|shàn yú} "to be good at", {知|zhī} for {了解|liǎo jiě} "to understand"), and particles like {之|zhī}, {者|zhě}
and {而|ér} carry the grammar. You know most of the characters already; what's new is how they combine.

## Laozi and his book

The 《{道德经|Dào dé jīng}》 is a short book of 81 brief chapters, about five thousand characters in all, in two parts:
the {道经|Dào jīng} (chapters 1–37) and the {德经|Dé jīng} (chapters 38–81). {道|dào} (dào, the Way) is its central idea: the way
the world works, which can't be fully named or explained; {德|dé} (dé) is the power or virtue that comes
from following it.

Tradition credits it to {老子|Lǎo zǐ} (Lǎo zǐ, "the Old Master"), said to have been an archivist at the Zhou court
in the 6th century BCE. Modern scholars are far less certain. Most see the book as a compilation put
together over a long time, as many early Chinese texts were, and some doubt that Laozi existed as one
historical person. The oldest copy found so far, on bamboo slips excavated at Guodian ({郭店|Guō diàn}) in 1993, is
dated to before about 300 BCE and is only part of the text we read today. So the honest answer to "who
wrote it, and when?" is: we don't know for sure.

What's certain is its influence. The 《{道德经|Dào dé jīng}》 is the founding text of the Daoist tradition, has been
read and argued over for more than two thousand years, and is one of the most translated books in the
world.

## {上|shàng}{善|shàn}{若|ruò}{水|shuǐ}

> {上|shàng}{善|shàn}{若|ruò}{水|shuǐ}。{水|shuǐ}{善|shàn}{利|lì}{万物|wàn wù}{而|ér}{不|bù}{争|zhēng}。
> (chapter 8)

### Words

| Word | Here | Modern Chinese |
|---|---|---|
| {上|shàng} | highest, supreme | {最|zuì}{高|gāo}{的|de} |
| {善|shàn} (first) | goodness, the good | {善|shàn}, {好|hǎo} |
| {若|ruò} | to be like | {像|xiàng}, {好像|hǎo xiàng} |
| {善|shàn} (second) | to be good at | {善于|shàn yú} |
| {利|lì} | to benefit | {有利|yǒu lì}{于|yú}, {帮助|bāng zhù} |
| {万物|wàn wù} | all things (lesson 17's word) | {万物|wàn wù} |
| {而|ér} | and yet | {却|què} |
| {不争|bù zhēng} | not to compete, not to contend | {不|bù}{争夺|zhēng duó}, {不|bù}{跟|gēn}{别人|bié ren}{争|zhēng} |

The first {善|shàn} is a noun (the good), the second a verb (to be good at): the same character doing two jobs
in one line, which classical Chinese does all the time. {不|bù} is bù here, before the first tone of {争|zhēng}.

### In modern Chinese

{最|zuì}{高|gāo}{的|de}{善|shàn}{就|jiù}{像|xiàng}{水|shuǐ}{一样|yí yàng}。{水|shuǐ}{善于|shàn yú}{帮助|bāng zhù}{万物|wàn wù}，{却|què}{不|bù}{跟|gēn}{万物|wàn wù}{争|zhēng}。

### Our translation

"The highest good is like water. Water is good at benefiting all things, and yet it does not contend."

The chapter goes on to say that water settles in the low places others dislike, and that this is
why it is close to the Way. The image is of a strength that works by giving way: water is soft, yet (as chapter 78 says)
nothing hard and strong can outdo it.

## {千|qiān}{里|lǐ}{之|zhī}{行|xíng}，{始|shǐ}{于|yú}{足|zú}{下|xià}

> {千里|qiān lǐ}{之|zhī}{行|xíng}，{始|shǐ}{于|yú}{足|zú}{下|xià}。
> (chapter 64)

### Words

| Word | Here | Modern Chinese |
|---|---|---|
| {千|qiān}{里|lǐ} | a thousand li (a long distance; a {里|lǐ} is half a kilometre today) | {很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}{的|de}{路|lù} |
| {之|zhī} | (the {的|de} of classical Chinese) | {的|de} |
| {行|xíng} | a journey | {路程|lù chéng}, {旅程|lǚ chéng} |
| {始|shǐ} | to begin | {开始|kāi shǐ} |
| {于|yú} | from, at (lesson 27's {于|yú}) | {从|cóng}, {在|zài} |
| {足|zú}{下|xià} | beneath one's feet | {脚下|jiǎo xià} |

{足|zú} is "foot" here, as in {足球|zú qiú}, and {足|zú}{下|xià} is "under the foot": where you're standing now. ({足|zú}{下|xià} was also a
polite way of saying "you" in old letters; that isn't its meaning here.)

### In modern Chinese

{走|zǒu}{一千|yì qiān}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{远|yuǎn}{路|lù}，{也|yě}{是|shì}{从|cóng}{脚下|jiǎo xià}{的|de}{第|dì}{一|yī}{步|bù}{开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de}。

### Our translation

"A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet."

English usually says "begins with a single step". The chapter leads up to the line with two other
images of great things growing from small ones: a tree too thick to put your arms round grows from a
tiny shoot, and a terrace nine storeys high rises from a heap of earth. The point is about how things
come about, and in context also about dealing with matters while they're still small.

## {知|zhī}{人|rén}{者|zhě}{智|zhì}，{自|zì}{知|zhī}{者|zhě}{明|míng}

> {知|zhī}{人|rén}{者|zhě}{智|zhì}，{自|zì}{知|zhī}{者|zhě}{明|míng}。
> (chapter 33)

### Words

| Word | Here | Modern Chinese |
|---|---|---|
| {知|zhī} | to know, understand | {了解|liǎo jiě} |
| {人|rén} | others | {别人|bié ren} |
| {者|zhě} | one who (HSK 4's suffix {者|zhě}) | …{的|de}{人|rén} |
| {智|zhì} | wise, clever | {有智慧|yǒu zhì huì}, {聪明|cōng ming} |
| {自|zì}{知|zhī} | to know oneself | {了解|liǎo jiě}{自己|zì jǐ} |
| {明|míng} | clear-sighted, enlightened | {明白|míng bai}, {清醒|qīng xǐng} |

The two halves are parallel, like a {成语|chéng yǔ}'s (lesson 28): {知|zhī}{人|rén} / {自|zì}{知|zhī}, {智|zhì} / {明|míng}. The pattern X {者|zhě} Y, "one who X is
Y", is everywhere in classical Chinese.

### In modern Chinese

{能|néng}{了解|liǎo jiě}{别人|bié ren}{的|de}{人|rén}{是|shì}{聪明|cōng ming}{的|de}，{能|néng}{了解|liǎo jiě}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{人才|rén cái}{是|shì}{真正|zhēn zhèng}{明白|míng bai}{的|de}。

### Our translation

"One who knows others is clever; one who knows oneself is clear-sighted."

The chapter continues in the same pattern: one who defeats others has strength, one who overcomes
oneself is truly strong. In each pair, the second half turns inwards and is held up as the higher
thing.

## Reading: old words, new places

A short essay in modern Chinese on how these lines live on.

> **{老子|Lǎo zǐ}{的话|de huà}，{今天|jīn tiān}{还|hái}{在|zài}{用|yòng}**
>

{流传|liú chuán} (liú chuán): to be handed down, spread; {书法|shū fǎ} (shū fǎ): calligraphy; {哲学|zhé xué} (zhé xué): philosophy; {项目|xiàng mù} (xiàng mù): a
project; {引用|yǐn yòng}: to quote; {学者|xué zhě} (xué zhě): a scholar.

1. Why, according to the essay, do people hang {上|shàng}{善|shàn}{若|ruò}{水|shuǐ} on their walls?
2. Who uses {千|qiān}{里|lǐ}{之|zhī}{行|xíng}，{始|shǐ}{于|yú}{足|zú}{下|xià}, and to say what?
3. What does the writer conclude from the order of {知|zhī}{人|rén} and {自|zì}{知|zhī}?
4. What is the writer's attitude to the 《{道德经|Dào dé jīng}》 in the last paragraph?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Not to study philosophy but because they like what they take it to mean: be like water, help others
   and don't compete with them; the writer adds that the original meaning goes deeper.
2. Teachers encouraging beginners, parents telling children not to fear difficulty, companies starting
   new projects: however long the road, it starts with the first step.
3. That Laozi thought knowing oneself harder and more important, since he put it second, in the
   place of the higher thing ({恰恰|qià qià}{说明|shuō míng}{他|tā}{认为|rèn wéi}{了解|liǎo jiě}{自己|zì jǐ}{更|gèng}{难|nán}，{也|yě}{更|gèng}{重要|zhòng yào}).
4. Balanced: we needn't agree with everything, and scholars still debate the meaning, but these lines last
   because their ideas aren't out of date.

"**Laozi's words, still in use today.** The *Daodejing* has only a little over five thousand
characters, yet it's one of the most widely handed-down ancient Chinese works. Many of its sentences,
after more than two thousand years, have become fixed expressions of everyday life; some people even
say they're 'like idioms'.

Walk into a Chinese home or office and you'll often see a piece of calligraphy on the wall with the four
large characters {上|shàng}{善|shàn}{若|ruò}{水|shuǐ}. The owner usually chose them not to study philosophy but because they like the
meaning: one should be like water, helpful to others without competing with them. Of course the original
meaning is deeper than that: water's 'not contending' touches on Laozi's view of the whole world. But that
one sentence can be understood this way by different people in different ages shows in itself how alive
it is.

'A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet' is probably the line used most. Teachers use it to
encourage beginners, parents to tell children not to fear difficulty, and companies like to quote it when
a new project starts. Its meaning is simple: however long the road, you start from the first step. Learners
of Chinese should know the feeling: thousands of characters, thousands of words, all began with one {你好|nǐ hǎo}.

'One who knows others is clever; one who knows oneself is clear-sighted' often appears in writing about
self-knowledge. Understanding others isn't easy; understanding yourself is harder. Many people can see
others' weaknesses but not their own problems. That Laozi puts 'knowing oneself' after 'knowing others' shows
precisely that he thought understanding oneself harder and more important.

Some people also use these lines in the wrong place. Some, for example, take 'not contending' to mean
that there's no need to make an effort at all, which misreads Laozi. In the *Daodejing*, water is soft,
yet nothing hard can outdo it. 'Not contending' isn't doing nothing: it's not comparing
yourself with others all the time, and putting your mind to doing your own work well.

Of course, reading the *Daodejing* today, we needn't agree with all its views, and scholars still debate
the meaning of many of its lines. The *Daodejing* is also one of the most translated books in the
world, and readers in every country understand it differently. But these few sentences have come down to us because what they say isn't out
of date: be modest, start things from small beginnings, and know yourself before you try to know the world."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# {老子|Lǎo zǐ}
{上|shàng}{善|shàn}{若|ruò}{水|shuǐ}。{水|shuǐ}{善|shàn}{利|lì}{万物|wàn wù}{而|ér}{不争|bù zhēng}。
= The highest good is like water. Water is good at benefiting all things, and yet it does not contend.
{千|qiān}{里|lǐ}{之|zhī}{行|xíng}，{始|shǐ}{于|yú}{足|zú}{下|xià}。
= A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet.
{知|zhī}{人|rén}{者|zhě}{智|zhì}，{自|zì}{知|zhī}{者|zhě}{明|míng}。
= One who knows others is clever; one who knows oneself is clear-sighted.
```

## Key points

- The 《{道德经|Dào dé jīng}》: 81 short chapters, about 5,000 characters, two parts ({道经|Dào jīng}, {德经|Dé jīng}); traditionally by {老子|Lǎo zǐ}, but
  its authorship and date are uncertain: probably a compilation; the oldest copy found (Guodian, 1993) dates
  from before about 300 BCE.
- {上|shàng}{善|shàn}{若|ruò}{水|shuǐ} (chapter 8): the highest good is like water: it benefits all things and doesn't contend.
- {千|qiān}{里|lǐ}{之|zhī}{行|xíng}，{始|shǐ}{于|yú}{足|zú}{下|xià} (chapter 64): a long journey begins where you stand.
- {知|zhī}{人|rén}{者|zhě}{智|zhì}，{自|zì}{知|zhī}{者|zhě}{明|míng} (chapter 33): knowing others is clever, knowing yourself is clear-sighted.
- Classical patterns: one character for a modern word ({善|shàn} = {善于|shàn yú}, {始|shǐ} = {开始|kāi shǐ}, {足|zú}{下|xià} = {脚下|jiǎo xià}), {之|zhī} for {的|de}, X {者|zhě} Y "one
  who X is Y", parallel halves.

lessons.title: The Peach Blossom Spring
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

《{桃花源记|Táo huā yuán jì}》 (*Táo huā yuán jì*, "The Peach Blossom Spring") is a short prose piece of about 320 characters by
the poet {陶渊明|Táo Yuān míng} (Táo Yuān míng, Tao Yuanming). It tells of a fisherman who follows a stream through a
forest of peach trees and finds a hidden village whose people have lived apart from the world for
centuries. Every Chinese schoolchild reads it, and it gave the language the idiom {世外桃源|shì wài táo yuán}: a peaceful
place cut off from the world.

This honors lesson reads its opening and the discovery of the village in the original, with notes, a
modern Chinese version and our own translation, then tells the rest of the story in our own Chinese.

## Tao Yuanming

{陶渊明|Táo Yuān míng} lived from about 365 to 427 (his birth year is uncertain), under the Eastern Jin dynasty ({东晋|Dōng Jìn})
and into the first years of the Song that followed it. He held minor official posts for some years,
then resigned and spent the rest of his life farming in the countryside, drinking with friends and
writing. His poems about fields, gardens and the quiet life ({田园诗|tián yuán shī}, poems of fields and gardens) made him
one of the best-loved poets in Chinese.

《{桃花源记|Táo huā yuán jì}》 was written late in his life (it's usually dated to about 421), as a preface ({记|jì}, an account) to
a poem on the same subject. The story is set in the {太元|Tài yuán} era (376–396) of the Jin.

## The fisherman finds the forest

> {晋|Jìn}{太元|Tài yuán}{中|zhōng}，{武陵|Wǔ líng}{人|rén}{捕|bǔ}{鱼|yú}{为|wéi}{业|yè}。{缘|yuán}{溪|xī}{行|xíng}，{忘|wàng}{路|lù}{之|zhī}{远近|yuǎn jìn}。{忽|hū}{逢|féng}{桃花|táo huā}{林|lín}，{夹|jiā}{岸|àn}{数|shù}{百|bǎi}{步|bù}，{中|zhōng}{无|wú}{杂|zá}{树|shù}，{芳草|fāng cǎo}{鲜美|xiān měi}，{落英|luò yīng}{缤纷|bīn fēn}。{渔人|yú rén}{甚|shèn}{异|yì}{之|zhī}。{复|fù}{前|qián}{行|xíng}，{欲|yù}{穷|qióng}{其|qí}{林|lín}。

### Words

| {武陵|Wǔ líng} | Wuling (a place name of the time) | {武陵|Wǔ líng} |
| {为业|wéi yè} wéi yè | as one's living ({为|wéi} wéi, "to be, act as") | {以|yǐ}…{为|wéi}{职业|zhí yè} |
| {缘|yuán} yuán | to follow, go along | {沿着|yán zhe} |
| {溪|xī} | a stream | {小|xiǎo}{河|hé} |
| {远近|yuǎn jìn} | far and near: how far | {远近|yuǎn jìn}, {多|duō}{远|yuǎn} |
| {忽逢|hū féng} | suddenly to come upon | {忽然|hū rán}{遇到|yù dào} |
| {夹|jiā}{岸|àn} | on both banks ({夹|jiā}, lesson 12: to hold between) | {两岸|liǎng àn} |
| {数|shù}{百|bǎi}{步|bù} shù bǎi bù | several hundred paces | {几|jǐ}{百|bǎi}{步|bù} |
| {杂树|zá shù} | other trees, mixed trees | {别的|bié de}{树|shù} |
| {芳草|fāng cǎo}{鲜美|xiān měi} | fragrant grass, fresh and lovely | {花|huā}{草|cǎo}{又|yòu}{香|xiāng}{又|yòu}{美|měi} |
| {落英|luò yīng}{缤纷|bīn fēn} | fallen petals everywhere | {落|luò}{下|xià}{的|de}{花瓣|huā bàn}{到处|dào chù}{都|dōu}{是|shì} |

### In modern Chinese

{晋朝|Jìn cháo}{太元|Tài yuán}{年|nián}{间|jiān}，{武陵|Wǔ líng}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{以|yǐ}{打鱼|dǎ yú}{为生|wéi shēng}{的|de}{人|rén}。{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{天|tiān}，{他|tā}{沿着|yán zhe}{小|xiǎo}{河|hé}{划|huá}{船|chuán}{往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}，{忘|wàng}{了|le}{走|zǒu}{了|le}{多|duō}{远|yuǎn}。{忽然|hū rán}，{他|tā}{遇到|yù dào}{一|yí}{片|piàn}{桃|táo}{花|huā}{林|lín}，
{河|hé}{的|de}{两岸|liǎng àn}{几|jǐ}{百|bǎi}{步|bù}{之|zhī}{内|nèi}，{除了|chú le}{桃|táo}{树|shù}{没有|méi yǒu}{别的|bié de}{树|shù}，{地|dì}{上|shàng}{的|de}{花|huā}{草|cǎo}{又|yòu}{香|xiāng}{又|yòu}{美|měi}，{落|luò}{下|xià}{的|de}{花瓣|huā bàn}{到处|dào chù}{都|dōu}{是|shì}。{渔人|yú rén}{觉得|jué de}{非常|fēi cháng}{奇怪|qí guài}，{又|yòu}{继续|jì xù}{往|wǎng}{前|qián}
{走|zǒu}，{想|xiǎng}{走|zǒu}{到|dào}{这|zhè}{片|piàn}{林子|lín zi}{的|de}{尽头|jìn tóu}。

### Our translation

"In the Taiyuan years of the Jin, a man of Wuling made his living by fishing. Following a stream, he
lost track of how far he had gone. Suddenly he came upon a forest of peach trees lining both banks
for several hundred paces, with no other trees among them; the fragrant grass was fresh and lovely,
and fallen petals lay thick everywhere. The fisherman thought it very strange, and went on, wanting
to see where the forest ended."

## The village

### Our translation

"Where the forest ended, at the stream's source, there was a hill, and in the hill a small opening
from which there seemed to come a light. He left his boat and went in through the opening. At first
it was very narrow, only just wide enough for one person. After a few dozen more paces it suddenly
opened out, wide and bright. The land was flat and open, the houses neat and orderly; there were
good fields and fine ponds, mulberry trees, bamboo and the like. Paths ran every way between the
fields, and cocks and dogs could be heard from farm to farm. Among them, people came and went,
sowing and working; the men's and women's clothes were just like those of people outside. The old
and the young alike were content and happy."

"The villagers, seeing the fisherman, were astonished and asked where he had come from. He answered
each question. They invited him into their homes, killed a chicken, set out wine and welcomed him
warmly. Hearing that a man from outside had come, everyone came to ask for news. They told him that
their ancestors, fleeing the wars of the Qin, had brought their families to this place, cut off from
the world, and had never gone out again, so they had lost touch with the world outside. They asked
what dynasty it was now: they had never heard of the Han, let alone the Wei and Jin that came after.
The fisherman told them everything he knew, and they all sighed at it.

The fisherman stayed some days. When he left, the villagers told him: 'What is here is not worth
telling people outside.' Once out, he found his boat and went back the way he had come, leaving marks
all along the route. Back in the prefecture town he went to see the prefect and told him the story.
The prefect at once sent men with him to look, but following the marks they lost their way and could
never find the path again.

Liu Ziji of Nanyang, a man of fine character, heard of it and happily planned to go and look for it,
but before he could set out he fell ill and died. After that no one ever asked the way to the Peach
Blossom Spring again."
